title: Compute Team Charter
heading: Mission
text:
# Compute Team Charter

**Team:** Compute (COMP), Platform Engineering
**Engineering manager:** Marcus Oyelaran
**Tech lead:** Lin Zhao

## Mission

Give every engineering team at TechSync a reliable, boring place to run and build software. When Compute is doing its job well, product teams rarely think about servers, clusters, or build machines.

title: Compute Team Charter
heading: What we own
text:
## What we own

| System | What it is |
|---|---|
| **Kestrel** | TechSync's internal Kubernetes platform, running on Amazon EKS in us-east-1, us-west-2, and eu-west-1 |
| **Forge** | The fleet of build runners that Gatekeeper CI uses to build and test code |

We also own the Kestrel node images, the cluster add-ons (autoscaling, DNS, admission controllers), and the Forge runner images.

title: Compute Team Charter
heading: What we don't own
text:
## What we don't own

- **Service mesh and ingress.** Meridian Mesh and EdgeGate belong to Networking.
- **Alerting and tracing.** Lookout and Tracewell belong to Observability.
- **Pipelines.** Gatekeeper CI and Scaffold belong to Developer Tooling. We run the machines; they run the pipeline logic.
- **Application code** running on Kestrel. That belongs to the teams who wrote it.

title: Compute Team Charter
heading: How to work with us
text:
## How to work with us

- **Requests:** the COMP project in Jira. We triage twice a week.
- **Questions:** #comp-help.
- **Urgent production problems:** page the COMP on-call through PagerDuty.

title: Compute Team Charter
heading: Goals for 2025
text:
## Goals for 2025

1. Finish moving all Kestrel node autoscaling to Karpenter.
2. Cut median Forge queue time in half.
3. Keep Kestrel within one minor version of the newest EKS release.
4. Publish runbooks for every Kestrel and Forge alert.

title: Compute Team Charter
heading: Team rituals
text:
## Team rituals

- Weekly planning on Mondays.
- Weekly patch sync on Wednesdays to review node-image updates.
- Monthly operational review covering incidents, alert noise, and capacity.

## Disaster recovery owners

Primary: Kestrel tech lead. Backup: senior SRE on the COMP rotation.

title: Kestrel Namespace Naming and Labeling Conventions
heading: Kestrel Namespace Naming and Labeling Conventions
text:
# Kestrel Namespace Naming and Labeling Conventions

Compute team standard. Written by Technical Writing with the Compute team.

Consistent names and labels let us route alerts, allocate cost, and find owners quickly during an incident. The Kestrel admission controller enforces the rules marked **required**.

title: Kestrel Namespace Naming and Labeling Conventions
heading: Namespace names
text:
## Namespace names

Format: `<team-code>-<system>` in lowercase, using hyphens.

| Good | Bad | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `pay-ledger-core` | `LedgerCore` | uppercase, no team code |
| `srch-quarry` | `search` | no system name |
| `mli-foundry` | `mli_foundry` | underscores aren't allowed |

Names are at most 40 characters. The environment isn't part of the name; dev, staging, and prod are separate clusters.

title: Kestrel Namespace Naming and Labeling Conventions
heading: Required labels
text:
## Required labels

Every namespace must carry:

- `techsync.io/team`: the team code, for example `WEB`.
- `techsync.io/org`: `PLAT`, `PROD`, or `DSEC`.
- `techsync.io/cost-center`: the finance cost center for the team.
- `techsync.io/oncall`: the PagerDuty service ID that should receive pages.

title: Kestrel Namespace Naming and Labeling Conventions
heading: Required labels on workloads
text:
## Required labels on workloads

Deployments and StatefulSets must carry:

- `app.kubernetes.io/name`
- `app.kubernetes.io/version`
- `techsync.io/team`

title: Kestrel Namespace Naming and Labeling Conventions
heading: Recommended labels
text:
## Recommended labels

- `techsync.io/data-region`: `us` or `eu`, for workloads handling EU customer data in eu-west-1.
- `techsync.io/experimental`: `true` for short-lived experiments.

title: Kestrel Namespace Naming and Labeling Conventions
heading: Renaming a namespace
text:
## Renaming a namespace

Kubernetes namespaces can't be renamed. Create the new namespace, migrate workloads, and ask COMP to delete the old one through a ticket.

## Questions

#comp-help

title: Kestrel Cluster Upgrade Runbook
heading: Overview
text:
# Kestrel Cluster Upgrade Runbook

**Owner:** Compute (COMP)
**Who runs this:** the COMP engineer assigned to the upgrade, with a second COMP engineer on watch

## Overview

We upgrade Kestrel clusters one EKS minor version at a time, always in the order dev, staging, prod. Each prod region is done separately. A full cycle usually takes three weeks.

title: Kestrel Cluster Upgrade Runbook
heading: Before you start
text:
## Before you start

- [ ] Read the EKS release notes for the target version and list deprecated Kubernetes APIs.
- [ ] Run `kestrel-apicheck` against every cluster to find workloads still using removed APIs. Open tickets for owning teams at least two weeks ahead.
- [ ] Confirm add-on versions (CoreDNS, VPC CNI, Karpenter, Meridian Mesh control plane) are compatible. Coordinate with NET for the mesh.
- [ ] Schedule the upgrade Tuesday to Thursday, during business hours.
- [ ] Post the plan in #platform-releases.

title: Kestrel Cluster Upgrade Runbook
heading: Procedure (per cluster)
text:
## Procedure (per cluster)

1. **Snapshot.** Take an etcd backup through the EKS console and record the cluster's current version.
2. **Control plane.** Run the Terraform change that bumps `cluster_version`. Wait for the EKS control-plane upgrade to finish (typically 20 to 40 minutes).
3. **Add-ons.** Apply the add-on version bumps.
4. **Node pools.** Update the Karpenter node class to the new node image. Karpenter replaces nodes gradually, respecting PodDisruptionBudgets.
5. **Watch.** Monitor the Kestrel control-plane dashboard and the cluster-wide error rate for one hour.
6. **Record.** Update the cluster version table on Confluence.

title: Kestrel Cluster Upgrade Runbook
heading: Rollback
text:
## Rollback

EKS control planes can't be downgraded. If something goes wrong after step 2, roll back add-ons and node images, and work the problem forward. This is why dev and staging go first.

## Common problems

- **Pods stuck terminating** during node replacement: usually a PDB that allows zero disruptions. Contact the owning team.
- **Webhook timeouts** after the control-plane upgrade: restart the admission controller pods.

title: Kestrel Control-Plane Alert Playbook
heading: KestrelAPIServerErrorRateHigh
text:
# Kestrel Control-Plane Alert Playbook

SRE runbook for the Compute rotation.

Each section below matches an alert name in Lookout. Start with **Impact**, then work down.

---

## KestrelAPIServerErrorRateHigh

**Impact:** deploys, autoscaling, and kubectl access may fail. Running pods usually keep serving traffic.

1. Open the Kestrel control-plane dashboard. Check whether errors are concentrated on one verb or resource.
2. Look for a client hammering the API server (`apiserver_request_total` by user agent). A runaway controller is the most common cause.
3. If one client is responsible, scale it to zero and contact the owning team.
4. If errors are broad, check the AWS Health Dashboard for EKS issues in the region.

title: Kestrel Control-Plane Alert Playbook
heading: KestrelEtcdDBSizeHigh
text:
## KestrelEtcdDBSizeHigh

**Impact:** writes to the cluster may start failing if the database hits its size limit.

1. Identify the largest object types. Large numbers of Events or Secrets are the usual suspects.
2. Check for a controller creating objects in a loop.
3. Open an AWS support case if compaction appears stuck.

title: Kestrel Control-Plane Alert Playbook
heading: KestrelSchedulerPendingPodsHigh
text:
## KestrelSchedulerPendingPodsHigh

**Impact:** new pods aren't starting. Scale-ups and deploys stall.

1. `kubectl get pods -A --field-selector=status.phase=Pending` and look at events.
2. Quota errors: point the team to the quota increase process.
3. "No nodes available": check Karpenter logs for provisioning failures, especially instance capacity errors.

title: Kestrel Control-Plane Alert Playbook
heading: KestrelNodeNotReady
text:
## KestrelNodeNotReady

**Impact:** pods on the node are rescheduled. Usually self-healing.

1. If one node: let Karpenter replace it; confirm within 15 minutes.
2. If many nodes in one AZ: suspect an AZ issue and check AWS Health.
3. If many nodes across AZs: suspect a bad node image. Pause the node-image rollout.

---

Escalate to the COMP tech lead if you're stuck for 30 minutes on anything customer-impacting.

title: Code Review Exception: Kestrel Node-Image Patch PRs
heading: Code Review Exception: Kestrel Node-Image Patch PRs
text:
# Code Review Exception: Kestrel Node-Image Patch PRs

**Status:** Approved
**Requested by:** Compute (COMP)
**Approved by:** Hannah Brecker (Engineering Manager, Developer Tooling, owner of the company code review policy) and Dana Whitfield (VP, Platform Engineering)
**Effective:** February 9, 2026
**Review date:** February 2027

title: Code Review Exception: Kestrel Node-Image Patch PRs
heading: Background
text:
## Background

Compute rebuilds the Kestrel node images every week to pick up OS and kernel security patches. An automated pipeline opens one pull request per week against the `kestrel-node-images` repository. Each PR bumps base-image digests and package versions. The diff is generated, the image is built and booted in dev and staging by Gatekeeper CI before the PR can merge, and the change is reviewed in aggregate during the weekly COMP patch sync.

Waiting for a second reviewer on these mechanical PRs has delayed security patches by up to four days in several weeks of 2025, mostly when the team is short-staffed during holidays.

title: Code Review Exception: Kestrel Node-Image Patch PRs
heading: Exception granted
text:
## Exception granted

Pull requests that meet **all** of the following conditions require **1 approval** from a COMP engineer before merge:

1. The PR is opened by the `kestrel-image-bot` service account.
2. The PR modifies only files under `images/node/` in the `kestrel-node-images` repository.
3. The PR changes only base-image digests, OS package pins, or kernel version pins.
4. The dev and staging boot checks in Gatekeeper CI passed.

title: Code Review Exception: Kestrel Node-Image Patch PRs
heading: What this exception does not cover
text:
## What this exception does not cover

- Any human-authored PR to `kestrel-node-images`, even if it touches only `images/node/`.
- Any change to the Kestrel control plane, scheduler, admission controllers, networking, or Terraform.
- Any other Compute-owned repository, including Forge.
- Any other team.

All of the above follow the standard company code review policy without modification.

title: Code Review Exception: Kestrel Node-Image Patch PRs
heading: Safeguards
text:
## Safeguards

- The bot PR template links the Gatekeeper CI test run and a package diff summary.
- COMP reviews all merged image PRs at the weekly patch sync and records it in the sync notes.
- If an image change causes a Sev1 or Sev2, this exception is suspended until Developer Tooling and the VP Platform Engineering re-review it.

title: Kestrel Workload Identity and Secrets Guide
heading: Why this exists
text:
# Kestrel Workload Identity and Secrets Guide

*Compute team, for anyone running services on Kestrel*

## Why this exists

Services on Kestrel constantly need credentials: a database password, an API token for a partner, a Kafka client cert for Streamline. We want every workload to get those from a short-lived source tied to its own identity, not from a long-lived secret pasted into a ConfigMap. This guide describes the supported path.

title: Kestrel Workload Identity and Secrets Guide
heading: Workload identity
text:
## Workload identity

Every pod on Kestrel runs with a Kubernetes service account. Kestrel maps each service account to a workload identity with the form:

```
kestrel://<cluster>/<namespace>/<service-account>
```

That identity is what other systems trust. Use one service account per service. Don't share a service account across deployments, and never use the `default` account in a namespace (the admission controller rejects it in staging and prod).

title: Kestrel Workload Identity and Secrets Guide
heading: Getting secrets into a pod
text:
## Getting secrets into a pod

1. Declare the secrets your service needs in the `secrets:` block of your Scaffold service manifest.
2. At deploy time, Gatekeeper CI wires up the Kestrel secrets sidecar for your pods.
3. On startup, the sidecar authenticates with the pod's workload identity, fetches the credentials from Vaultline, and writes them to an in-memory volume at `/var/run/secrets/app/`.
4. The sidecar refreshes credentials in the background before they expire. Your process should re-read the file on change (most of our Go and Python libraries do this already).

title: Kestrel Workload Identity and Secrets Guide
heading: Credential lifetime
text:
## Credential lifetime

Secrets issued to workloads can live up to 4 hours. The sidecar renews them well before that point, so a healthy pod never sees an expired credential. If your service caches a credential in memory, size the cache TTL comfortably under that ceiling and rely on the file watcher.

title: Kestrel Workload Identity and Secrets Guide
heading: Common mistakes
text:
## Common mistakes

- **Baking secrets into images.** Sentinel will flag this, and the build will fail.
- **Reading the secret once at boot and never again.** Long-running pods will eventually present an expired credential. Watch the file.
- **Using one identity for many services.** You lose the audit trail, and a compromise of one service exposes all of them.

title: Kestrel Workload Identity and Secrets Guide
heading: Debugging
text:
## Debugging

```
kubectl -n <namespace> logs <pod> -c kestrel-secrets
```

Look for `renewed` lines. Repeated `auth denied` usually means the service account isn't bound to a Vaultline role; ask in #comp-help.

## Related

- Kestrel Namespace Provisioning Runbook
- Vaultline documentation (owned by AppSec)

title: Postmortem: Kestrel CoreDNS Saturation (Sev2, Apr 2025)
heading: Postmortem: Kestrel CoreDNS Saturation (Sev2, Apr 2025)
text:
# Postmortem: Kestrel CoreDNS Saturation (Sev2, Apr 2025)

**Severity:** Sev2
**Duration:** 47 minutes
**Owning team:** Compute
**Author:** SRE, Compute rotation

title: Postmortem: Kestrel CoreDNS Saturation (Sev2, Apr 2025)
heading: Summary
text:
## Summary

On April 15, 2025, CoreDNS pods in the us-east-1 prod Kestrel cluster became saturated. Services saw intermittent DNS lookup failures, which surfaced as elevated `5xx` rates on several customer-facing APIs, including Ledger usage ingestion and parts of Console.

title: Postmortem: Kestrel CoreDNS Saturation (Sev2, Apr 2025)
heading: Customer impact
text:
## Customer impact

About 3% of API requests to affected services failed over 47 minutes. Some Ledger usage events were retried and delivered late but none were lost, because Meterflow buffers on Streamline.

## Timeline (PT)

- 10:12: Search deploys a new Sieve indexer version that opens a fresh connection per document.
- 10:19: CoreDNS CPU climbs; first Lookout alert on DNS latency.
- 10:24: Compute on-call joins #incident-room; Sev2 declared.
- 10:38: Sieve identified as the source of the query spike.
- 10:44: Search rolls Sieve back through Gatekeeper CI.
- 10:59: DNS latency back to normal; incident resolved.

title: Postmortem: Kestrel CoreDNS Saturation (Sev2, Apr 2025)
heading: Contributing factors
text:
## Contributing factors

1. CoreDNS replicas were fixed at 6 and didn't scale with query volume.
2. No per-namespace DNS query metrics existed, so finding the source took 14 minutes.
3. Sieve's HTTP client wasn't reusing connections.

title: Postmortem: Kestrel CoreDNS Saturation (Sev2, Apr 2025)
heading: What went well
text:
## What went well

- Search responded fast once identified.
- Meterflow's buffering prevented data loss.

## Action items

| Item | Owner | Ticket |
|---|---|---|
| Autoscale CoreDNS by query rate | COMP | COMP-4412 |
| Add NodeLocal DNSCache to all clusters | COMP | COMP-4413 |
| Per-namespace DNS query dashboard | OBS | OBS-2290 |
| Fix connection reuse in Sieve | SRCH | SRCH-1187 |

title: Service Capacity Runbook
heading: How services are hosted
text:
# Service Capacity Runbook

Core Engineering, Compute Infrastructure group

This runbook explains how a new production service gets machines. Read it before you schedule a launch date, because capacity takes time to arrive.

## How services are hosted

Every production service runs on its own pool of virtual machines in us-east-1. Pools are built from the standard Compute base image (Ubuntu with our config-management agent baked in) and sit behind an internal load balancer. Services do not share VMs with other services.

title: Service Capacity Runbook
heading: Minimum pool
text:
## Minimum pool

Each new service receives a **minimum pool of 3 VMs**, spread across three availability zones so one AZ outage can't take the service down. Small services almost never need more than the minimum at launch. Larger services can request a bigger starting pool.

title: Service Capacity Runbook
heading: Requesting capacity
text:
## Requesting capacity

1. Fill out a **Compute capacity request** in Jira (project: COMPUTE). Include the service name, expected requests per second, memory footprint per process, and your launch date.
2. Compute Infrastructure reviews requests every Tuesday and Thursday.
3. Once approved, we provision the pool, register it with the load balancer, and add it to the config-management inventory. Plan for **5 to 7 business days** from approval to usable machines.

If your launch is fixed and the request is late, talk to the Compute Infrastructure on-call. We can sometimes pull VMs from the shared spare pool, but no promises.

title: Service Capacity Runbook
heading: Instance sizes
text:
## Instance sizes

| Size | vCPU | Memory | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|
| small | 2 | 4 GB | internal tools, cron-style workers |
| medium | 4 | 16 GB | most API services |
| large | 8 | 32 GB | Ship build coordinators, data-heavy services |

title: Service Capacity Runbook
heading: Growing a pool
text:
## Growing a pool

Add VMs through another capacity request. Mention current CPU and memory usage from the monitoring dashboards. Pools can't be shrunk below 3.

## Decommissioning

When a service is shut down, file a capacity release request so the VMs return to the spare pool. Unused pools get flagged in the quarterly capacity review.

## Contacts

Compute Infrastructure on-call (pager), or the #compute-infra channel.

title: Kestrel Namespace Provisioning Runbook
heading: Kestrel Namespace Provisioning Runbook
text:
# Kestrel Namespace Provisioning Runbook

**Owner:** Compute (COMP) · **Audience:** any team onboarding a new service or a new team to Kestrel · **On-call contact:** #comp-oncall

title: Kestrel Namespace Provisioning Runbook
heading: Purpose
text:
## Purpose

This runbook covers how a team gets a home on Kestrel, TechSync's internal Kubernetes platform on EKS. Every service at TechSync runs inside a Kestrel namespace. If you are standing up a brand-new team or launching your first service, this is where you start.

Compute owns this process end to end. Please don't create namespaces by hand with `kubectl` or by copying another team's Terraform; namespaces created outside this flow are missing quota, network policy, and cost tags, and they get cleaned up by the weekly reconciler.

title: Kestrel Namespace Provisioning Runbook
heading: Before you start
text:
## Before you start

You will need:

- A team code (for example `WEB`, `DATA`) and the engineering manager's approval on the request ticket.
- A cost-allocation tag. See the *Kestrel Namespace Naming and Labeling Conventions* doc for the required labels.
- At least one service scaffolded with Scaffold, or a plan to do so in the first sprint.

title: Kestrel Namespace Provisioning Runbook
heading: Step 1: File the request
text:
## Step 1: File the request

Open a Jira ticket in the **COMP** project using the *New Kestrel Namespace* template. Fill in:

| Field | Example |
|---|---|
| Team code | `SRCH` |
| Namespace name | `srch-quarry` |
| Environments | dev, staging, prod |
| Expected services | Quarry query API, Quarry workers |
| Owning manager | Engineering Manager, Search |

Tickets are triaged by the COMP on-call within two business days.

title: Kestrel Namespace Provisioning Runbook
heading: Step 2: What you get by default
text:
## Step 2: What you get by default

When the namespace is created, Compute applies the standard team baseline:

- **40 CPU cores** of request quota per new team namespace, in each environment.
- A matching memory quota, sized by the reconciler from the CPU quota.
- Default network policies (deny-all ingress, allow from Meridian Mesh sidecars and EdgeGate).
- Lookout alert routing to the team's PagerDuty service.
- Tracewell collector injection.

Most teams run comfortably inside the default for their first two or three quarters.

title: Kestrel Namespace Provisioning Runbook
heading: Step 3: Requesting more capacity
text:
## Step 3: Requesting more capacity

Quota increases go through a ticket to COMP. Use the *Kestrel Quota Increase* template in the COMP Jira project and include:

1. The namespace and environment.
2. The new CPU and memory totals you are asking for.
3. A link to a Lookout dashboard showing current utilization (we look for sustained usage above roughly 70% of quota).
4. Whether the need is permanent or tied to a launch or migration.

Please don't ask in Slack for a quota bump and don't edit the `ResourceQuota` object directly. Manual edits are reverted by the reconciler within the hour, and the ticket is how we keep capacity planning honest across all three orgs.

title: Kestrel Namespace Provisioning Runbook
heading: Step 4: Verify
text:
## Step 4: Verify

Once the ticket is resolved, confirm:

```
scaffold ns describe <namespace> --env prod
```

You should see the quota, network policies, and labels listed. Deploy your first service through Gatekeeper CI and confirm it schedules.

title: Kestrel Namespace Provisioning Runbook
heading: Troubleshooting
text:
## Troubleshooting

- **Pods stuck in `Pending` with "exceeded quota":** you've hit the namespace quota. File a quota increase ticket (Step 3).
- **Namespace missing labels:** re-run the request; the reconciler will repair labels but not cost tags.
- **Need a namespace for a short-lived experiment:** use the dev environment only and mark the ticket "experimental."

## Revision history

- 2026-06-18: Refreshed templates and the verification command for the current Scaffold CLI.
- 2025-09-03: Added memory-quota sizing note.

title: Forge Build Runner Fleet Overview
heading: Forge Build Runner Fleet Overview
text:
# Forge Build Runner Fleet Overview

Compute (COMP), Forge tech lead

Forge is the pool of machines that runs build and test jobs for Gatekeeper CI. Developer Tooling owns the pipeline logic; Compute owns the runners: their images, capacity, and health.

title: Forge Build Runner Fleet Overview
heading: Runner pools
text:
## Runner pools

| Pool | Instance family | Architecture | Typical jobs |
|---|---|---|---|
| `forge-standard` | c7i | x86 | Most Go, Python, and TypeScript builds |
| `forge-large` | c7i.8xlarge | x86 | Monorepo builds, large integration suites |
| `forge-large-arm` | c8g | ARM (Graviton) | Multi-arch images |
| `forge-macos` | mac2 | ARM | TechSync Mobile iOS builds |
| `forge-gpu` | g6 | x86 + GPU | Foundry model tests |

All pools run in us-east-1. A smaller standby fleet in us-west-2 can be scaled up if needed.

title: Forge Build Runner Fleet Overview
heading: Scheduling
text:
## Scheduling

Gatekeeper CI submits each job with a pool label. Forge places it on an idle runner or queues it. Runners are ephemeral: one job per runner, then the runner is destroyed. This prevents state from leaking between jobs.

title: Forge Build Runner Fleet Overview
heading: Scaling
text:
## Scaling

Pools autoscale on queue depth. During business hours in the US we keep a warm buffer of idle runners in `forge-standard` to keep queue times low. Overnight, pools shrink to a small floor.

## Caching

- **Dependency cache:** shared S3-backed cache for Go modules, pip, npm, and Gradle.
- **Docker layer cache:** per-pool, on local NVMe of each runner, prewarmed from the latest base layers.

See the *Forge Build Cache Troubleshooting FAQ* for cache problems.

title: Forge Build Runner Fleet Overview
heading: Health metrics we watch
text:
## Health metrics we watch

- Median and p95 queue time per pool
- Runner boot time
- Job failure rate attributable to infrastructure (not test failures)

## Contacting us

#comp-forge for questions; page COMP on-call if all builds are failing.

title: Forge Build Cache Troubleshooting FAQ
heading: Forge Build Cache Troubleshooting FAQ
text:
# Forge Build Cache Troubleshooting FAQ

Compute, Forge

**My build is suddenly much slower than usual. Is the cache broken?**

Maybe. Look at the job log header for `cache: hit` or `cache: miss` lines. A full miss usually means one of three things: your lockfile changed (expected), the runner image was updated and base layers were rebuilt (expected for a day or two after a release), or the cache key includes something that changes every build, like a timestamp. Check your pipeline's `cache.key`.

**I'm getting checksum errors restoring Go modules.**

This is almost always a corrupted entry from an interrupted upload. Re-run the job with `FORGE_CACHE_BYPASS=1`; the next successful run will write a fresh entry. If it keeps happening, post the job URL in #comp-forge.

**Docker says "no space left on device".**

The runner's NVMe filled up. This happens with very large images or many intermediate layers. Use multi-stage builds, clean package caches in the same `RUN` step, or move the job to `forge-large`, which has bigger disks.

**Can I share a cache between two repositories?**

title: Forge Build Cache Troubleshooting FAQ
heading: Forge Build Cache Troubleshooting FAQ
text:
**I'm getting checksum errors restoring Go modules.**

**Docker says "no space left on device".**

**Can I share a cache between two repositories?**

Yes, if they use the same `cache.namespace` in the pipeline file. Only do this for repos owned by the same team; cache poisoning across teams is a real risk.

**How long are cache entries kept?**

Entries that aren't read for 14 days are evicted. Frequently used entries stay indefinitely.

**Can I clear the cache for my repo?**

Run `forge cache purge --repo <org/repo>`. It takes effect for the next job.

**Is the cache shared between regions?**

No. The standby us-west-2 runners have their own, colder cache.

**Who do I talk to?**

#comp-forge. Include the job URL, runner pool, and image version.

title: Kestrel GPU Node Pools: Architecture Notes
heading: Context
text:
# Kestrel GPU Node Pools: Architecture Notes

Author: Staff Engineer, Compute. Status: approved.

## Context

ML Infrastructure runs training and online inference for Foundry on Kestrel. Until early 2025 these workloads shared generic node pools with a handful of manually managed GPU nodes. As Foundry usage grew, we needed dedicated, autoscaled GPU capacity with clear isolation from general workloads.

title: Kestrel GPU Node Pools: Architecture Notes
heading: Design
text:
## Design

### Separate pools by workload shape

| Pool | Instances | Used for |
|---|---|---|
| `gpu-train` | p5 | Distributed training jobs |
| `gpu-infer` | g6 | Online inference behind FeatureHub-backed services |
| `gpu-batch` | g6, spot | Batch scoring, evaluation jobs |

title: Kestrel GPU Node Pools: Architecture Notes
heading: Isolation
text:
### Isolation

- GPU nodes carry a `nvidia.com/gpu` taint. Only pods that tolerate it and request GPUs land there.
- Each pool is restricted by node affinity to Foundry namespaces (`mli-*`).

title: Kestrel GPU Node Pools: Architecture Notes
heading: Autoscaling
text:
### Autoscaling

Karpenter provisions GPU nodes on demand. `gpu-train` scales to zero when idle because p5 capacity is expensive; `gpu-infer` keeps a minimum of two nodes per AZ so inference doesn't cold-start.

title: Kestrel GPU Node Pools: Architecture Notes
heading: Drivers and runtime
text:
### Drivers and runtime

The NVIDIA driver and container toolkit are baked into a dedicated GPU node image, rebuilt alongside the standard Kestrel node images.

## Capacity reservations

For `gpu-train`, MLI and Compute jointly maintain AWS capacity reservations in us-east-1. Reservations are reviewed quarterly against Foundry's training calendar.

title: Kestrel GPU Node Pools: Architecture Notes
heading: Open questions
text:
## Open questions

- Should `gpu-batch` move to eu-west-1 for models trained on EU data? Pending a decision from MLI.
- Multi-instance GPU partitioning for small inference models is being evaluated.

## Owners

Compute owns the pools and images. ML Infrastructure owns Foundry and decides how capacity is split among its workloads.

title: Kestrel Pod Disruption Budget Guidelines
heading: Why PDBs matter
text:
# Kestrel Pod Disruption Budget Guidelines

Compute team standard

## Why PDBs matter

Kestrel replaces nodes all the time: weekly node-image patches, Karpenter consolidation, cluster upgrades, spot interruptions. A PodDisruptionBudget (PDB) tells Kubernetes how many of your pods can be taken down voluntarily at once. Without one, a node drain can evict all your replicas together. With a badly written one, drains get stuck and block cluster maintenance for everyone.

title: Kestrel Pod Disruption Budget Guidelines
heading: Rules of thumb
text:
## Rules of thumb

1. **Every Deployment with 2 or more replicas needs a PDB.** Scaffold templates generate one.
2. **Use `maxUnavailable`, not `minAvailable`.** `maxUnavailable: 1` (or 25% for large services) keeps working as your replica count changes.
3. **Never set `maxUnavailable: 0`.** It blocks all voluntary evictions. Our admission controller rejects it in staging and prod.
4. **Single-replica services:** don't add a PDB. Accept the brief disruption, or run 2 replicas.
5. **Stateful services** (Kafka brokers in Streamline, OpenSearch nodes): use `maxUnavailable: 1` and make sure readiness probes reflect actual data health, not just process health.

title: Kestrel Pod Disruption Budget Guidelines
heading: Examples
text:
## Examples

```yaml
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata:
  name: quarry-api
spec:
  maxUnavailable: 25%
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app.kubernetes.io/name: quarry-api
```

title: Kestrel Pod Disruption Budget Guidelines
heading: What happens when a drain is blocked
text:
## What happens when a drain is blocked

Karpenter retries for up to 1 hour, then pages the COMP on-call. We'll contact the owning team. Repeated blocked drains are raised at the Platform monthly operational review.

## Checking your PDBs

```
kubectl get pdb -n <namespace>
```

`ALLOWED DISRUPTIONS` should be at least 1 during normal operation.

title: ADR: Adopt Karpenter for Kestrel Node Autoscaling
heading: ADR: Adopt Karpenter for Kestrel Node Autoscaling
text:
# ADR: Adopt Karpenter for Kestrel Node Autoscaling

**Status:** Accepted
**Date:** November 2024
**Deciders:** Compute engineering manager, Compute tech lead, two Compute staff engineers
**Consulted:** ML Infrastructure, Networking

title: ADR: Adopt Karpenter for Kestrel Node Autoscaling
heading: Context
text:
## Context

Kestrel uses the Kubernetes Cluster Autoscaler with fixed managed node groups: one per instance type per AZ, about 60 node groups across our clusters. Problems we've hit:

- Scale-up is slow (often 4 to 6 minutes) because node groups scale independently.
- Bin-packing is poor. We pay for a lot of idle capacity.
- Adding a new instance type means new node groups and Terraform changes.
- GPU and spot capacity are awkward to manage.

title: ADR: Adopt Karpenter for Kestrel Node Autoscaling
heading: Decision
text:
## Decision

Replace Cluster Autoscaler with **Karpenter** on all Kestrel clusters. Define capacity with a small number of NodePools (general, memory-heavy, GPU, spot) instead of per-instance node groups.

title: ADR: Adopt Karpenter for Kestrel Node Autoscaling
heading: Consequences
text:
## Consequences

**Positive**
- Faster scale-up, usually under 90 seconds.
- Karpenter chooses from many instance types, improving bin-packing and spot availability.
- Consolidation removes underused nodes automatically.

**Negative**
- Consolidation means more frequent voluntary pod evictions. Teams need correct PodDisruptionBudgets.
- A new component to operate and upgrade.

title: ADR: Adopt Karpenter for Kestrel Node Autoscaling
heading: Rollout
text:
## Rollout

1. dev clusters, December 2024
2. staging, January 2025
3. prod, one region at a time, Q1 2025

## Alternatives considered

- **Tuning Cluster Autoscaler.** Helps scale-up speed a little, doesn't fix bin-packing.
- **Fargate.** Doesn't support our sidecar and GPU needs.

title: VPC Peering and Transit Gateway Request Process
heading: VPC Peering and Transit Gateway Request Process
text:
# VPC Peering and Transit Gateway Request Process

Networking (NET)

Most services never need this: anything running on Kestrel already reaches other Kestrel services through Meridian Mesh. You need this process when a workload outside Kestrel (a managed AWS service, a data warehouse VPC, a vendor's PrivateLink endpoint) has to talk to something in another VPC.

title: VPC Peering and Transit Gateway Request Process
heading: Which option do I need?
text:
## Which option do I need?

| Situation | What we use |
|---|---|
| Two TechSync VPCs in the same region | Transit Gateway attachment |
| Two TechSync VPCs in different regions | Transit Gateway peering between regional TGWs |
| A vendor or SaaS endpoint | AWS PrivateLink |
| A one-off VPC peering connection | Not offered; use the Transit Gateway |

We stopped creating direct VPC peering connections in 2023. They don't scale and they're hard to audit.

title: VPC Peering and Transit Gateway Request Process
heading: How to request
text:
## How to request

1. Open a ticket in the NET Jira project using *Network Connectivity Request*.
2. Include source and destination VPC IDs, the CIDR ranges, the ports and protocols, and the business reason.
3. If either side handles EU customer data in eu-west-1, say so. Cross-region paths out of eu-west-1 need AppSec review.
4. NET reviews requests every Monday and Thursday.

title: VPC Peering and Transit Gateway Request Process
heading: What NET checks
text:
## What NET checks

- No overlapping CIDRs.
- The narrowest possible security group and route table rules.
- Routes are added in Terraform, never by hand in the AWS console.

## Turnaround

Same-region attachments: about 3 business days. Cross-region or PrivateLink: about 1 to 2 weeks, depending on the vendor.

## Removing connectivity

When a connection isn't needed anymore, file a ticket so we can remove the routes. We audit unused attachments every quarter.

title: Networking Team Charter

title: EdgeGate Release Guide
heading: EdgeGate Release Guide
text:
# EdgeGate Release Guide

Networking team runbook. Use this for every change to EdgeGate itself: gateway binaries, global configuration, plugins, and TLS settings. It doesn't cover individual route onboarding; see the *EdgeGate Route Onboarding Guide* for that.

title: EdgeGate Release Guide
heading: Release path
text:
## Release path

All EdgeGate changes go through Gatekeeper CI in this order:

1. **dev**: deploy automatically on merge to `main`.
2. **staging**: promote once dev checks pass.
3. **staging soak**: a **20-minute** soak in staging under replayed production traffic.
4. **prod canary**: one EdgeGate cell in us-east-1.
5. **prod**: remaining cells, then eu-west-1, then the us-west-2 standby cells.

title: EdgeGate Release Guide
heading: Staging soak
text:
## Staging soak

During the 20-minute soak we watch the EdgeGate staging dashboard in Lookout:

- `5xx` rate stays within 0.1 percentage points of the pre-deploy baseline.
- p99 latency stays within 10% of baseline.
- No new TLS handshake errors.
- Memory per gateway pod is flat (watch for slow leaks after plugin changes).

If any check fails, roll back staging and stop. Don't "push through" to prod to see whether it was noise.

title: EdgeGate Release Guide
heading: Who can release
text:
## Who can release

Any NET engineer who has shadowed two releases. The release author shouldn't also be the only person watching the canary; grab a second NET engineer or the NET on-call.

## Rollback

```
gatekeeper rollback edgegate --env prod --to <previous-release>
```

Rollback takes about four minutes across all cells. Announce it in #net-releases and #incident-room if customers were affected.

title: EdgeGate Release Guide
heading: Checklist
text:
## Checklist

- [ ] Change description and Jira ticket linked in the release
- [ ] Staging soak passed (20 min)
- [ ] Canary cell healthy for 10 minutes
- [ ] Release notes posted in #net-releases

## Contacts

NET on-call via PagerDuty, or #net-edgegate.

title: EdgeGate Rate Limiting Reference
heading: EdgeGate Rate Limiting Reference
text:
# EdgeGate Rate Limiting Reference

Networking, EdgeGate

EdgeGate enforces rate limits at the edge so a single noisy client can't degrade TechSync for everyone. This page explains the policy types and how to configure them for your routes.

title: EdgeGate Rate Limiting Reference
heading: Policy types
text:
## Policy types

| Type | Key | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| `per_api_key` | API key or token | Public APIs for Ship and Ledger |
| `per_ip` | Client IP | Unauthenticated endpoints such as login and signup |
| `per_org` | Customer org ID | Fair-share limits across a customer's users |
| `global` | Route | Protecting a fragile backend |

Limits use a token bucket: a sustained rate plus a burst size.

title: EdgeGate Rate Limiting Reference
heading: Configuring a route
text:
## Configuring a route

Rate limits live in the route's EdgeGate config in the owning team's repo:

```yaml
route: /v2/ledger/usage
rate_limits:
  - type: per_api_key
    rate: 200/s
    burst: 400
  - type: per_org
    rate: 1000/s
    burst: 2000
```

Changes go through Gatekeeper CI like any other config.

title: EdgeGate Rate Limiting Reference
heading: Tier-based defaults
text:
## Tier-based defaults

Customer plans (Free, Team, Enterprise) map to default limit profiles maintained by the Product teams. EdgeGate reads the customer's plan from the auth token, so you usually only set route-specific overrides.

title: EdgeGate Rate Limiting Reference
heading: What clients see
text:
## What clients see

Requests over the limit get HTTP `429` with `Retry-After` and `X-RateLimit-*` headers. Make sure your public API docs describe them.

## Monitoring

The `edgegate_ratelimit_rejections_total` metric is labeled by route and policy type. Sudden spikes usually mean a customer integration is retrying in a tight loop. Contact the account team before raising limits.

## Getting help

#net-edgegate.

title: EdgeGate Production Change Windows
heading: EdgeGate Production Change Windows
text:
# EdgeGate Production Change Windows

Networking team. Last reviewed May 2024.

EdgeGate is the front door for every customer request to TechSync Ship, Ledger, Insight, and Console. A bad change here is visible to every customer immediately, so we're deliberate about when production changes go out.

title: EdgeGate Production Change Windows
heading: When we ship to prod
text:
## When we ship to prod

**Preferred window:** Tuesday through Thursday, 9 AM to 3 PM PT. This is when the most NET engineers are online and the product teams are around to help verify.

**Allowed:** Monday and Friday during business hours, as long as you follow the company freeze rule below.

**Not allowed:**

- No production deploys after **4 PM PT on Friday**, through the weekend. This follows the company production deploy freeze.
- No production deploys on company holidays.
- No deploys during an active Sev1 or Sev2 incident unless the change is the fix.

title: EdgeGate Production Change Windows
heading: Emergency changes
text:
## Emergency changes

If an EdgeGate change is needed to fix or mitigate an active incident, it can go out at any time. The incident commander approves it in the incident channel, and the NET on-call ships it. Document it in the incident timeline.

title: EdgeGate Production Change Windows
heading: Large customer events
text:
## Large customer events

For planned high-traffic events (for example a large Enterprise customer's launch or end-of-quarter billing runs in Ledger), the NET engineering manager may declare an extra no-change window. These are posted in #net-announcements at least a week in advance.

title: EdgeGate Production Change Windows
heading: Before any prod change
text:
## Before any prod change

- Confirm the release passed staging.
- Make sure a second NET engineer is available to watch the rollout.
- Check #incident-room for anything ongoing.

## Questions

Ask in #net-edgegate or ping the NET engineering manager.

title: Meridian Mesh Configuration Reference
heading: Meridian Mesh Configuration Reference
text:
# Meridian Mesh Configuration Reference

Maintained by Networking (NET). Applies to every service that runs with a Meridian Mesh sidecar on Kestrel, in dev, staging, and prod.

This page lists the defaults the mesh applies when a service doesn't override them. NET owns these values. If you need something different for a route, override it in your service's `mesh.yaml` (see "Overrides" below) rather than asking us to change the global default.

title: Meridian Mesh Configuration Reference
heading: Traffic defaults
text:
## Traffic defaults

| Setting | Default | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Per-route request timeout | **15 s** | Applies to each HTTP and gRPC route. The timer starts when the sidecar sends the request upstream. |
| Retries | 2 | Only on connect failures, `503`, and gRPC `UNAVAILABLE`. Never on `POST` unless the route opts in. |
| Retry per-try timeout | 5 s | |
| Retry budget | 20% of active requests | Prevents retry storms during partial outages. |
| Connection idle timeout | 60 min | |
| Max concurrent requests per upstream host | 1,024 | |

title: Meridian Mesh Configuration Reference
heading: Security defaults
text:
## Security defaults

| Setting | Default |
|---|---|
| mTLS mode | STRICT in staging and prod, PERMISSIVE in dev |
| Peer authentication | Workload identity from Kestrel service accounts |
| Authorization policy | Deny by default between namespaces; allow within a namespace |

title: Meridian Mesh Configuration Reference
heading: Load balancing
text:
## Load balancing

- Algorithm: least-request.
- Locality-aware routing is on by default; traffic stays in the caller's availability zone while that zone is healthy.
- Outlier detection ejects a host after 5 consecutive `5xx` responses, for 30 s initially.

title: Meridian Mesh Configuration Reference
heading: Overrides
text:
## Overrides

Add a `mesh.yaml` next to your service manifest:

```yaml
routes:
  - match: /v1/reports/export
    timeout: 45s
    retries: 0
```

Overrides are reviewed by Gatekeeper CI policy checks. Timeouts above 120 s need a NET reviewer on the PR.

title: Meridian Mesh Configuration Reference
heading: Observability
text:
## Observability

Every sidecar exports request metrics to Lookout and spans to Tracewell. Look for the `meridian_route_timeouts_total` metric when debugging slow upstreams.

## Change log

- 2026-07-14: Clarified retry per-try timeout and outlier ejection settings.
- 2026-01-20: Raised max concurrent requests per host from 512 to 1,024.

Questions: #net-mesh.

title: EdgeGate Route Onboarding Guide
heading: Before you begin
text:
# EdgeGate Route Onboarding Guide

*Written by Technical Writing with the Networking team*

This guide walks you through exposing a new API route to customers or to TechSync Mobile through EdgeGate.

## Before you begin

- Your service is running on Kestrel and reachable through Meridian Mesh.
- You know the public path, for example `/v2/insight/queries`.
- You've decided how the route is authenticated.

title: EdgeGate Route Onboarding Guide
heading: Step 1: Add the route config
text:
## Step 1: Add the route config

In your service repo, create `edgegate/routes.yaml`:

```yaml
- path: /v2/insight/queries
  methods: [GET, POST]
  upstream: srch-quarry/quarry-api
  auth: customer_token
  rate_limits: default
```

title: EdgeGate Route Onboarding Guide
heading: Step 2: Choose authentication
text:
## Step 2: Choose authentication

| Option | When |
|---|---|
| `customer_token` | Customer API calls with a TechSync API token |
| `console_session` | Calls from the Console web app |
| `mobile_session` | Calls from TechSync Mobile |
| `none` | Public endpoints like health or status (rare; needs NET review) |

title: EdgeGate Route Onboarding Guide
heading: Step 3: Open a PR
text:
## Step 3: Open a PR

Gatekeeper CI validates the config: path conflicts, valid upstream, auth set. A NET engineer is auto-assigned as a reviewer for new routes.

## Step 4: Test in staging

Once merged, the route appears on the staging EdgeGate. Test with:

```
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $STAGING_TOKEN" https://api.staging.techsync.io/v2/insight/queries
```

title: EdgeGate Route Onboarding Guide
heading: Step 5: Promote
text:
## Step 5: Promote

Promotion to prod happens through the normal Gatekeeper CI flow.

## Step 6: Document

Update the public API reference for customer-facing routes, and add the route to your service's runbook.

## Help

#net-edgegate, or file a ticket in the NET Jira project.

title: ADR: Locality-Aware Load Balancing in Meridian Mesh
heading: ADR: Locality-Aware Load Balancing in Meridian Mesh
text:
# ADR: Locality-Aware Load Balancing in Meridian Mesh

**Status:** Accepted
**Date:** March 2025
**Deciders:** Networking tech lead, Networking engineering manager, Networking staff engineers
**Consulted:** Compute, Observability, Payments

title: ADR: Locality-Aware Load Balancing in Meridian Mesh
heading: Context
text:
## Context

Meridian Mesh distributes requests evenly across all healthy upstream pods regardless of availability zone. In us-east-1, roughly two-thirds of service-to-service calls cross AZ boundaries. That adds about 1 to 2 ms per hop and is a significant part of our AWS data transfer bill.

title: ADR: Locality-Aware Load Balancing in Meridian Mesh
heading: Decision
text:
## Decision

Enable locality-aware load balancing in the mesh by default:

- Requests go to upstream pods in the caller's AZ when that AZ has enough healthy endpoints.
- If healthy endpoints in the local AZ drop below 70% of normal, traffic spills over to other AZs proportionally.
- Services can opt out per route.

title: ADR: Locality-Aware Load Balancing in Meridian Mesh
heading: Consequences
text:
## Consequences

**Positive**
- Lower p50 latency for chatty call chains.
- Large reduction in cross-AZ data transfer cost.

**Negative**
- Uneven load if a service's pods are unevenly spread across AZs. Teams must use topology spread constraints (Scaffold templates now include them).
- Harder to reason about traffic during partial AZ failures.

title: ADR: Locality-Aware Load Balancing in Meridian Mesh
heading: Rollout
text:
## Rollout

Dev in April 2025, staging in May, prod clusters one at a time through June. Observability added per-AZ request panels to the standard dashboards.

## Alternatives considered

- **Do nothing.** Rejected because of cost.
- **Topology-aware routing in Kubernetes Services.** Doesn't apply to mesh-routed traffic.

title: Internal DNS Architecture Overview
heading: Zones
text:
# Internal DNS Architecture Overview

Networking. Author: Staff Engineer.

## Zones

| Zone | Used for | Hosted in |
|---|---|---|
| `techsync.io` | Public names (API, Console, status page) | Route 53 public hosted zone |
| `internal.techsync.io` | Internal tools and services outside Kestrel | Route 53 private hosted zones, per region |
| `svc.kestrel` | Services inside Kestrel clusters | CoreDNS in each cluster |

title: Internal DNS Architecture Overview
heading: Split-horizon names
text:
## Split-horizon names

Some names, like `console.techsync.io`, resolve differently inside and outside our network. Internally they point to private EdgeGate listeners so internal traffic doesn't hairpin through the public internet.

## Resolution path from a Kestrel pod

1. The pod queries the node-local DNS cache.
2. Cache miss: CoreDNS in the cluster.
3. Names under `svc.kestrel` are answered by CoreDNS.
4. Everything else is forwarded to the VPC resolver, which answers `internal.techsync.io` from the private hosted zones and public names from the internet.

title: Internal DNS Architecture Overview
heading: Cross-region
text:
## Cross-region

Private hosted zones are associated with VPCs in us-east-1, us-west-2, and eu-west-1. During a regional failover, records for failed-over services are updated by the traffic shift runbook.

title: Internal DNS Architecture Overview
heading: Making changes
text:
## Making changes

All zones are managed in Terraform in the `net-dns` repository. Changes need a NET reviewer. Never edit Route 53 records in the console; the next Terraform apply will overwrite them.

## Common pitfalls

- High TTLs on records that may change during failover. Keep failover-sensitive records at 60 seconds or less.
- Assuming `svc.kestrel` names work outside Kestrel. They don't.

title: Meridian Mesh mTLS Certificate Rotation Runbook
heading: Meridian Mesh mTLS Certificate Rotation Runbook
text:
# Meridian Mesh mTLS Certificate Rotation Runbook

Networking, SRE rotation

Meridian Mesh uses mTLS between every pair of services. Each sidecar gets a short-lived leaf certificate from the mesh certificate authority (CA). Leaf certificates renew automatically; nobody needs to do anything. This runbook is for rotating the **CA itself**, which is a planned operation, and for recovering if leaf issuance breaks.

title: Meridian Mesh mTLS Certificate Rotation Runbook
heading: Planned CA rotation
text:
## Planned CA rotation

The mesh uses an intermediate CA signed by the TechSync root CA (managed by AppSec). We rotate the intermediate on the schedule AppSec sets.

1. **Generate the new intermediate.** Request a signing ceremony with AppSec. The new intermediate is stored in Vaultline.
2. **Distribute trust.** Add the new intermediate to the mesh trust bundle alongside the current one. Roll this to every cluster and wait for all sidecars to pick up the new bundle (check `meridian_trust_bundle_version`).
3. **Switch issuance.** Point the mesh CA at the new intermediate. New leaf certificates are now signed by it.
4. **Wait.** Leave both intermediates trusted until every leaf certificate signed by the old one has expired.
5. **Remove the old intermediate** from the trust bundle.

Do each step in dev, then staging, then prod.

title: Meridian Mesh mTLS Certificate Rotation Runbook
heading: Leaf issuance failures
text:
## Leaf issuance failures

Symptoms: new pods fail readiness; sidecar logs show `certificate request failed`.

1. Check that the mesh CA pods are running in `net-mesh-system`.
2. Check the CA's connection to Vaultline. Auth failures here need AppSec.
3. Existing pods keep working until their leaf certificate expires, so act quickly.

## Escalation

NET tech lead and AppSec on-call.

title: EdgeGate WAF Rule Change Process
heading: EdgeGate WAF Rule Change Process
text:
# EdgeGate WAF Rule Change Process

Networking with AppSec. Author: Security Engineer.

EdgeGate's web application firewall (WAF) blocks malicious traffic before it reaches our services. WAF changes can easily block real customers, so we treat them with the same care as code.

title: EdgeGate WAF Rule Change Process
heading: Who can request a change
text:
## Who can request a change

- **AppSec**, for new threats or findings from Sentinel and penetration tests.
- **Any service team**, for false positives affecting their routes.
- **Support**, on behalf of customers, through a Jira ticket.

title: EdgeGate WAF Rule Change Process
heading: Process
text:
## Process

1. **Request.** File a ticket in the NET Jira project using *WAF Rule Change*. Include the route, the example request (redact customer data), and the desired behavior.
2. **Draft.** The NET engineer on WAF duty writes the rule in the `edgegate-waf` repository.
3. **Review.** Every rule change needs review from one NET engineer and one AppSec engineer.
4. **Count mode.** New blocking rules first run in **count mode** in prod for at least 24 hours. Count mode logs what would be blocked without blocking it.
5. **Analyze.** Check the count-mode hits in Tracewell. Make sure legitimate traffic isn't caught.
6. **Enforce.** Switch the rule to block mode through Gatekeeper CI.

title: EdgeGate WAF Rule Change Process
heading: Emergency rules
text:
## Emergency rules

During an active attack, the NET on-call can deploy a blocking rule directly to enforce mode with AppSec approval in the incident channel. The rule gets a normal review within one business day afterward.

## False positives

If customers report blocked requests, first check `edgegate_waf_blocks_total` by rule ID. Disabling a single rule is preferred over loosening the whole rule group.

## Records

All WAF changes are tracked in Jira and logged to Compass for audit evidence.

title: Meridian Mesh Sidecar Troubleshooting FAQ
heading: Meridian Mesh Sidecar Troubleshooting FAQ
text:
# Meridian Mesh Sidecar Troubleshooting FAQ

Networking, SRE

**My service returns 503s, but the upstream pods look healthy.**

Check whether the upstream's readiness probe is passing. The mesh only routes to ready pods. Also check outlier detection: if a pod returned a run of `5xx` errors, the mesh may have ejected it temporarily. Look at `meridian_outlier_ejections_total`.

**I see "upstream connect error or disconnect/reset before headers".**

The connection to the upstream failed before a response arrived. Common causes: the upstream process crashed, it isn't listening on the port in the Service definition, or it closed an idle keepalive connection the sidecar was reusing. If it's the last one, make sure your server's idle timeout is longer than the mesh's connection idle timeout.

**The sidecar wasn't injected into my pod.**

Check that the namespace has the `meridian.techsync.io/inject=enabled` label, and that your pod doesn't have the opt-out annotation. Then restart the pod; injection only happens at creation time.

**My pod takes a long time to become ready after the sidecar was added.**

title: Meridian Mesh Sidecar Troubleshooting FAQ
heading: Meridian Mesh Sidecar Troubleshooting FAQ
text:
# Meridian Mesh Sidecar Troubleshooting FAQ

Networking, SRE

**The sidecar wasn't injected into my pod.**

**My pod takes a long time to become ready after the sidecar was added.**

The sidecar needs to fetch its certificate and config before traffic flows. Set `holdApplicationUntilProxyStarts: true` (Scaffold templates already do).

**Jobs never finish because the sidecar keeps running.**

Use the `meridian-quit` helper at the end of your job, or use native sidecar containers on Kestrel.

**mTLS errors between two services.**

One side may be in a namespace without the mesh, or calling the pod IP directly instead of the Service name. Always call the Service name.

**Who can help?**

#net-mesh. Include namespace, pod name, and a sample request ID from Tracewell.

title: Postmortem: EdgeGate TLS Certificate Expiry (Sev1, Jul 2025)
heading: Postmortem: EdgeGate TLS Certificate Expiry (Sev1, Jul 2025)
text:
# Postmortem: EdgeGate TLS Certificate Expiry (Sev1, Jul 2025)

**Severity:** Sev1
**Duration:** 26 minutes
**Owning team:** Networking
**Author:** SRE, NET rotation

title: Postmortem: EdgeGate TLS Certificate Expiry (Sev1, Jul 2025)
heading: Summary
text:
## Summary

On July 10, 2025, the TLS certificate for the EdgeGate listener serving `api.eu.techsync.io` expired. Customers calling TechSync APIs through the EU endpoint got TLS errors until a renewed certificate was deployed.

title: Postmortem: EdgeGate TLS Certificate Expiry (Sev1, Jul 2025)
heading: Customer impact
text:
## Customer impact

All API traffic through the EU endpoint failed for 26 minutes. Ship deploys for EU customers stalled, and Ledger usage events from EU customers were rejected. Clients retried, and Meterflow accepted the backlog once service was restored.

title: Postmortem: EdgeGate TLS Certificate Expiry (Sev1, Jul 2025)
heading: Timeline (UTC)
text:
## Timeline (UTC)

- 08:00: Certificate for `api.eu.techsync.io` expires.
- 08:03: Lookout alert on EU EdgeGate `5xx` and TLS handshake failures.
- 08:06: Sev1 declared; NET on-call is incident commander.
- 08:14: Expired certificate identified.
- 08:21: Renewed certificate issued manually and deployed.
- 08:26: Error rates back to normal.

title: Postmortem: EdgeGate TLS Certificate Expiry (Sev1, Jul 2025)
heading: Root cause
text:
## Root cause

The EU listener's certificate had been issued manually in 2023, when eu-west-1 EdgeGate was first set up, and was never moved to the automated renewal system used everywhere else. No alert existed for certificate expiry on that listener.

title: Postmortem: EdgeGate TLS Certificate Expiry (Sev1, Jul 2025)
heading: Contributing factors
text:
## Contributing factors

- No inventory of which certificates were managed by automation.
- The expiry alert only covered certificates the automation knew about.

## What went well

- Detection in three minutes.
- Clear ownership; the right engineer was paged first.

title: Postmortem: EdgeGate TLS Certificate Expiry (Sev1, Jul 2025)
heading: Action items
text:
## Action items

| Item | Owner | Ticket |
|---|---|---|
| Move all EdgeGate certificates to automated issuance | NET | NET-3021 |
| Alert on any certificate under 21 days to expiry, from live scans | OBS | OBS-2411 |
| Certificate inventory dashboard | NET | NET-3022 |
| Status page update template for regional API outages | SRE guild | SRE-588 |

title: Cross-Region Traffic Shift Runbook (us-east-1 to us-west-2)
heading: Cross-Region Traffic Shift Runbook (us-east-1 to us-west-2)
text:
# Cross-Region Traffic Shift Runbook (us-east-1 to us-west-2)

Networking, SRE rotation

Use this runbook to move customer traffic from us-east-1 to us-west-2, either during a regional disaster recovery event or a planned exercise. The SRE guild decides when to shift. NET executes the network steps.

title: Cross-Region Traffic Shift Runbook (us-east-1 to us-west-2)
heading: Preconditions
text:
## Preconditions

- The SRE guild incident commander has called for the shift.
- Kestrel clusters in us-west-2 are up and the target services report healthy.
- EdgeGate cells in us-west-2 are scaled up (they run at reduced capacity normally).

title: Cross-Region Traffic Shift Runbook (us-east-1 to us-west-2)
heading: Steps
text:
## Steps

1. **Scale EdgeGate in us-west-2.** Set the cell autoscaler minimums to production levels and wait for pods to be ready.
2. **Lower DNS TTLs** if they aren't already at 60 seconds (they should be).
3. **Shift public traffic.** Update the Route 53 weighted records for `api.techsync.io` and `console.techsync.io` in steps: 10%, 50%, 100% to us-west-2. Watch error rates for at least five minutes at each step.
4. **Shift internal names.** Update `internal.techsync.io` records for failed-over internal tools.
5. **Mesh failover.** Confirm Meridian Mesh in us-west-2 has the full set of service endpoints.
6. **Verify.** Run the synthetic checks in Lookout for Ship, Ledger, Insight, and Console.
7. **Announce** in #incident-room and on the status page.

EU traffic through eu-west-1 is not affected by this runbook.

title: Cross-Region Traffic Shift Runbook (us-east-1 to us-west-2)
heading: Shifting back
text:
## Shifting back

Reverse the steps once us-east-1 is healthy and the CTO approves failback. Shift back gradually, the same way.

## Notes from past exercises

- Step 1 is the slowest; start it as soon as a shift looks likely.
- Some Enterprise customers allowlist our IPs. The us-west-2 EdgeGate IPs are published in the customer docs, but warn the support team anyway.

title: Lookout On-Call Standard
heading: Lookout On-Call Standard
text:
# Lookout On-Call Standard

**Team:** Observability (OBS)
**Owner:** Ingrid Solheim, Engineering Manager, Observability
**Applies to:** the OBS on-call rotation

title: Lookout On-Call Standard
heading: Why OBS has its own standard
text:
## Why OBS has its own standard

Lookout is the system that pages everyone else. If Lookout is degraded, other teams' alerts may be delayed or lost, and they won't know it. That makes a Lookout outage uniquely dangerous: an incident can be happening anywhere in the company with nobody being paged. We hold ourselves to a tighter response than a typical service.

This standard applies in addition to the company on-call policy. Everything in the company policy still applies to the OBS rotation; this page adds to it.

title: Lookout On-Call Standard
heading: Acknowledgment
text:
## Acknowledgment

- **Sev1 pages on Lookout must be acknowledged within 3 minutes.**
- If the primary hasn't acknowledged in 3 minutes, PagerDuty escalates to the secondary automatically.
- Tracewell pages follow the company on-call policy.

title: Lookout On-Call Standard
heading: Heartbeat monitoring
text:
## Heartbeat monitoring

Lookout sends a heartbeat to an external monitor every 60 seconds. If heartbeats stop, the external monitor pages the OBS primary and secondary directly through PagerDuty (not through Lookout). Treat a missed-heartbeat page as Sev1 until proven otherwise.

title: Lookout On-Call Standard
heading: During a Lookout incident
text:
## During a Lookout incident

1. Acknowledge and join #incident-room.
2. Post in #eng-announce that paging may be delayed, and ask other teams' on-calls to watch their dashboards manually.
3. Check the Lookout evaluation queue and PagerDuty integration health first; they are the most common failure points.
4. Once paging is restored, replay any alerts that fired during the gap.

title: Lookout On-Call Standard
heading: Handoffs
text:
## Handoffs

Handoff notes go in the #obs-oncall channel at the end of each shift, including any silenced alerts and open tickets.

## Readiness

New OBS engineers shadow one full rotation before joining as primary.
