title: Platform SLO Policy
heading: Which systems need SLOs
text:
# Platform SLO Policy

**Owner:** SRE, Platform Engineering
**Scope:** internal service level objectives for Platform systems

## Which systems need SLOs

Every system in the Platform Service Catalog must publish at least one SLO:

| System | Example SLIs |
|---|---|
| Kestrel | API server availability, pod scheduling latency |
| Forge | Job queue time |
| Meridian Mesh | Sidecar-added latency |
| EdgeGate | Availability, added latency |
| Lookout | Alert evaluation delay, notification delivery |
| Tracewell | Ingestion delay |
| Gatekeeper CI | Pipeline dispatch time, deploy success rate |

title: Platform SLO Policy
heading: Requirements
text:
## Requirements

1. SLOs are defined in Lookout using the SLO Definition Guide.
2. Each SLO has a burn-rate alert.
3. SLO targets are reviewed every six months by the owning team and the Platform staff engineers.
4. SLO dashboards are linked from the Platform Service Catalog.

title: Platform SLO Policy
heading: Error budget policy
text:
## Error budget policy

- When a Platform system exhausts its error budget for the 28-day window, the owning team prioritizes reliability work over new features until the budget recovers.
- The team's engineering manager decides which work pauses.
- Repeated budget exhaustion is raised at the Platform quarterly review.

title: Platform SLO Policy
heading: Customer-facing commitments
text:
## Customer-facing commitments

Customer contracts are managed by the CTO office and are out of scope here. Internal SLOs should be tighter than anything customers depend on.

## Reporting

A monthly SLO report covering every Platform system is posted in #platform.

title: Incident Commander Handbook
heading: What the IC does
text:
# Incident Commander Handbook

**Owner:** SRE guild
**Applies to:** anyone acting as incident commander (IC) at TechSync

## What the IC does

The incident commander coordinates the response. The IC doesn't usually fix the problem; they make sure the right people are working on it, decisions get made, and everyone knows what's happening.

title: Incident Commander Handbook
heading: Taking command
text:
## Taking command

1. Declare yourself: "I'm IC for this incident" in the incident channel.
2. Confirm the severity using the *Incident Severity Definitions*. Raise or lower it as you learn more.
3. Open a dedicated channel: `#inc-<date>-<short-name>`.
4. Start the incident doc from the template and assign a scribe.

title: Incident Commander Handbook
heading: Running the response
text:
## Running the response

- **Assign roles.** Operations lead (hands on keyboard), communications lead, scribe. For small incidents one person may hold several roles.
- **Set a rhythm.** Ask for status updates at regular intervals. Keep them short: what we know, what we're trying, what's next.
- **Make decisions.** If responders disagree on an approach, the IC decides. Rolling back is usually the right first move.
- **Pull in help.** Page other teams early. It's cheaper to release someone than to wait for them.
- **Protect responders.** Keep spectators out of the working channel. Answer leadership in a separate thread.

title: Incident Commander Handbook
heading: Communicating
text:
## Communicating

The communications lead posts updates to #incident-room and, for customer-impacting incidents, the status page, following the *Incident Communication Standard*.

## Handing off

For long incidents, hand off IC every four hours. Do it explicitly in the channel and summarize the current state.

title: Incident Commander Handbook
heading: Ending the incident
text:
## Ending the incident

1. Confirm impact has ended and metrics are normal.
2. Announce resolution in the channel and #incident-room.
3. Assign a postmortem owner for incidents that need one.

## Becoming an IC

Shadow two incidents, then lead one with an experienced IC as backup. The SRE guild runs IC training each quarter.

title: Code Review Guidelines for Authors and Reviewers
heading: Code Review Guidelines for Authors and Reviewers
text:
# Code Review Guidelines for Authors and Reviewers

**Owner:** Developer Tooling, with input from Staff Engineers across all orgs

Code review is how we share knowledge, catch mistakes, and keep our codebase healthy. These guidelines describe what good review looks like at TechSync. Approval requirements are covered in the separate Code Review Policy.

title: Code Review Guidelines for Authors and Reviewers
heading: For authors
text:
## For authors

- **Keep PRs small.** Under 400 lines of change is a good target. Split refactors from behavior changes.
- **Explain why.** The description should say what problem you're solving and how you tested it.
- **Review your own diff first.** Catch the debug prints and stray files before others do.
- **Link the ticket.** Reviewers should be able to find the context.
- **Respond to every comment,** even if just "done."

title: Code Review Guidelines for Authors and Reviewers
heading: For reviewers
text:
## For reviewers

- **Respond within one business day.** A first pass counts.
- **Review the design, not just the lines.** Does this belong here? Is there a simpler approach?
- **Be specific and kind.** Suggest a fix, not just a problem.
- **Mark nits as nits.** Use the `nit:` prefix for things that shouldn't block merging.
- **Check tests.** Are the important cases covered? Do the tests actually fail when the code is wrong?

title: Code Review Guidelines for Authors and Reviewers
heading: Things to look for
text:
## Things to look for

- Error handling and timeouts on network calls.
- Logging customer data (don't).
- Backwards compatibility for APIs, config, and database schemas.
- Missing alerts or dashboards for new functionality.

title: Code Review Guidelines for Authors and Reviewers
heading: Disagreements
text:
## Disagreements

Talk it out on a call if a thread goes back and forth more than twice. If you still disagree, ask the tech lead of the code's owning team.

## Speed versus thoroughness

Both matter. Large or risky changes deserve a slow, careful review. Mechanical changes deserve a quick one.

title: Disaster Recovery Plan (2023)
heading: Disaster Recovery Plan (2023)
text:
# Disaster Recovery Plan (2023)

> **Deprecated.** This plan was deprecated on January 14, 2025, and is superseded by the current *Disaster Recovery Policy*, which tightens the Tier 0 and Tier 1 RTO. Kept for historical reference.

**Owner:** SRE guild
**Originally approved:** 2023

title: Disaster Recovery Plan (2023)
heading: Scope
text:
## Scope

Covers recovery of TechSync production services in the event that the primary region (us-east-1) is unavailable for an extended period.

## Recovery targets

| Service tier | RPO | RTO |
|---|---|---|
| Tier 0 and Tier 1 | 15 minutes | 8 hours |
| Tier 2 | 24 hours | 72 hours |
| Tier 3 | Best effort | Best effort |

title: Disaster Recovery Plan (2023)
heading: Failover region
text:
## Failover region

Production fails over to us-west-2. EU customer data remains in eu-west-1, which has its own regional recovery plan.

## Responsibilities

- SRE guild: coordinates the failover and owns this plan.
- Each service-owning team: maintains its own failover runbook and data replication.

title: Disaster Recovery Plan (2023)
heading: Declaring a disaster
text:
## Declaring a disaster

The SRE guild on-call lead declares a regional disaster after confirming with AWS that us-east-1 recovery isn't expected within the RTO window. The CTO is informed at declaration.

## Recovery order

1. Core platform (Kestrel, Meridian Mesh, EdgeGate)
2. Identity and secrets (Keystone, Vaultline)
3. Customer-facing products (Ship, Ledger, Insight, Console)
4. Internal tools

## Testing

An annual company-wide failover test, plus team-level tabletop exercises.

title: Postmortem Writing Guide and Template
heading: Principles
text:
# Postmortem Writing Guide and Template

*Technical Writing, with the SRE guild*

A good postmortem helps the whole company learn from an incident. This guide explains how to write one, and includes the template.

## Principles

- **Blameless.** Describe what people did and why it made sense to them at the time. Focus on the system that allowed the mistake.
- **Specific.** Times, numbers, links to graphs.
- **Honest about luck.** If something went well by accident, say so.
- **Action-oriented.** Every contributing factor should lead to an action item or an explicit decision not to act.

title: Postmortem Writing Guide and Template
heading: Template
text:
## Template

**Title:** Postmortem: <short description> (<Sev>, <Month Year>)

**Summary.** Two or three sentences: what broke, for how long, and the impact.

**Customer impact.** Who was affected and how. Numbers if possible.

**Timeline.** Times in one time zone, stated at the top. Include detection, escalation, key decisions, mitigation, and resolution.

**Contributing factors.** Usually several. Avoid "root cause" as a single thing; incidents rarely have one.

**What went well.**

**What didn't go well.**

**Where we got lucky.**

**Action items.** A table with item, owner (team), and Jira ticket.

title: Postmortem Writing Guide and Template
heading: Tips
text:
## Tips

- Start the timeline during the incident; the scribe's notes are your best source.
- Pull graphs before they age out of hot storage.
- Ask "why did that make sense?" not "why did you do that?"
- Get a reviewer from another team. Outsiders spot assumptions.

## Publishing

Publish in Confluence under the owning team's postmortem section and link it in #incident-room.

title: Incident Communication Standard
heading: Internal updates
text:
# Incident Communication Standard

**Owner:** SRE guild, with Customer Support and Technical Program Management
**Applies to:** all Sev1 and Sev2 incidents, and any incident with customer impact

## Internal updates

Post updates in #incident-room:

| Severity | Update interval |
|---|---|
| Sev1 | Every 30 minutes, or sooner when something changes |
| Sev2 | Every 60 minutes |
| Sev3 / Sev4 | At start and resolution |

Each update follows the format:

> **Status:** investigating / identified / mitigating / monitoring / resolved
> **Impact:** who is affected and how
> **Next update:** time

title: Incident Communication Standard
heading: Customer-facing updates
text:
## Customer-facing updates

For incidents affecting customers, the communications lead posts to the status page:

1. **First post** within 15 minutes of declaring a customer-impacting Sev1 or Sev2. It's fine to say "we're investigating."
2. **Updates** at the same interval as internal updates.
3. **Resolution post** when impact ends.

Name the affected products (Ship, Ledger, Insight, Console, Mobile) and regions. Don't speculate about causes in public posts.

title: Incident Communication Standard
heading: Enterprise customers
text:
## Enterprise customers

Customer Support notifies Enterprise account contacts directly for incidents affecting them, using the template in the Support handbook.

## Leadership

For Sev1 incidents, the IC or communications lead sends a brief summary to the CTO within 30 minutes of declaration, then at each major change.

title: Incident Communication Standard
heading: After the incident
text:
## After the incident

A customer-facing incident summary is published for Sev1 incidents within one week, reviewed by the CTO office and Support.

## Templates

Status page and Enterprise email templates live in Confluence under *Incident Communication*.

title: Code Review Policy
heading: Required approvals
text:
# Code Review Policy

**Policy owner:** Developer Tooling
**Applies to:** all code merged into production repositories at TechSync

## Required approvals

The number of approvals required before merge depends on the tier of the service the code belongs to:

| Service tier | Required approvals |
|---|---|
| Tier 0 (core platform) | **2** |
| Tier 1 (customer-facing) | **2** |
| Tier 2 (internal) | **1** |
| Tier 3 (experimental) | **1** |

Approvals must come from engineers other than the author. At least one approver must be listed in the repository's CODEOWNERS for the files changed.

If a PR touches services of different tiers, the highest tier applies.

title: Code Review Policy
heading: Enforcement
text:
## Enforcement

GitHub Enterprise branch protection enforces the approval count on each repository's default branch. Developer Tooling syncs branch protection from the service catalog nightly, so the required count follows the service's tier automatically.

## Self-approval and bypass

- Authors cannot approve their own PRs.
- Admin bypass of branch protection is disabled on production repositories.
- Changes needed during an active Sev1 incident still require the normal approvals, but reviewers in the incident channel should prioritize them.

title: Code Review Policy
heading: Exceptions
text:
## Exceptions

Teams may request an exception for a narrowly defined class of changes. Exceptions must be approved by the Developer Tooling engineering manager and the VP of the requesting team's org, must name the exact repositories and change types covered, and must be recorded on Confluence.

## Related

- Code Review Guidelines for Authors and Reviewers

title: Disaster Recovery Policy
heading: Recovery targets
text:
# Disaster Recovery Policy

**Policy owner:** SRE guild
**Effective:** January 14, 2025
**Applies to:** all production services at TechSync

## Recovery targets

| Service tier | Recovery point objective (RPO) | Recovery time objective (RTO) |
|---|---|---|
| Tier 0 (core platform) | **15 minutes** | **4 hours** |
| Tier 1 (customer-facing) | **15 minutes** | **4 hours** |
| Tier 2 (internal) | 24 hours | 72 hours |
| Tier 3 (experimental) | Best effort | Best effort |

title: Disaster Recovery Policy
heading: Regions
text:
## Regions

- **Primary:** us-east-1
- **Disaster recovery:** us-west-2
- **EU customer data:** eu-west-1, recovered within the EU only

## Requirements for Tier 0 and Tier 1 services

1. **Replication.** State is replicated to us-west-2 continuously or at least every 15 minutes.
2. **Infrastructure as code.** All infrastructure can be recreated in us-west-2 from Terraform.
3. **Runbook.** A tested failover runbook exists and was exercised in the last 12 months.
4. **Dependencies.** Each service documents which Tier 0 services it needs to recover first.

title: Disaster Recovery Policy
heading: Roles
text:
## Roles

- **SRE guild** declares a regional disaster, coordinates the failover, and owns this policy.
- **Service-owning teams** execute their runbooks and confirm recovery.
- **CTO** is informed at declaration and approves failback.

## Testing

- An annual company-wide failover exercise, coordinated by the SRE guild.
- Team tabletop exercises at least twice a year.

Results are recorded in Compass as compliance evidence.

## Questions

#sre-guild

title: Incident Postmortem Policy
heading: When a postmortem is required
text:
# Incident Postmortem Policy

**Policy owner:** SRE guild
**Applies to:** all incidents at TechSync

## When a postmortem is required

A written postmortem is required for every **Sev1** and **Sev2** incident. Postmortems for Sev3 and Sev4 incidents are encouraged when there's something worth learning, but not required.

title: Incident Postmortem Policy
heading: Deadline
text:
## Deadline

Postmortems for Sev1 and Sev2 incidents are **due within 5 business days** of the incident being resolved. "Due" means the document is complete, reviewed by the owning team's engineering manager, and published on Confluence.

title: Incident Postmortem Policy
heading: Content
text:
## Content

Every postmortem includes:

- A summary and customer impact
- A timeline
- Contributing factors
- What went well and what didn't
- Action items, each with an owner and a Jira ticket

Use the company postmortem template.

title: Incident Postmortem Policy
heading: Ownership
text:
## Ownership

The team that owns the system where the incident started owns the postmortem. If several teams were involved, the incident commander names one owning team before the incident channel is closed. Other teams contribute sections for their parts of the timeline.

title: Incident Postmortem Policy
heading: Review
text:
## Review

Each org runs a regular incident review meeting where completed postmortems are presented. Postmortems with customer impact are also shared with Customer Support.

## Blamelessness

Postmortems describe what happened and why the system allowed it. They don't assign blame to individuals.

## Follow-through

The SRE guild tracks open action items from Sev1 and Sev2 postmortems and reports on them monthly to the CTO.

## Questions

#sre-guild

title: Disaster Recovery Game Day Program
heading: Purpose
text:
# Disaster Recovery Game Day Program

**Owner:** SRE guild, coordinated by Technical Program Management
**Applies to:** all teams owning Tier 0 and Tier 1 services

## Purpose

A disaster recovery plan that hasn't been tested isn't a plan. This program sets how TechSync exercises its regional recovery.

title: Disaster Recovery Game Day Program
heading: Exercise types
text:
## Exercise types

| Type | Frequency | Scope |
|---|---|---|
| Tabletop | Twice a year per team | Walk through the team's failover runbook as a discussion |
| Component failover | Once a year per team | Fail one service over to us-west-2 in a controlled window |
| Company failover | Once a year | Shift production traffic for all Tier 0 and Tier 1 services to us-west-2 |

title: Disaster Recovery Game Day Program
heading: Company failover exercise
text:
## Company failover exercise

- Scheduled by the SRE guild at least six weeks in advance.
- Announced to customers through the status page one week ahead.
- Runs during a low-traffic window, never during a freeze or holiday period.
- Uses the real failover runbooks, including the cross-region traffic shift.
- Has a go/no-go check with the CTO before the shift begins.

title: Disaster Recovery Game Day Program
heading: What we measure
text:
## What we measure

- Time taken for each step of the recovery order.
- Data replication lag at the moment of the shift.
- Every runbook step that was unclear or wrong.

## After each exercise

1. Debrief within one week.
2. Every gap becomes a Jira ticket with an owner.
3. Results are stored as compliance evidence in Compass.

## Readiness checklist for teams

- Failover runbook reviewed in the last six months.
- Terraform for us-west-2 applied successfully in the last six months.
- Named primary and backup DR owners.

title: Production Deploy Freeze Policy
heading: Policy
text:
# Production Deploy Freeze Policy

**Policy owner:** VP Platform Engineering
**Effective:** March 3, 2025
**Applies to:** all production deploys at TechSync, all orgs and teams

## Policy

TechSync freezes production deploys at these times:

1. **Fridays, beginning at 2 PM PT**, through the end of Sunday.
2. **Company holidays**, beginning at 2 PM PT on the last working day before the holiday, through the end of the holiday.

During a freeze, no changes may be deployed to production. Deploys to dev and staging are unaffected.

title: Production Deploy Freeze Policy
heading: Why
text:
## Why

Most of our serious incidents in 2024 began with a deploy late in the week, when fewer engineers were online to notice and respond. An earlier Friday cutoff gives teams time to watch their changes through the afternoon while the full team is still working.

title: Production Deploy Freeze Policy
heading: What counts as a production deploy
text:
## What counts as a production deploy

- Any Gatekeeper CI deploy to the prod environment.
- Production configuration changes, including feature flag changes that alter customer-visible behavior.
- Infrastructure changes to production through Terraform.

## Emergency changes

Changes needed to resolve or mitigate an active Sev1 or Sev2 incident may be deployed during a freeze. The incident commander approves the change in the incident channel, and the change is recorded in the incident timeline.

title: Production Deploy Freeze Policy
heading: Enforcement
text:
## Enforcement

Gatekeeper CI blocks production deploys during freeze windows. Incident commanders can unlock a single deploy using the emergency override, which is logged and reviewed weekly by Platform Engineering.

## Holiday calendar

The company holiday calendar is published by People Operations each December for the following year and is loaded into Gatekeeper CI automatically.

## Questions

#platform-releases

title: Incident Severity Definitions
heading: Incident Severity Definitions
text:
# Incident Severity Definitions

**Owner:** SRE guild
**Applies to:** all incidents at TechSync

Use these definitions to choose a severity when declaring an incident. When unsure between two levels, pick the higher one. You can lower it later.

title: Incident Severity Definitions
heading: Sev1: Critical
text:
## Sev1: Critical

A major customer-facing outage or a serious security or data event.

Examples:
- Ship, Ledger, Insight, or Console unavailable or failing for a large share of customers.
- Ledger producing incorrect invoices.
- Confirmed customer data exposure.
- A complete failure of paging (Lookout down).

title: Incident Severity Definitions
heading: Sev2: Major
text:
## Sev2: Major

Significant degradation, or an outage affecting a subset of customers or a key internal system.

Examples:
- A product unavailable in one region.
- Major features failing for many customers.
- Deploys blocked company-wide.
- Logs and traces delayed for all teams.

title: Incident Severity Definitions
heading: Sev3: Minor
text:
## Sev3: Minor

Limited impact with a workaround available.

Examples:
- One non-critical feature failing.
- Elevated errors for a small number of customers.
- An internal tool down for one team.

## Sev4: Low

Minimal impact. Often found before anyone notices.

Examples:
- A cosmetic bug in Console.
- A failed batch job that can be rerun.

title: Incident Severity Definitions
heading: Who declares
text:
## Who declares

Anyone can declare an incident. The on-call for the affected system becomes the initial incident commander unless someone else takes command.

## Changing severity

The IC can raise or lower severity at any time. Record the change and the reason in the incident channel.

title: On-Call Policy (v3)
heading: Rotations
text:
# On-Call Policy (v3)

**Policy owner:** SRE guild
**Effective:** August 12, 2025
**Applies to:** every engineer on an on-call rotation at TechSync

## Rotations

- Rotations are **1 week** long, handing off Monday at 10 AM local time of the primary.
- No engineer is primary on-call more than **1 week in every 4 weeks**. Teams that can't staff this should pair with another team or raise it with their engineering manager.
- Each rotation has a primary and a secondary.

title: On-Call Policy (v3)
heading: Acknowledgment
text:
## Acknowledgment

- **Sev1 pages on Tier 0 and Tier 1 services must be acknowledged within 5 minutes.**
- If the primary doesn't acknowledge in time, PagerDuty escalates to the secondary, then to the team's engineering manager.
- Lower-severity pages and pages on Tier 2 and Tier 3 services should be acknowledged within business-appropriate time and handled during working hours where possible.

title: On-Call Policy (v3)
heading: Expectations while on call
text:
## Expectations while on call

- Keep your laptop and a working network connection within reach.
- Join #incident-room for any Sev1 or Sev2.
- Hand off clearly at the end of your week: open incidents, silenced alerts, anything unusual.

title: On-Call Policy (v3)
heading: Compensation and recovery
text:
## Compensation and recovery

On-call engineers receive the on-call stipend set by People Operations. After a night with a Sev1 page, take the next morning off.

## What changed in version 3

Rotations are now one week instead of two, and Sev1 acknowledgment is faster than in version 2. Shorter rotations reduce fatigue; faster acknowledgment reflects our customer commitments.

## Questions

#sre-guild

title: Console Production Deploy Runbook
heading: Overview
text:
# Console Production Deploy Runbook

**Team:** WEB  **Audience:** engineers on the Console release rota

## Overview

Console is deployed to production by the `console-prod` Jenkins job. A deploy takes about twelve minutes end to end. Rollbacks are done with `jenkins-ctl`.

title: Console Production Deploy Runbook
heading: Before you deploy
text:
## Before you deploy

1. Confirm that the build you want has passed on the main branch and is green in staging.  
2. Check the on-call channel for any ongoing incident.  
3. Post in #prod-web that you are about to deploy.

title: Console Production Deploy Runbook
heading: Deploying
text:
## Deploying

1. Open Jenkins and find the job `console-prod`.  
2. Choose **Build with Parameters** and enter the release tag (for example `console-2025.06.3`).  
3. Leave `CANARY_PERCENT` at 10 unless the release notes say otherwise.  
4. Start the job and watch the console output. The job pauses after the canary stage.  
5. Check the error-rate and latency dashboards for five minutes. If they look normal, approve the pause to continue to full rollout.

title: Console Production Deploy Runbook
heading: Rolling back
text:
## Rolling back

If the canary or full rollout misbehaves:

```
jenkins-ctl rollback console-prod --to previous
```

Wait for the job to report success, then confirm the dashboards recover. Post the result in #prod-web.

title: Console Production Deploy Runbook
heading: After the deploy
text:
## After the deploy

- Update the release notes page with the deploy time and tag.  
- If you rolled back, open a ticket describing what happened.

## Troubleshooting

- **Job stuck at canary:** check that the canary pods are ready.  
- **`jenkins-ctl` cannot authenticate:** refresh your token from the Jenkins user page.

title: Console Session Lifetime Notes
heading: Session lifetime
text:
# Console Session Lifetime Notes

**Audience:** Web engineers, Support

This page explains how long a signed-in Console session lasts and what happens when it ends.

## Session lifetime

Console sessions last **up to 12 hours** from sign-in. After that, the user is returned to the sign-in page and must authenticate again.

title: Console Session Lifetime Notes
heading: Idle behavior
text:
## Idle behavior

A user who is inactive for 30 minutes sees a prompt to continue. If they do not respond within five minutes, the session ends sooner than the maximum.

## What the user sees

- During the last five minutes of a session, a banner offers to save work.
- Unsaved dashboard edits are stored as local drafts and offered again at the next sign-in.
- Long-running exports continue in the background after a session ends.

title: Console Session Lifetime Notes
heading: Implementation notes
text:
## Implementation notes

- The session cookie is `HttpOnly` and `Secure`.
- Session state is stored server-side; the browser holds only an opaque identifier.
- Sign-out ends the session immediately on all tabs in the same browser.

title: Console Session Lifetime Notes
heading: Common support questions
text:
## Common support questions

**"I was signed out in the middle of the day."** Check how long the session had been open and whether the user was idle.

**"Can I stay signed in longer?"** Console does not offer a longer session option.

## Contact

Questions go to #prod-web.

title: Prism Component Contribution Guide
heading: Before you propose
text:
# Prism Component Contribution Guide

Prism is TechSync's design system, and the Web team stewards it. Anyone at the company can propose a component. This guide explains how.

## Before you propose

Check the component library. Many needs are met by an existing component with different options. If you are not sure, ask in #prism.

title: Prism Component Contribution Guide
heading: Proposal
text:
## Proposal

1. Open a Jira ticket in the Prism project with a short description, a sketch or screenshot, and examples of where it would be used.
2. A Web Tech Lead or Staff Engineer will triage the ticket within a week.
3. If accepted, you and a Prism maintainer agree on an API (props, events, accessibility behavior).

title: Prism Component Contribution Guide
heading: Building
text:
## Building

- Write the component in TypeScript with React.
- Add stories showing every variant and state.
- Use design tokens, never hard-coded colors or spacing.
- Meet the Accessibility Standard for Product UIs: keyboard operable, labeled, correct contrast.

title: Prism Component Contribution Guide
heading: Review
text:
## Review

Two reviewers, including one Prism maintainer, must approve the pull request. Visual regression tests must pass.

## Release

Prism releases twice a month. Release notes list new components and any breaking changes.

## Getting help

Office hours with a maintainer are held Thursdays at 11:00 Pacific.

title: Prism Color Tokens and Theming Reference
heading: Why tokens
text:
# Prism Color Tokens and Theming Reference

## Why tokens

Design tokens give a name to each color so that themes can change without touching components. Components refer to tokens, never to raw values.

## Token families

| Family | Example | Used for |
|---|---|---|
| `color.bg` | `color.bg.surface` | Page and card backgrounds |
| `color.text` | `color.text.primary` | Body and heading text |
| `color.border` | `color.border.subtle` | Dividers and outlines |
| `color.accent` | `color.accent.default` | Buttons and links |
| `color.status` | `color.status.danger` | Success, warning, danger, info |

title: Prism Color Tokens and Theming Reference
heading: Themes
text:
## Themes

Prism ships a light theme and a dark theme. Each theme maps every token to a value. A component that uses only tokens works in both.

## Dark mode

- Do not invert colors automatically; use the dark values defined for each token.
- Check status colors on dark backgrounds, because yellows and reds often need adjusting.
- Images with transparent backgrounds should be checked in both themes.

title: Prism Color Tokens and Theming Reference
heading: Adding a token
text:
## Adding a token

Propose it in a Jira ticket with the intended use and values for both themes. New tokens must meet contrast requirements in both.

## Where tokens live

Tokens are defined in the `prism-tokens` package and compiled to CSS variables and a TypeScript map.

title: Console Feature Flag Conventions
heading: Console Feature Flag Conventions
text:
# Console Feature Flag Conventions

**Q: Why do we use feature flags?**
So we can ship code before a feature is ready for everyone, test with a small group, and turn something off without a new release.

**Q: How do I name a flag?**
Use lower kebab case with a team prefix and the feature: `web-new-dashboard-layout`. Avoid dates and the word "test."

**Q: What kinds of flags are there?**
- *Release flags* hide unfinished work and are short lived.
- *Experiment flags* split users between variants.
- *Ops flags* let us disable expensive behavior in an emergency and may live for a long time.

**Q: Who owns a flag?**
The engineer who creates it. Put your name and a cleanup date in the flag description.

**Q: When do I remove a flag?**
A release flag should be removed within two sprints of reaching everyone. A reminder is posted in #prod-web on the cleanup date.

**Q: Can flags depend on each other?**
Avoid it. If you must, document the dependency in both descriptions.

**Q: What should the default be?**
Off. Flags are enabled deliberately.

**Q: How do I test with a flag on?**
Use the flag override panel in staging, or set the flag for your own user.

title: Console Frontend Performance Budget
heading: Purpose
text:
# Console Frontend Performance Budget

## Purpose

A budget keeps Console fast as it grows. Each page has targets; a pull request that pushes a page over its budget needs a conversation before merging.

## Budgets

| Metric | Target |
|---|---|
| Initial JavaScript (gzipped) | 250 KB |
| Largest Contentful Paint (p75) | 2.5 s |
| Interaction to Next Paint (p75) | 200 ms |
| Cumulative Layout Shift (p75) | 0.1 |

Measured on a mid-range laptop on a typical broadband connection.

title: Console Frontend Performance Budget
heading: How it is enforced
text:
## How it is enforced

- The CI pipeline reports bundle sizes on every pull request.
- A bot comments when the initial bundle grows by more than 5 KB.
- Real-user measurements from production feed weekly dashboards.

## Common ways to stay within budget

1. Split code by route and load heavy components on demand.
2. Prefer lightweight libraries; check size before adding a dependency.
3. Avoid layout shifts by reserving space for images and tables.
4. Cache API responses where it is safe.

## Exceptions

If a feature genuinely needs more, the Tech Lead can approve a temporary increase. Record it in the pull request with a plan to recover the budget.

## Review

The budget is reviewed each November.

title: Postmortem: Console Dashboard Load Regression
heading: Postmortem: Console Dashboard Load Regression
text:
# Postmortem: Console Dashboard Load Regression

**Severity:** Sev3  **Date of incident:** 2026-05-12  **Authors:** Staff Engineer (WEB), with input from the on-call engineer

title: Postmortem: Console Dashboard Load Regression
heading: Summary
text:
## Summary

For about six hours, Console dashboards with many widgets took more than twenty seconds to load. No data was lost, and all views remained usable once loaded.

## Impact

Roughly 4% of dashboard views were affected. Support received nine tickets.

title: Postmortem: Console Dashboard Load Regression
heading: Timeline (Pacific)
text:
## Timeline (Pacific)

- **09:10** A release containing a change to widget loading went out.
- **11:40** Support reported slow dashboards.
- **12:05** The on-call engineer reproduced the problem with a dashboard of 40 widgets.
- **13:20** The cause was found: widget data was requested one at a time instead of in parallel.
- **15:05** A fix was released and load times returned to normal.

title: Postmortem: Console Dashboard Load Regression
heading: Root cause
text:
## Root cause

A refactor accidentally serialized widget requests. The existing test used a dashboard with three widgets, so it did not notice.

## What went well

Support's early report; a clear reproduction; a quick fix once the cause was known.

title: Postmortem: Console Dashboard Load Regression
heading: What went badly
text:
## What went badly

No alert existed for slow dashboard loads, and tests did not cover large dashboards.

## Action items

1. Add a performance test with a 40-widget dashboard (owner: Tech Lead).
2. Add an alert on the p75 dashboard load time (owner: SRE).
3. Review other places where requests are made in loops.

title: Prism Accessibility Testing Checklist
heading: Automated
text:
# Prism Accessibility Testing Checklist

Use this checklist when you add or change a Prism component. Automated checks catch some problems; the manual steps catch the rest.

## Automated

- [ ] The component passes axe checks in Storybook for every story.
- [ ] Unit tests cover keyboard interactions.
- [ ] Visual tests render correctly in light and dark themes.

title: Prism Accessibility Testing Checklist
heading: Keyboard
text:
## Keyboard

- [ ] Every interactive part can be reached with Tab and Shift+Tab, in a logical order.
- [ ] Enter and Space activate buttons; arrow keys move within composite widgets.
- [ ] Focus is never trapped, except in modals, which return focus when closed.
- [ ] A visible focus indicator appears on every focusable element.

title: Prism Accessibility Testing Checklist
heading: Screen reader
text:
## Screen reader

- [ ] The component's role, name and state are announced.
- [ ] Dynamic changes use live regions where needed.
- [ ] Decorative icons are hidden from assistive technology.

## Visual

- [ ] Text contrast is at least 4.5:1 (3:1 for large text).
- [ ] The component works at 200% zoom without losing content.
- [ ] Information is not conveyed by color alone.

## Record the result

Add a short note to the pull request describing what you tested and with which screen reader.

title: App-Store Submissions During the Production Freeze
heading: Summary
text:
# App-Store Submissions During the Production Freeze

**Status:** Approved, March 2025
**Approved by:** VP Dana Whitfield and VP Carlos Mendoza
**Owner:** Mobile (MOB)

## Summary

The Mobile team has an approved exception that lets it submit mobile applications to the app stores during the production deploy freeze. The exception is limited to store submissions.

title: App-Store Submissions During the Production Freeze
heading: Why
text:
## Why

Apple and Google review and release applications on their own schedules. Store release trains are fixed, and missing a train can delay a customer-facing fix by days. Submitting during the freeze does not change anything running in TechSync's production environment.

title: App-Store Submissions During the Production Freeze
heading: What the exception allows
text:
## What the exception allows

**App-store submissions may go out during the freeze.** That covers uploading a build to App Store Connect or Google Play Console, submitting it for review, and releasing it once it is approved.

title: App-Store Submissions During the Production Freeze
heading: What it does not allow
text:
## What it does not allow

All other Mobile deploys stay frozen, including deploys of Pushline. Backend services, configuration changes and Pushline releases wait until the freeze ends.

## How to use the exception

1. Tell #prod-mobile that you are submitting during the freeze.
2. Confirm in the release ticket that the change contains no backend or Pushline deploy.
3. Record the submission in the release log.

## Scope

This exception applies only to the Mobile team. No other team may rely on it.

## Review

The Engineering Manager reviews this exception each March and reports to both approving VPs.

title: Pushline Operations Runbook
heading: What Pushline does
text:
# Pushline Operations Runbook

**Owner:** Mobile (MOB)  **Audience:** on-call engineers and SREs supporting Pushline

## What Pushline does

Pushline accepts notification requests from TechSync services, queues them, and hands them to Apple Push Notification service (APNs) or Firebase Cloud Messaging (FCM) for delivery to phones.

title: Pushline Operations Runbook
heading: Delivery pipeline
text:
## Delivery pipeline

1. A service calls the Pushline API with a recipient, payload and priority.
2. Pushline validates the request and writes it to the delivery queue.
3. Workers pick up messages and send them to APNs or FCM.
4. Delivery receipts are recorded.

title: Pushline Operations Runbook
heading: Retry behavior
text:
## Retry behavior

When a delivery attempt fails with a retryable error, Pushline retries the delivery. **A failed delivery is retried at most 3 times; after the third failed retry the message is moved to the dead-letter queue.** Retries use exponential backoff starting at 5 seconds.

title: Pushline Operations Runbook
heading: Dead-letter queue
text:
## Dead-letter queue

- Messages in the dead-letter queue are kept for seven days.
- The queue size is graphed on the Pushline dashboard. Investigate if it grows quickly.
- To replay a message, use the replay tool with the message ID.

title: Pushline Operations Runbook
heading: Common alerts
text:
## Common alerts

| Alert | First action |
|---|---|
| Delivery success rate low | Check APNs/FCM status pages and recent Pushline releases |
| Queue depth high | Check worker health and scale workers |
| Dead-letter queue growing | Inspect recent messages for a shared error |

## Escalation

Page the Mobile on-call engineer through Lookout. For platform problems, escalate to Platform Compute.

title: Mobile Architecture Overview
heading: Goals
text:
# Mobile Architecture Overview

## Goals

Two native apps, one product. We want iOS and Android to feel native, share behavior where it helps and stay easy to test.

## Platform stacks

- **iOS:** Swift, SwiftUI, Combine.
- **Android:** Kotlin, Jetpack Compose, coroutines.

title: Mobile Architecture Overview
heading: Module layout
text:
## Module layout

Both apps use the same module boundaries:

| Module | Responsibility |
|---|---|
| `core` | Networking, authentication, storage |
| `alerts` | Alert list, detail and acknowledge flows |
| `approvals` | Deploy approval requests and decisions |
| `settings` | Preferences and quiet hours |
| `ui-kit` | Shared visual components |

title: Mobile Architecture Overview
heading: Shared contracts
text:
## Shared contracts

The team keeps a shared API schema, and both apps generate their network models from it. Analytics events are defined once in the Analytics Event Catalog.

## Data flow

Screens observe view models, which call use cases, which call repositories. Repositories decide between the network and local storage.

title: Mobile Architecture Overview
heading: Notifications
text:
## Notifications

The apps register for push notifications on first launch. Incoming notifications open the relevant alert or approval screen.

## Testing

Unit tests for view models and use cases; snapshot tests for key screens; a small suite of UI tests for core journeys.

## Decisions pending

Moving shared business rules into a common library is under discussion.

title: Deploy Approvals Feature: User Guide
heading: What are deploy approvals?
text:
# Deploy Approvals Feature: User Guide

## What are deploy approvals?

When a release is waiting for a person to say yes, TechSync can send the request to your phone. You review what is changing and approve or reject it.

title: Deploy Approvals Feature: User Guide
heading: Getting requests
text:
## Getting requests

1. Turn on notifications for TechSync Mobile when prompted.
2. In **Settings > Approvals**, choose which pipelines you want to hear about.
3. When a request arrives, tap the notification to open it.

title: Deploy Approvals Feature: User Guide
heading: Reviewing a request
text:
## Reviewing a request

The screen shows the service, the version, who started the release, the list of changes, and the checks that have passed. Tap **View details** to see the full change list.

## Approving or rejecting

- **Approve** continues the release to the next stage.
- **Reject** stops it and lets the author know. You can add a comment.

title: Deploy Approvals Feature: User Guide
heading: Frequently asked questions
text:
## Frequently asked questions

**Can someone else approve for me?**
Only people named as approvers for the pipeline can approve.

**What if I miss the notification?**
Open the app and look under **Approvals**. Pending requests stay there until they are decided.

**Is my decision recorded?**
Yes. Decisions appear in the same audit trail as decisions made in the web console.

**Can I undo an approval?**
No. If something is wrong, ask the author to stop the release.

title: Alert Preferences UX Spec
heading: Problem
text:
# Alert Preferences UX Spec

**Status:** Approved for implementation

## Problem

Users on call want fewer, better notifications. Today, preferences are a single list, which makes it hard to tell which settings matter.

## Goals

1. Let people choose alerts by severity.
2. Let them set quiet hours without turning everything off.
3. Make the effect of each setting obvious.

title: Alert Preferences UX Spec
heading: Screens
text:
## Screens

### Preferences home
A list of groups: Alerts, Approvals, Quiet hours. Each row shows its current summary (for example, "Sev1 and Sev2").

### Alerts
A control for each severity, Sev1 to Sev4, with three options: **Interrupt**, **Quiet**, **Off**. A preview line shows what each choice means ("Sound and banner" and so on).

title: Alert Preferences UX Spec
heading: Quiet hours
text:
### Quiet hours
Start time, end time and days. A toggle allows Sev1 alerts to break through.

### Approvals
Pipelines the user can approve, each with an on/off toggle.

## Behavior

- Changes save immediately and show a brief confirmation.
- Preferences sync across the user's devices.
- Defaults: Sev1 and Sev2 interrupt; Sev3 quiet; Sev4 off.

## Accessibility

All controls are labeled and operable with a screen reader. Option summaries are read aloud.

## Open questions

Do we need per-service overrides in the first release?

title: Mobile Crash Triage Runbook
heading: Where crashes come from
text:
# Mobile Crash Triage Runbook

**Owner:** Mobile SRE  **Audience:** on-call and release engineers

## Where crashes come from

Crash reports flow into the crash reporting dashboard from both apps. Each report has the app version, OS version, device model and a stack trace.

title: Mobile Crash Triage Runbook
heading: Daily triage
text:
## Daily triage

1. Open the dashboard and sort by affected users.
2. Look at new crash groups first, then those growing quickly.
3. Assign each significant group to an engineer in Jira.

## Severity mapping

| Crash profile | Severity |
|---|---|
| App cannot start for many users | Sev1 |
| Crash in a core flow (alerts, approvals) affecting many users | Sev2 |
| Crash in a secondary screen | Sev3 |
| Rare crash on an unusual device | Sev4 |

title: Mobile Crash Triage Runbook
heading: Investigating
text:
## Investigating

- Reproduce on a device or simulator matching the report.
- Check whether the crash began in a specific release.
- Look for correlations with OS version or device model.

## Fixing

Fix in the next release unless it is Sev1 or Sev2, in which case discuss an expedited release with the Tech Lead.

## Closing

Mark the crash group resolved with the release number. Confirm it does not recur after rollout.

title: Postmortem: Android Alert Delay under Doze
heading: Postmortem: Android Alert Delay under Doze
text:
# Postmortem: Android Alert Delay under Doze

**Severity:** Sev2  **Incident date:** 2026-04-21  **Published:** 2026-04-28  **Author:** SRE (MOB)

title: Postmortem: Android Alert Delay under Doze
heading: Summary
text:
## Summary

Some Android users received alerts up to 40 minutes late when their phones were idle. No alerts were lost. The delay affected roughly 6% of Android users that day.

## Timeline (Pacific)

- **08:15** Support noted a few reports of late alerts.
- **09:30** The on-call engineer compared send and receive times and saw delays only on Android.
- **10:50** The pattern pointed to devices in battery-saving Doze mode.
- **13:10** A change to message priority was prepared.
- **15:30** The change reached all users.

title: Postmortem: Android Alert Delay under Doze
heading: Root cause
text:
## Root cause

A release the previous week changed how the app requested high-priority delivery. Messages were sent with normal priority, which Android may batch while a device is in Doze mode.

## What went well

Support spotted the trend early; engineers compared timestamps rather than guessing.

title: Postmortem: Android Alert Delay under Doze
heading: What went badly
text:
## What went badly

We had no test that measured delivery delay on an idle device. The release notes did not mention the priority change.

## Action items

1. Add a test that sends alerts to an idle device and checks delay (owner: Tech Lead).
2. Add a delivery delay graph by platform (owner: SRE).
3. Add a line about delivery priority to the release checklist template.

title: Mobile Accessibility Guidelines
heading: VoiceOver (iOS)
text:
# Mobile Accessibility Guidelines

Everyone should be able to acknowledge an alert or approve a release from their phone. These guidelines apply to both apps.

## VoiceOver (iOS)

- Give every control an `accessibilityLabel` that describes its purpose, not its appearance.
- Use `accessibilityTraits` correctly: buttons are buttons, headers are headers.
- Group related elements so that a card is read as one item.
- Announce changes such as a new alert using `UIAccessibility.post`.

title: Mobile Accessibility Guidelines
heading: TalkBack (Android)
text:
## TalkBack (Android)

- Set `contentDescription` on icons and image buttons; mark decorative images as not important for accessibility.
- Use semantic roles in Compose (`Role.Button`, `heading()`).
- Merge descendants where a row should be a single focus target.

title: Mobile Accessibility Guidelines
heading: Text and layout
text:
## Text and layout

- Support dynamic type on iOS and font scaling on Android; layouts must not clip at the largest sizes.
- Touch targets are at least 44 points on iOS and 48 dp on Android.
- Keep contrast at least 4.5:1 for text.

## Motion and sound

Respect the system settings for reduced motion. Do not rely on sound alone to convey an alert.

## Testing

Before each release, one engineer walks through alerts, approvals and settings with each screen reader.

title: Internal Beta Distribution Program

text:

title: Mobile Strings and Localization Workflow
heading: Principles
text:
# Mobile Strings and Localization Workflow

How text gets from a developer's keyboard to a translated app.

## Principles

- No user-visible text is hard-coded in views.
- Every string has a key and a comment for translators.
- Sentences are never built by joining pieces.

title: Mobile Strings and Localization Workflow
heading: iOS
text:
## iOS

Strings live in `Localizable.strings` and `Localizable.stringsdict` (for plurals). Use `String(localized:)` in code.

## Android

Strings live in `res/values/strings.xml` with translations in `values-xx/`. Use plurals resources for counts.

title: Mobile Strings and Localization Workflow
heading: Steps
text:
## Steps

1. Add the string in the base language with a comment.
2. Run the sync script to push new strings to the translation tool.
3. Translators work on the new strings. Reviewers check them in context using screenshots.
4. When translations are complete, the sync script opens a pull request.
5. A teammate reviews the pull request and merges it.

title: Mobile Strings and Localization Workflow
heading: Checking your work
text:
## Checking your work

Use the pseudo-localization build to find hard-coded text and layouts that break with long words.

## Languages

The current language list is kept in the repository's `LANGUAGES.md`.

## Contact

title: Design Doc: Offline Alert Cache
heading: Context
text:
# Design Doc: Offline Alert Cache

**Author:** Staff Engineer (MOB)  **Status:** Approved by the Mobile Tech Lead

## Context

When a phone has no signal, the alerts screen is empty even for alerts the user has already seen. People on call often check alerts in basements, elevators or on planes.

title: Design Doc: Offline Alert Cache
heading: Goals
text:
## Goals

- Show the most recent alerts without a network connection.
- Keep the data fresh when the network returns.
- Keep storage small and secure.

## Non-goals

Acknowledging alerts offline. That needs separate design.

## Proposal

Store the latest 200 alerts in an on-device database (SQLite via Room on Android and Core Data on iOS). Each alert records its ID, title, severity, time and state.

On launch, the app shows cached alerts immediately and refreshes in the background. When the refresh completes, the list updates in place.

title: Design Doc: Offline Alert Cache
heading: Security
text:
## Security

The database is stored in the app's protected storage and cleared on sign-out. Alert bodies are not cached, only summaries.

## Alternatives

1. **No cache.** Simple, but poor experience.
2. **Cache everything.** More useful, but a bigger privacy and storage cost.

## Risks

Stale data may mislead. The screen will show "last updated" and an offline badge.

## Rollout

Behind a feature flag; internal beta first.

title: Ledger Invoice Data Handling and Classification
heading: Classification
text:
# Ledger Invoice Data Handling and Classification

**Owner:** Payments (PAY)  **Applies to:** everyone with access to Ledger Core invoice records

## Classification

Ledger invoice data is classified **Restricted**. That includes invoice line items, billing contact details on an invoice, tax amounts, totals, payment status and the generated PDF of an invoice.

title: Ledger Invoice Data Handling and Classification
heading: Handling rules
text:
## Handling rules

1. **Access.** Only members of the Payments team and approved Finance Systems staff may read invoice data in production. Access is requested through the access portal and reviewed quarterly.
2. **Storage.** Invoice data is stored only in Ledger Core's encrypted databases and the invoice archive bucket. Do not copy invoice data into spreadsheets, tickets or chat.
3. **Transit.** Use only internal services and TLS when moving invoice data between systems.
4. **Test data.** Use generated sample invoices in development and staging. Production invoice data must not be loaded into non-production environments.
5. **Logs.** Never write full invoice contents to logs. Log the invoice ID and status only.
6. **Support.** Support staff see a masked view. Requests to see more go to the on-call Payments engineer.

title: Ledger Invoice Data Handling and Classification
heading: Exports
text:
## Exports

Customers can download their own invoices through Ledger. Internal exports require approval from the Payments Engineering Manager and are logged.

## Incidents

If invoice data may have been exposed, page the Payments on-call engineer and notify the security team immediately.

## Questions

#prod-payments, or the Payments Staff Engineer.

title: Ledger Core Service Credentials Runbook
heading: Scope
text:
# Ledger Core Service Credentials Runbook

**Team:** Payments  **Audience:** SREs and engineers who operate Ledger Core

## Scope

This runbook covers the service API keys that Ledger Core uses to call internal services and external payment providers.

title: Ledger Core Service Credentials Runbook
heading: Where keys live
text:
## Where keys live

Keys are stored in Vaultline. Applications read them at start-up through the secrets sidecar. No key should appear in code, environment files or tickets.

## Rotation schedule

**Ledger Core service API keys rotate every 180 days.** The rotation calendar is kept in the Payments on-call handbook, and a reminder is created in Jira 14 days before each rotation.

title: Ledger Core Service Credentials Runbook
heading: Rotation steps
text:
## Rotation steps

1. Create a new key version in Vaultline with the same permissions as the current one.
2. Deploy the new version to staging and run the integration tests.
3. Roll the new version to production one instance at a time.
4. Watch error rates for 30 minutes.
5. Disable the old key version, and delete it after seven days if nothing has failed.
6. Record the rotation in the credentials log.

title: Ledger Core Service Credentials Runbook
heading: If a key is exposed
text:
## If a key is exposed

Rotate it immediately, outside the calendar, and tell the security team. Review access logs for the period the key was exposed.

## Checks

After each rotation, confirm that both Ledger Core and Meterflow report healthy and that billing jobs ran on schedule.

## Contacts

Payments on-call engineer; AppSec for questions about Vaultline.

title: Billing Alerts Integration Guide (Pushline)
heading: Overview
text:
# Billing Alerts Integration Guide (Pushline)

**Team:** Payments  **Audience:** engineers working on billing alerts

## Overview

Ledger sends alerts to customers about billing events, such as an approaching usage limit or a failed payment. Alerts reach mobile users through Pushline.

title: Billing Alerts Integration Guide (Pushline)
heading: How it works
text:
## How it works

1. Ledger Core detects a billing event.
2. The alert service builds a message with the customer's notification preferences.
3. The message is sent to the Pushline API with a priority and an idempotency key.
4. Pushline delivers the message to the customer's phones.

title: Billing Alerts Integration Guide (Pushline)
heading: Message priorities
text:
## Message priorities

| Event | Priority |
|---|---|
| Payment failed | High |
| Usage limit reached | High |
| Usage limit approaching | Normal |
| Invoice available | Normal |

## Handling delivery failures

Pushline retries a failed delivery **up to 5 times** before moving the message to its dead-letter queue. Design alert flows with that in mind: a message may arrive minutes after it was first sent, so alert text should not rely on the exact time of delivery.

If a message reaches the dead-letter queue, Ledger falls back to sending an email. The fallback is triggered by a dead-letter notification from Pushline.

title: Billing Alerts Integration Guide (Pushline)
heading: Idempotency
text:
## Idempotency

Always send the same idempotency key when you resend an alert, so the customer does not receive duplicates.

## Testing

Use the Pushline sandbox in staging. It lets you simulate failures and check the fallback.

## Contacts

Payments Tech Lead for this guide; Mobile team for Pushline questions.

title: Ledger Public API: Version Lifecycle and Deprecation
heading: Why we are careful
text:
# Ledger Public API: Version Lifecycle and Deprecation

**Owner:** Payments (PAY)  **Applies to:** the Ledger public API

## Why we are careful

Customers build billing and finance processes on top of the Ledger API. Changing it too fast can break their month-end close. This policy sets how Ledger retires versions.

title: Ledger Public API: Version Lifecycle and Deprecation
heading: Lifecycle
text:
## Lifecycle

| Stage | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Current | Recommended for new integrations |
| Deprecated | Still works, but customers are asked to move |
| Sunset | No longer served |

## Support period

**A deprecated Ledger API version remains supported for 12 months after the deprecation notice is published.** During that time it receives security fixes and critical bug fixes.

title: Ledger Public API: Version Lifecycle and Deprecation
heading: What we do when we deprecate
text:
## What we do when we deprecate

1. Publish a notice on the developer portal and in the changelog.
2. Email every customer account that has called the version in the previous 90 days.
3. Add `Deprecation` and `Sunset` headers to responses.
4. Offer a migration guide with side-by-side examples.
5. Remind customers at 6 months and at 90 days before sunset.

## Exceptions

A version may be sunset earlier only for a serious security reason, with approval from the Payments Engineering Manager and notice to customers.

## Approval

Approved by the Payments Engineering Manager and Tech Lead.

title: Ledger Core Architecture Decision Requirements
heading: Purpose
text:
# Ledger Core Architecture Decision Requirements

**Owner:** Payments (PAY)  **Approved by:** Payments Engineering Manager and Tech Lead

## Purpose

Ledger Core produces invoices that customers pay and auditors read. Mistakes are expensive and hard to undo. For this reason, Payments records the reasoning behind important design choices in Architecture Decision Records (ADRs).

title: Ledger Core Architecture Decision Requirements
heading: Requirement
text:
## Requirement

**An ADR is required for any change to the Ledger Core invoice schema or the Ledger public API, even when only the Payments team is affected.**

The ADR must be approved by the Payments Engineering Manager and the Payments Tech Lead before work starts.

title: Ledger Core Architecture Decision Requirements
heading: What the ADR should cover
text:
## What the ADR should cover

- The change and why it is needed
- Impact on stored invoices and on customers' integrations
- Migration and rollback plan
- Tests that show the change is safe
- Effect on reports and exports

## Process

1. The author drafts the ADR in the architecture records space and tags both approvers.
2. Approvers review within three working days.
3. Once both approve, the ADR is marked Accepted and linked in the pull request.

## Out of scope

Changes that do not touch the invoice schema or the public API follow normal review.

## Review

This requirement is reviewed each March.

title: Meterflow Usage Event Ingestion Design
heading: Problem
text:
# Meterflow Usage Event Ingestion Design

**Author:** Staff Engineer (PAY)  **Status:** Approved

## Problem

Customers send millions of usage events per hour. We must count each event exactly once, even when senders retry or networks fail.

title: Meterflow Usage Event Ingestion Design
heading: Overview
text:
## Overview

Events arrive at the ingestion API, are validated, and are published to Kafka on Streamline. Aggregation workers consume the topic and update usage totals.

## Components

1. **Ingestion API.** Validates the schema, authenticates the sender and assigns a receipt ID.
2. **Kafka topic.** Partitioned by customer ID so one customer's events stay in order.
3. **Deduplicator.** Uses the event's idempotency key and a rolling window in Redis to drop duplicates.
4. **Aggregator.** Writes hourly counts to PostgreSQL.

title: Meterflow Usage Event Ingestion Design
heading: Idempotency
text:
## Idempotency

Senders include an `event_id`. The deduplicator remembers IDs for 72 hours. Events with an unseen ID are accepted; seen IDs are acknowledged but not counted again.

## Failure handling

- If Kafka is unavailable, the API returns a retryable error.
- If the deduplicator is down, events are accepted and deduplicated later by a reconciliation job.

## Scaling

Add partitions and consumers together. The system has been tested at four times current peak.

## Alternatives considered

Deduplicating in the database alone was simpler but too slow at peak.

title: Meterflow Aggregation Windows Reference
heading: Windows
text:
# Meterflow Aggregation Windows Reference

## Windows

Meterflow rolls up usage into fixed windows.

| Window | Boundary | Used for |
|---|---|---|
| Hourly | Top of the hour, UTC | Near-real-time dashboards |
| Daily | 00:00 UTC | Usage exports, daily summaries |
| Billing period | Customer's billing cycle | Invoices |

title: Meterflow Aggregation Windows Reference
heading: Late events
text:
## Late events

Events can arrive after their window closes. Meterflow accepts late events for 48 hours and updates the affected window. After that, they go to a correction queue reviewed by the Payments team.

## Time zones

All windows are in UTC. Customers see their own time zone in the user interface, but windows are never shifted.

title: Meterflow Aggregation Windows Reference
heading: Rounding
text:
## Rounding

Quantities are stored as decimals with six places and rounded only when an invoice is produced.

## Querying

The aggregates API returns windows with `start`, `end`, `quantity` and a `final` flag. A window is final once its late-event period has passed.

title: Meterflow Aggregation Windows Reference
heading: Common questions
text:
## Common questions

**Why did the hourly total change?** A late event arrived within the 48-hour period.

**Why do daily totals differ slightly from the sum of hours?** They shouldn't; if they do, open a ticket with the customer ID and date.

## Owner

Meterflow Staff Engineer.

title: Ledger Core Invoice Finalization Runbook
heading: What finalization does
text:
# Ledger Core Invoice Finalization Runbook

**Team:** Payments  **Audience:** on-call engineers and finance operations

## What finalization does

At the end of each billing period, Ledger Core locks the period's usage, applies pricing, and produces a final invoice. After finalization, an invoice can only change through a credit note.

title: Ledger Core Invoice Finalization Runbook
heading: Timing
text:
## Timing

**Invoices finalize 3 days after the billing period ends.** This leaves time for late usage events to arrive and for customers' disputes to be raised before invoices are locked.

## Daily job

The finalization job runs at 02:00 UTC. It selects billing periods that ended exactly three days earlier.

title: Ledger Core Invoice Finalization Runbook
heading: Checks before finalizing
text:
## Checks before finalizing

1. Meterflow reports all windows for the period as final.
2. Reconciliation shows no unresolved differences.
3. Pricing plan versions for the period are unchanged.

## If the job fails

- Check the job log for the first error.
- Fix the cause and rerun the job; it is safe to rerun, as finalization is idempotent.
- If more than one hour passes, tell the finance operations channel.

title: Ledger Core Invoice Finalization Runbook
heading: Manual finalization
text:
## Manual finalization

Requires approval from the Payments Engineering Manager. Run `ledgerctl finalize --period <id> --reason <ticket>` and record the ticket.

## After finalization

Invoices are published to customers and the archive. Confirm that the publication count matches the number of finalized invoices.

title: Postmortem: Duplicate Usage Events during Kafka Rebalance
heading: Postmortem: Duplicate Usage Events during Kafka Rebalance
text:
# Postmortem: Duplicate Usage Events during Kafka Rebalance

**Severity:** Sev2  **Incident date:** 2026-03-09  **Published: 2026-03-16**  **Author:** SRE (PAY)

title: Postmortem: Duplicate Usage Events during Kafka Rebalance
heading: Summary
text:
## Summary

During a Kafka consumer rebalance, a set of usage events was processed twice for about 25 minutes. Roughly 0.3% of that period's events were double counted. The error was corrected before any invoice was finalized.

title: Postmortem: Duplicate Usage Events during Kafka Rebalance
heading: Detection
text:
## Detection

A reconciliation alert showed that usage totals for several customers exceeded the number of events received.

## Timeline (UTC)

- **14:02** A scaling change added consumers, triggering a rebalance.  
- **14:05** Some consumers committed offsets late, so events were redelivered.  
- **14:31** The reconciliation alert fired.  
- **14:40** The on-call engineer paused aggregation.  
- **15:20** The deduplication window was extended and aggregation resumed.  
- **17:00** A correction job fixed the affected totals.

title: Postmortem: Duplicate Usage Events during Kafka Rebalance
heading: Root cause
text:
## Root cause

The deduplicator relied on a short in-memory window that was reset by the rebalance. Redelivered events were seen as new.

## What went well

The reconciliation alert caught the problem quickly. Correction was done without customer impact.

title: Postmortem: Duplicate Usage Events during Kafka Rebalance
heading: What went badly
text:
## What went badly

The scaling change was made without considering consumer rebalance behavior.

## Action items

1. Persist the deduplication window outside the process (owner: Staff Engineer).  
2. Add a rebalance-safe scaling procedure to the runbook (owner: SRE).  
3. Alert on duplicate rate (owner: SRE).

title: Payment Reconciliation Job Troubleshooting
heading: What reconciliation does
text:
# Payment Reconciliation Job Troubleshooting

**Team:** Payments  **Audience:** on-call engineers

## What reconciliation does

Every night, the reconciliation job compares usage received by Meterflow with usage counted in Ledger Core, and compares invoices against payment provider records. It reports differences.

title: Payment Reconciliation Job Troubleshooting
heading: Reading the report
text:
## Reading the report

The job writes a summary to the `#prod-payments-recon` channel:

- **Matched:** counts agree.
- **Unmatched usage:** Ledger Core has usage that Meterflow does not.
- **Unmatched payments:** a payment exists with no matching invoice, or the reverse.

title: Payment Reconciliation Job Troubleshooting
heading: Common failures
text:
## Common failures

| Symptom | Likely cause | Action |
|---|---|---|
| Job did not run | Scheduler issue | Check the scheduler; rerun the job |
| Job timed out | Large backlog after an incident | Rerun with a smaller date range |
| Many unmatched payments | Provider settlement delay | Wait a day and rerun |
| A few unmatched usage rows | Late events | Check the correction queue |

title: Payment Reconciliation Job Troubleshooting
heading: Rerunning
text:
## Rerunning

```
reconcile --date 2026-05-10 --customer-batch 1
```

Reruns are safe and do not change data; they only recompute the report.

## Escalating

If differences persist after two reruns, open a ticket in the Payments queue and tag the Staff Engineer. For possible customer impact, page the on-call engineer.

title: Ledger Core PostgreSQL Migration Playbook
heading: Principles
text:
# Ledger Core PostgreSQL Migration Playbook

**Owner:** Tech Lead, Payments

## Principles

Never take Ledger Core offline for a database change. Every migration should be reversible, observable and small.

## The expand and contract pattern

1. **Expand:** add new columns, tables or indexes in a way that old code still works.
2. **Migrate:** backfill data in batches and deploy code that writes to both old and new structures.
3. **Switch:** change reads to the new structure.
4. **Contract:** after a stable period, remove the old structure.

title: Ledger Core PostgreSQL Migration Playbook
heading: Practical rules
text:
## Practical rules

- Add columns as nullable; set defaults in a later step.
- Create indexes with `CONCURRENTLY`.
- Backfill in batches of 10,000 rows with a pause between batches.
- Use lock timeouts so that a migration never blocks traffic.
- Test on a staging copy that is at least as large as production.

title: Ledger Core PostgreSQL Migration Playbook
heading: Before running
text:
## Before running

- [ ] Migration reviewed by a second engineer.
- [ ] Rollback script written and tested.
- [ ] Dashboards open for lock waits, replication lag and error rates.

## During

Run during a low-traffic period, watch the dashboards, and stop at the first sign of trouble.

## After

Record the migration in the change log and delete temporary scripts.

title: Meterflow Usage Export FAQ
heading: Meterflow Usage Export FAQ
text:
# Meterflow Usage Export FAQ

*For customers and Support.*

**What is a usage export?**
A file that lists the usage Meterflow recorded for your account over a period you choose.

**How do I request one?**
In Console, open **Usage > Exports**, choose a date range and format, and select **Create export**. You will get an email when it is ready.

**Which formats are available?**
CSV and JSON.

**How far back can I export?**
As far back as your account has data, up to the limit in your plan.

**How long does an export take?**
Most finish in a few minutes. Large ranges can take longer.

**Why do my numbers differ from my invoice?**
Exports show raw recorded usage. Invoices apply pricing, minimums and credits. Compare the usage totals first, then check the pricing plan.

**Can I schedule exports?**
Yes. In **Usage > Exports**, choose **Schedule** and select daily, weekly or monthly.

**Will late events change an export?**
Recent windows can change slightly as late events arrive. The export marks windows as final or not final.

**Who can I ask?**
Contact support, or the Payments team if you are an internal user.

title: Ledger Core Tax Rate Table Update Procedure
heading: Background
text:
# Ledger Core Tax Rate Table Update Procedure

**Owner:** Tech Lead, Payments  **Frequency:** quarterly

## Background

Ledger Core calculates tax using a table of rates by jurisdiction. Rates change; we update the table each quarter, effective the first day of the quarter.

title: Ledger Core Tax Rate Table Update Procedure
heading: Timeline
text:
## Timeline

| When | Step |
|---|---|
| Six weeks before | Finance supplies the new rates file |
| Five weeks before | Engineer loads the file into staging and runs validation |
| Four weeks before | Finance reviews staging results |
| Two weeks before | Load into production with an effective date |
| Quarter start | New rates take effect automatically |

title: Ledger Core Tax Rate Table Update Procedure
heading: Steps
text:
## Steps

1. Download the rates file from the shared finance folder and verify the checksum.
2. Run the validation script:
   ```
   taxctl validate --file rates-2026Q4.csv
   ```
3. Review the diff report. Large changes should be explained by Finance.
4. Load into staging with `taxctl load --env staging`.
5. Compare sample invoices before and after.
6. After approval, load into production.

title: Ledger Core Tax Rate Table Update Procedure
heading: Rollback
text:
## Rollback

Production loads are versioned. Roll back with `taxctl activate --version <previous>`, effective immediately for future calculations.

## Records

Save the validation report, the diff and the approvals in the quarter's folder.

title: Quarry Query API Reference
heading: Overview
text:
# Quarry Query API Reference

**Owner:** Search (SRCH)  **Audience:** engineers calling Quarry

## Overview

Quarry executes search and analytics queries over data indexed by Sieve. This page documents the query endpoint and its limits.

title: Quarry Query API Reference
heading: Endpoint
text:
## Endpoint

```
POST /v1/query
```

### Request

| Field | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `query` | string | Query in Quarry Query Language |
| `time_range` | object | `start` and `end`, ISO 8601 |
| `limit` | integer | Maximum rows to return (default 1,000; maximum 10,000) |
| `timeout_ms` | integer | Optional per-request timeout |

title: Quarry Query API Reference
heading: Response
text:
### Response

Returns `rows`, `stats` (scanned, matched, took_ms) and a `cursor` when more rows are available.

## Limits

- **Default query timeout: 120 seconds.** A request may set a lower `timeout_ms`; it may not exceed the maximum configured for the account.
- Maximum query length: 8,192 characters.
- Concurrent queries per account: 20.

title: Quarry Query API Reference
heading: Errors
text:
## Errors

| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `INVALID_QUERY` | The query could not be parsed |
| `TIMEOUT` | The query ran longer than the timeout |
| `RATE_LIMITED` | Too many concurrent queries |

## Pagination

Pass the `cursor` from a response to fetch the next page.

## Versioning

This is version 1 of the API. Changes follow the Product API Versioning Standard.

title: Insight Search: Query Limits (Help Center Article)
heading: Insight Search: Query Limits
text:
# Insight Search: Query Limits

*Help Center article for TechSync Insight customers.*

## Overview

To keep searches fast for everyone, Insight sets limits on how long a search can run and how much it can return. This article explains what you can expect.

title: Insight Search: Query Limits (Help Center Article)
heading: Search time limit
text:
## Search time limit

**By default, a search stops after 60 seconds.** If your search is stopped, you will see a message saying it timed out, along with any partial results.

## Tips if your search times out

1. **Narrow the time range.** Searching one hour is faster than searching a week.
2. **Add filters early.** Start your query with the fields that remove the most data.
3. **Use saved searches** for expensive queries you run often.
4. **Break a large question into parts.** Run each part and compare results.

title: Insight Search: Query Limits (Help Center Article)
heading: Result limits
text:
## Result limits

A search returns up to 1,000 rows in the table view. Use **Export** to download more.

## Concurrent searches

You can run several searches at once. If you run many together, some may wait briefly.

## Need more?

If you often reach these limits, contact your account team to talk about your plan.

## Related articles

- Writing your first Insight search
- Saving and sharing searches
- Understanding search results
