title: Sieve Indexing Pipeline Overview
heading: Purpose
text:
# Sieve Indexing Pipeline Overview

**Author:** Staff Engineer (SRCH)  **Status:** Approved

## Purpose

Sieve turns incoming data into searchable indexes. This document describes the path from ingest to a query-ready index.

title: Sieve Indexing Pipeline Overview
heading: Stages
text:
## Stages

1. **Collect.** Data arrives from customers' agents and integrations through the ingestion gateway.
2. **Parse.** Records are parsed into fields using the account's schema mapping. Unparseable records go to a quarantine stream.
3. **Enrich.** Optional enrichment adds fields (for example, geographic data for IP addresses).
4. **Batch.** Records are grouped into batches by account and time window.
5. **Index.** Batches are written to OpenSearch shards.
6. **Publish.** When a batch is searchable, Sieve updates the metadata that Quarry reads.

title: Sieve Indexing Pipeline Overview
heading: Latency
text:
## Latency

Typical time from arrival to searchable is under a minute. Under heavy load it can be a few minutes.

## Failure handling

Each stage commits progress, so a failed worker restarts from the last committed point. Quarantined records are visible in Console so customers can fix their data.

## Scaling

Parse and index stages scale independently. The index stage is limited by OpenSearch write capacity, which is monitored.

## Open topics

Smarter batching for very small accounts is an idea we plan to explore.

title: Quarry Query Planner Internals
heading: What the planner does
text:
# Quarry Query Planner Internals

**Audience:** Search engineers  **Status:** Approved design reference

## What the planner does

Given a parsed query, the planner chooses how to run it: which shards to read, in what order, which filters to push down, and how to combine partial results.

title: Quarry Query Planner Internals
heading: Stages
text:
## Stages

1. **Parse and validate.** Produce a syntax tree and check field names against the schema.
2. **Normalize.** Rewrite equivalent expressions into a canonical form, so that planning rules apply consistently.
3. **Estimate.** Use shard statistics to estimate how many rows each filter will match.
4. **Choose a plan.** Compare candidate plans using a cost model.
5. **Execute.** Run sub-queries on shards and merge.

title: Quarry Query Planner Internals
heading: Cost model
text:
## Cost model

Costs combine estimated rows scanned, rows returned, and the number of shards touched. The model is deliberately simple. We prefer plans that read less data over those that look clever.

## Pushdown rules

- Time range filters are always pushed to shard selection.
- Equality filters on indexed fields are applied first.
- Aggregations are computed per shard and merged.

title: Quarry Query Planner Internals
heading: Known limits
text:
## Known limits

- The planner has no statistics for brand-new fields until a batch has been indexed.
- Very wide `OR` expressions can produce large plans.

## Testing

Planner changes are tested with a corpus of 2,000 saved queries; the plan and results must match the previous release unless intended.

title: Sieve Reindexing Runbook
heading: Choose the type
text:
# Sieve Reindexing Runbook

**Owner:** Search SRE  **When to use:** after schema mapping changes or index corruption

## Choose the type

- **Partial reindex** rebuilds a time range or one account. Use for small corrections.
- **Full reindex** rebuilds every index for an account. Use when the mapping changes in a way that affects existing data.

title: Sieve Reindexing Runbook
heading: Before you start
text:
## Before you start

1. Confirm approval in the Jira ticket from the Search Tech Lead.
2. Check OpenSearch capacity; reindexing doubles write load.
3. Notify #prod-search and Support.

## Partial reindex

```
sieve reindex --account <id> --from 2026-05-01 --to 2026-05-07
```

The job reads the source data, rewrites documents into a new index, and switches an alias when it finishes.

title: Sieve Reindexing Runbook
heading: Full reindex
text:
## Full reindex

1. Create the new index with the updated mapping.
2. Start the reindex job with `--full`.
3. Watch progress on the Sieve dashboard.
4. When the job reports complete, compare document counts between old and new indexes.
5. Switch the alias.
6. Keep the old index for 48 hours, then delete it.

title: Sieve Reindexing Runbook
heading: Troubleshooting
text:
## Troubleshooting

- **Job stalls:** look for a bulk rejection in OpenSearch; lower the batch size.
- **Counts differ:** rerun the affected range.

## After

Record the work in the ticket and update the account's mapping version.

title: OpenSearch Cluster Capacity Planning
heading: Why plan
text:
# OpenSearch Cluster Capacity Planning

**Author:** SRE (SRCH)  **Status:** Approved

## Why plan

Search clusters run out of capacity slowly and then suddenly. Planning ahead avoids emergency expansions.

## Key quantities

| Quantity | Guidance |
|---|---|
| Shard size | Target 30 to 50 GB |
| Shards per node | Fewer than 20 per GB of heap |
| Disk headroom | Keep at least 25% free |
| Heap | Half of memory, up to 31 GB |

title: OpenSearch Cluster Capacity Planning
heading: Estimating growth
text:
## Estimating growth

1. Take the daily ingest volume from the Sieve dashboard.
2. Multiply by the replication factor.
3. Multiply by retention days to get the storage needed.
4. Add 25% headroom.
5. Divide by usable disk per node.

title: OpenSearch Cluster Capacity Planning
heading: Review cadence
text:
## Review cadence

Review each cluster monthly. Raise a ticket when projected usage will pass 70% within 90 days.

## Expansion

Add nodes in pairs across availability zones. Rebalancing takes hours; schedule expansions off-peak and watch search latency.

## Warning signs

Rising rejected-bulk counts, long garbage collection pauses, or shards stuck relocating.

## Cost

The finance partner reviews cluster costs each quarter. Savings usually come from shard sizing and index lifecycle choices.

title: Postmortem: Quarry Slow Queries after Shard Rebalance
heading: Postmortem: Quarry Slow Queries after Shard Rebalance
text:
# Postmortem: Quarry Slow Queries after Shard Rebalance

**Severity:** Sev2  **Incident date:** 2026-06-15  **Published:** 2026-06-22  **Author:** SRE (SRCH)

title: Postmortem: Quarry Slow Queries after Shard Rebalance
heading: Summary
text:
## Summary

After an automatic shard rebalance, query latency for a group of accounts rose sharply for about 90 minutes. Searches completed, but many were several times slower than normal.

## Impact

Around 12% of queries were affected. Dashboards that refresh frequently were slow to update.

title: Postmortem: Quarry Slow Queries after Shard Rebalance
heading: Timeline (UTC)
text:
## Timeline (UTC)

- **13:00** OpenSearch began moving shards after a node was added.
- **13:25** Latency alerts fired for the affected accounts.
- **13:40** The on-call engineer found heavy relocation traffic on two nodes.
- **14:10** Relocation was throttled.
- **14:35** Latency returned to normal.

title: Postmortem: Quarry Slow Queries after Shard Rebalance
heading: Root cause
text:
## Root cause

Rebalancing ran at its default concurrency while the cluster was under normal query load. Several large shards moved at once and competed with search for disk and network.

## What went well

Alerts fired early. The mitigation was simple and quick once the cause was identified.

title: Postmortem: Quarry Slow Queries after Shard Rebalance
heading: What went badly
text:
## What went badly

We expanded the cluster during busy hours and had no limit on rebalance concurrency.

## Action items

1. Set a lower default relocation concurrency (owner: SRE).
2. Update the capacity planning guide to recommend off-peak expansions (owner: Tech Lead).
3. Add a dashboard panel for shard relocations.

title: Relevance Tuning Basics FAQ
heading: Relevance Tuning Basics FAQ
text:
# Relevance Tuning Basics FAQ

**What is relevance?**
How well search results match what the user was looking for. Better relevance means the right result is near the top.

**What can I tune?**
- Which fields are searched
- How much each field counts (boosts)
- How text is split into terms (analyzers)
- How recent results are ranked

**What is a boost?**
A multiplier on a field's contribution. A match in the title might count three times as much as a match in the body.

**What is an analyzer?**
The recipe for breaking text into terms: lowercasing, splitting on spaces, removing endings (stemming) and so on.

**How do I know a change helped?**
Use the evaluation harness. It runs a set of sample queries and compares ranking quality before and after.

**Why did my change break something?**
Relevance is a trade-off. A boost that helps one query can hurt another. Always run the whole set.

**Should I tune per customer?**
Rarely. Start with defaults, and only add account-specific settings when there is a clear reason.

**Where do I ask for help?**
#prod-search, or find the Tech Lead during office hours on Wednesdays.

title: Quarry Query Language Syntax Guide
heading: Basic form
text:
# Quarry Query Language Syntax Guide

A short reference to the Quarry Query Language (QQL).

## Basic form

```
source=app-logs level=error | stats count() by service
```

A query is a source, optional filters, then pipe-separated commands.

title: Quarry Query Language Syntax Guide
heading: Filters
text:
## Filters

| Syntax | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `field=value` | Equals |
| `field!=value` | Not equals |
| `field>10` | Greater than |
| `field~"abc*"` | Wildcard match |
| `field in (a,b,c)` | One of a list |

Combine filters with `AND`, `OR` and parentheses. A space between filters means `AND`.

title: Quarry Query Language Syntax Guide
heading: Commands
text:
## Commands

- `stats count() by field`: group and count.
- `sort -field`: sort descending.
- `head 20`: first 20 rows.
- `fields a,b`: keep only these columns.
- `rename a as b`: rename a column.
- `dedup field`: remove duplicate values.
- `eval total=a+b`: compute a new field.

title: Quarry Query Language Syntax Guide
heading: Time
text:
## Time

Use the time range control or `earliest=-1h latest=now` in the query.

## Examples

Errors by service in the last hour:
```
source=app-logs level=error earliest=-1h | stats count() by service | sort -count
```

Slowest requests:
```
source=requests | sort -duration_ms | head 10
```

## Tips

Put the most selective filters first, and select only the fields you need.

title: Sieve Schema Mapping Guide
heading: What is a mapping?
text:
# Sieve Schema Mapping Guide

> Draft. Not reviewed. Examples may change.

## What is a mapping?

A mapping tells Sieve how to turn incoming records into fields in an index: names, types and whether a field is searchable.

title: Sieve Schema Mapping Guide
heading: Default mapping
text:
## Default mapping

If an account has no mapping, Sieve uses dynamic mapping: strings become text and keyword fields, numbers become numeric, and timestamps are detected.

## Defining your own

A mapping file looks like this:

```
fields:
  - name: timestamp
    type: date
  - name: level
    type: keyword
  - name: message
    type: text
  - name: duration_ms
    type: long
```

title: Sieve Schema Mapping Guide
heading: Field types
text:
## Field types

| Type | Use for |
|---|---|
| `keyword` | Exact matches, grouping |
| `text` | Full-text search |
| `long`, `double` | Numbers |
| `date` | Time values |
| `ip` | IP addresses |

title: Sieve Schema Mapping Guide
heading: Changing a mapping
text:
## Changing a mapping

Adding a field is easy. Changing the type of an existing field needs a reindex.

title: Search Relevance Evaluation Harness
heading: What it is
text:
# Search Relevance Evaluation Harness

## What it is

A set of tools that measure how good our search ranking is. You give it queries and the results people consider correct; it reports how well Quarry ranks them.

## Inputs

- **Query set:** a CSV of sample queries (about 500).
- **Judgments:** for each query, a list of documents with a relevance grade from 0 to 3.
- **Configuration:** the ranking settings to test.

title: Search Relevance Evaluation Harness
heading: Metrics
text:
## Metrics

| Metric | Meaning |
|---|---|
| nDCG@10 | Quality of the top ten, weighted by position |
| Recall@50 | Share of relevant documents in the top fifty |
| MRR | How high the first relevant result appears |

title: Search Relevance Evaluation Harness
heading: Running it
text:
## Running it

```
relevance-eval run --queries queries.csv --judgments judgments.csv --config candidate.yaml
```

The tool prints a table and writes a detailed report. Use `--baseline baseline.yaml` to compare two configurations side by side.

title: Search Relevance Evaluation Harness
heading: Interpreting results
text:
## Interpreting results

Small changes can be noise. Look at the whole query set and at the worst-hit queries, not only the average.

## Adding judgments

Judges grade results in the review tool. Aim for at least two graders per query.

## Limits

Judgments reflect today's content and may need refreshing.

title: Design Doc: Quarry Result Caching
heading: Context
text:
# Design Doc: Quarry Result Caching

**Author:** Staff Engineer (SRCH)  **Status:** Approved

## Context

Dashboards run the same queries repeatedly. Quarry re-executes them each time, which uses shard capacity unnecessarily.

title: Design Doc: Quarry Result Caching
heading: Goals
text:
## Goals

- Reduce repeated work for identical queries over unchanged data.
- Never return results that are staler than the data's freshness allows.
- Keep memory use predictable.

## Proposal

Add two cache layers:

1. **Result cache** keyed by account, normalized query and time range. Entries are valid until new data arrives for that window.
2. **Shard-level cache** for partial aggregates over closed time windows. Closed windows never change, so entries can live longer.

title: Design Doc: Quarry Result Caching
heading: Invalidation
text:
## Invalidation

Sieve publishes an event when it indexes a batch. Quarry invalidates cache entries that overlap the batch's time range. Windows older than the indexing delay are treated as closed.

## Sizing

The result cache uses up to 2 GB per node, with a least-recently-used policy. The shard cache uses up to 4 GB.

title: Design Doc: Quarry Result Caching
heading: Risks
text:
## Risks

- Cache stampedes on popular queries; mitigated by request coalescing.
- Subtle staleness bugs; mitigated by tests comparing cached and uncached results.

## Alternatives

A cache outside Quarry was simpler but lacked visibility into data freshness.

## Rollout

Enable for a few internal accounts, then compare latency and hit rates.

title: Product API Versioning Standard
heading: 1. Version numbers
text:
# Product API Versioning Standard

**Applies to:** every public and partner-facing API owned by a Product Engineering team.

## 1. Version numbers

APIs use semantic versioning. The major version appears in the request path (for example `/v2/`). Minor and patch changes must stay backward compatible within a major version.

title: Product API Versioning Standard
heading: 2. What counts as a breaking change
text:
## 2. What counts as a breaking change

Removing or renaming a field, changing a field's type, tightening validation, changing an error code, or changing default behavior in a way that alters results.

## 3. Deprecation

When a team decides to retire a version, it must:

1. Publish a deprecation notice in the API changelog and on the developer portal.
2. Add `Deprecation` and `Sunset` headers to responses from the affected version.
3. Notify customers who have called the version in the previous 30 days.

**A deprecated version remains supported for a minimum of 6 months after the deprecation notice is published.** Teams may support it longer; they may not support it for less time without written approval from the VP of Product Engineering.

title: Product API Versioning Standard
heading: 4. Sunset
text:
## 4. Sunset

On the sunset date the version may return `410 Gone`. Sunset dates are published at least 30 days before they take effect.

## 5. Changelog

Every team keeps a changelog in the developer portal with the date, version and a plain-language summary of each change.

## 6. Questions

Ask in #prod-api-standards or contact the owning Staff Engineer.

title: Product Release Readiness Checklist
heading: Before the release
text:
# Product Release Readiness Checklist

Use this checklist for any release that customers will notice. It is short on purpose; teams add their own steps on top.

## Before the release

- [ ] Changes have been exercised in staging and a named engineer has signed off.
- [ ] A rollback plan is written down and has been read by the person releasing.
- [ ] Release notes are drafted in plain language and reviewed by the Tech Lead.
- [ ] Feature flags are configured so that new behavior can be switched off without a new build.
- [ ] Dashboards and alerts for the affected service have been checked.
- [ ] Support has been told about customer-visible changes.

title: Product Release Readiness Checklist
heading: During the release
text:
## During the release

- [ ] The releasing engineer announces start and finish in the team channel.
- [ ] Error rates and latency are watched for at least thirty minutes.

## After the release

- [ ] Release notes are published.
- [ ] Flags that are no longer needed are scheduled for cleanup.
- [ ] Anything surprising is written up in the team's notes for the next planning meeting.

## Ownership

The TPM function owns this checklist and reviews it each January. Suggestions are welcome in #prod-release.

title: Product Design Review Process
heading: Purpose
text:
# Product Design Review Process

## Purpose

A design review is a short, structured conversation that lets other engineers find problems while they are cheap to fix. It is not an approval gate for every change.

## When to hold one

Hold a design review when a change introduces a new service, a new data store, a new external dependency, or a significant change to how a component behaves. If you are unsure, ask your Tech Lead.

title: Product Design Review Process
heading: How it runs
text:
## How it runs

1. The author writes a design document using the standard template (context, goals, proposal, alternatives, risks).
2. The author shares it at least two working days before the review.
3. A Staff Engineer acts as reviewer-of-record and invites two or three other engineers with relevant experience.
4. The review lasts 45 minutes. The author presents for ten minutes; the rest is discussion.
5. The reviewer-of-record posts a written summary of decisions and open questions within two working days.

title: Product Design Review Process
heading: What reviewers look for
text:
## What reviewers look for

Clear goals, honest alternatives, operability (how will we know it is broken?), and the cost of changing course later.

## Records

Design documents and summaries are stored in the team's Confluence space. Link them from the pull request that implements the design.

## Questions

Contact a Staff Engineer in your team or ask in #prod-design-review.

title: Customer-Facing Incident Communication Template
heading: Stages
text:
# Customer-Facing Incident Communication Template

Use this template for status page updates and customer emails during an incident. Plain words, short sentences, no internal system names unless customers see them.

## Stages

1. **Investigating:** We know something is wrong and are looking into it.
2. **Identified:** We know the cause and are working on a fix.
3. **Monitoring:** A fix is in place and we are watching to be sure.
4. **Resolved:** The issue is over.

title: Customer-Facing Incident Communication Template
heading: Wording
text:
## Wording

**Investigating**
> We are investigating reports of [symptom] affecting [product or feature]. We will post another update within [time].

**Identified**
> We have identified the cause of [symptom] and are working on a fix. [Workaround, if any.]

**Monitoring**
> A fix has been applied. We are monitoring and will confirm when we are confident the issue is resolved.

**Resolved**
> The issue affecting [product or feature] has been resolved as of [time, with time zone]. We will publish a summary within [timeframe].

title: Customer-Facing Incident Communication Template
heading: Update cadence
text:
## Update cadence

For Sev1 incidents, post an update at least every 30 minutes. For Sev2, at least every hour. For Sev3 and Sev4, post when the status changes.

## Tone

Be direct. Say what customers can and cannot do right now. Do not speculate about cause until it is confirmed.

title: Product Engineering Quarterly Planning Process

text:

title: Error Handling and Logging Conventions
heading: Errors
text:
# Error Handling and Logging Conventions

## Errors

- Every API error returns a JSON body with `code`, `message` and `request_id`.
- Error codes are upper snake case and stable: `INVALID_ARGUMENT`, `NOT_FOUND`, `RATE_LIMITED`.
- Messages are written for the caller, not for us. Never include stack traces, SQL or internal hostnames.
- Retryable errors should say so with a `retryable` flag.

title: Error Handling and Logging Conventions
heading: Logs
text:
## Logs

Services write structured JSON logs to standard output. Required fields:

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `ts` | UTC timestamp, ISO 8601 |
| `level` | debug, info, warn or error |
| `service` | Service name |
| `request_id` | Correlation ID, propagated across services |
| `msg` | Short human-readable message |

title: Error Handling and Logging Conventions
heading: Levels
text:
## Levels

- **error:** something failed and needs attention.
- **warn:** something unexpected happened but the request succeeded.
- **info:** normal significant events.
- **debug:** developer detail, off by default in production.

title: Error Handling and Logging Conventions
heading: What never goes in a log
text:
## What never goes in a log

Passwords, tokens, full payment card numbers, and message bodies containing customer content. If in doubt, log an identifier instead.

## Tracing

Propagate the trace context headers on every outbound call so that Tracewell can stitch a request together.

title: Accessibility Standard for Product UIs
heading: Target
text:
# Accessibility Standard for Product UIs

## Target

All customer-facing web and mobile interfaces meet WCAG 2.2 Level AA.

## Requirements

1. **Keyboard:** every interactive element is reachable and usable with a keyboard alone, with a visible focus indicator.
2. **Contrast:** text has a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 against its background; large text at least 3:1.
3. **Labels:** every form control has a programmatic label. Icons used as buttons have accessible names.
4. **Structure:** pages use semantic headings and landmarks.
5. **Motion:** animations can be reduced or turned off through the operating system setting.
6. **Mobile:** touch targets are at least 44 by 44 points; screen readers announce state changes.

title: Accessibility Standard for Product UIs
heading: Use shared components
text:
## Use shared components

Web interfaces should use Prism components, which include accessibility behavior by default. Mobile apps follow the platform guidelines and the Mobile team's accessibility guide.

## Audits

Each product is audited twice a year. Findings are logged in Jira with the label `a11y` and are prioritized with other work.

## Ownership

Staff Engineers in Web and Mobile jointly maintain this standard.

title: Product API Design Guidelines
heading: Resources and naming
text:
# Product API Design Guidelines

A consistent API is easier to learn. These guidelines cover shape and naming. They do not cover the lifecycle of versions.

## Resources and naming

- Use plural nouns for collections: `/invoices`, `/queries`.
- Use lower snake case for field names; use ISO 8601 for timestamps in UTC.
- Identifiers are opaque strings. Do not encode meaning in them.

title: Product API Design Guidelines
heading: Pagination
text:
## Pagination

Collections use cursor-based pagination. Responses include `next_cursor`; clients pass it back as `cursor`. Page size is set with `limit`, with a documented default and maximum.

title: Product API Design Guidelines
heading: Filtering and sorting
text:
## Filtering and sorting

Filter with query parameters named for the field (`status=open`). Sort with `sort=created_at` or `sort=-created_at` for descending.

## Errors

Use the standard error body from the Error Handling and Logging Conventions. Use HTTP status codes for the class of error and the `code` field for the specific cause.

title: Product API Design Guidelines
heading: Idempotency
text:
## Idempotency

`POST` operations that create billable or irreversible effects accept an `Idempotency-Key` header and return the original result when it is repeated.

## Documentation

Every endpoint is described in OpenAPI, with an example request and response, before it ships.

title: Technical Documentation Standard
heading: Every document needs
text:
# Technical Documentation Standard

Good documentation saves hours. This standard applies to documents kept in the shared Confluence spaces and repositories.

## Every document needs

1. A title that says what the document is for.
2. An owner team and the author's role.
3. A status: draft, approved, deprecated, or unmarked for working notes.
4. A last-updated date.
5. A short opening paragraph that says who the document is for.

title: Technical Documentation Standard
heading: Templates
text:
## Templates

Technical Writing provides templates for runbooks, design documents, postmortems, onboarding guides, FAQs and policies. Start from the template; delete sections you do not need.

## Writing style

- Prefer short sentences and plain words.
- Put the most important instruction first.
- Use numbered steps for procedures and tables for reference values.
- Define abbreviations on first use.

title: Technical Documentation Standard
heading: Review
text:
## Review

Documents that other teams will rely on are reviewed by a peer before they are marked approved. Technical Writing is happy to review any document on request.

## Upkeep

Owners review their approved documents at least once a year and update the last-updated date when they do.

title: Engineer Interview Loop Guide

title: Dependency and Library Upgrade Cadence
heading: Policy
text:
# Dependency and Library Upgrade Cadence

## Policy

Product Engineering teams upgrade third-party dependencies on a quarterly cadence so that updates stay small and predictable.

## Upgrade windows

Each quarter has a two-week upgrade window, starting the second Monday of the quarter. During the window, teams:

1. Review the dependency report produced by Sentinel.
2. Upgrade minor and patch versions of direct dependencies.
3. Plan major-version upgrades as separate work with their own tickets.
4. Run the full test suite and the staging checks before merging.

title: Dependency and Library Upgrade Cadence
heading: Keeping it manageable
text:
## Keeping it manageable

- Upgrade one ecosystem at a time (for example, Go modules, then npm packages).
- Keep upgrade pull requests free of unrelated changes.
- Record notable behavior changes in the pull request description.

## Out-of-cycle upgrades

A team may upgrade outside the window when it needs a specific fix. It should tell its Tech Lead and note the reason in the pull request.

## Ownership

Staff Engineers across the four teams maintain this policy. Suggested changes go to #prod-engineering-standards.

title: Customer Escalation Handling with Support
heading: Severity levels
text:
# Customer Escalation Handling with Support

This runbook describes how Support brings customer problems to Product Engineering and what Support can expect in return.

## Severity levels

| Level | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Sev1 | Widespread customer-facing impact |
| Sev2 | Significant impact for one or more customers |
| Sev3 | Limited impact, workaround available |
| Sev4 | Question or minor issue |

title: Customer Escalation Handling with Support
heading: Steps
text:
## Steps

1. **Support triages** the ticket and chooses a severity based on the table above.
2. **Sev3 and Sev4:** Support files a Jira ticket in the owning team's queue, using the product component field.
3. **Sev1 and Sev2:** Support pages the owning team's on-call engineer through Lookout and opens an incident channel.
4. **The on-call engineer** confirms the severity, starts the incident process and tells Support who is leading.
5. **Support relays updates** to the customer using the Customer-Facing Incident Communication Template.
6. **After resolution,** Support closes the ticket with a plain-language summary.

## Finding the right team

Use the Product Engineering Team Directory to map a product area to a team.

## Feedback loop

Each month, the TPM and the Support lead review recurring tickets and decide which to fix at the source.

title: Product Test Strategy Standard
heading: Principles
text:
# Product Test Strategy Standard

## Principles

Tests exist to give us confidence to change code. Prefer fast, reliable tests close to the code, and a few end-to-end tests for the journeys customers depend on.

## The test pyramid

| Layer | Purpose | Share of tests |
|---|---|---|
| Unit | Logic in isolation | Most |
| Integration | Components with real dependencies such as a database | Some |
| End-to-end | Key customer journeys | Few |

title: Product Test Strategy Standard
heading: Expectations
text:
## Expectations

- New code ships with tests. Bug fixes ship with a test that fails without the fix.
- Teams aim for at least 80% line coverage on new code. Coverage is a prompt for conversation, not a goal in itself.
- Tests must not depend on the network, wall-clock time or execution order.
- A flaky test is fixed or removed within one sprint.

title: Product Test Strategy Standard
heading: Environments
text:
## Environments

Integration tests run against containers in CI. End-to-end tests run in staging after each merge to the main branch.

## Reporting

Each team reviews its flaky-test list and test duration at the end of every sprint.

## Questions

Ask a Staff Engineer on your team, or post in #prod-quality.

title: Q2 2026 Delivery Retrospective

title: Working with the SRE Guild and TPM: FAQ
heading: Working with the SRE Guild and TPM: FAQ
text:
# Working with the SRE Guild and TPM: FAQ

**What is the SRE guild?**
A group of SREs from across the three engineering orgs. They share reliability practice and look after policies that apply to every team. Each product team has SREs who work with it day to day.

**When should I involve an SRE?**
When you are designing something that must stay up, when you want help setting alerts, when you are preparing for a large launch, or when an incident needs more hands.

**What is a TPM?**
A Technical Program Manager. TPMs coordinate work that crosses team boundaries, keep planning calendars and run dependency reviews.

**When should I involve a TPM?**
When your work depends on another team, when a deadline slips and others are affected, or when you are not sure which team owns something.

**How do I reach them?**
Post in #prod-tpm or #sre-guild-help. For urgent production problems, page the on-call engineer instead.

**Can the SRE guild or TPMs approve my change?**
They advise and help you find the right people. Approvals follow the policy that applies to your change.

**Where do I learn more?**
The Engineering Handbook describes cross-org functions, and the Product Engineering Team Directory lists contacts.

title: TechSync Company Overview
heading: Who we are
text:
# TechSync Company Overview

## Who we are

TechSync Software builds developer-platform products for businesses that ship software at scale. The company was founded in 2014 as TechSync Labs and is headquartered in Denver, Colorado. Since 2020 we have been remote-first: most of our roughly 2,400 employees work from home offices across many time zones, and about 900 of them are in engineering.

title: TechSync Company Overview
heading: A short history
text:
## A short history

TechSync Labs started with a small team and a single idea: release automation should not require a dedicated team to babysit it. That idea became **TechSync Ship**, which launched in 2016. In 2019 we moved our own infrastructure from virtual machines to Kubernetes, a move that shaped how we build everything since. Remote-first working began in 2020, and in 2021 we launched **TechSync Ledger** for usage metering and billing. In 2022 engineering was reorganized into three organizations, which is the structure we use today. In 2023 we completed SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001 audits. **TechSync Insight**, our logs, metrics, traces and search product, followed in 2024.

title: TechSync Company Overview
heading: What we sell
text:
## What we sell

- **TechSync Ship**: CI/CD and release orchestration.
- **TechSync Ledger**: usage metering and billing.
- **TechSync Insight**: logs, metrics, traces and search.
- **TechSync Console**: the shared web console that fronts our products.
- **TechSync Mobile**: alerts and deploy approvals on your phone.

Customers buy on one of three tiers: Free, Team and Enterprise. Each product has its own overview page in the company library.

title: TechSync Company Overview
heading: How we run
text:
## How we run

TechSync runs on AWS. Our primary region is us-east-1, disaster recovery lives in us-west-2, and customer data that must stay in the European Union is hosted in eu-west-1. Our day-to-day stack includes Kubernetes on EKS, Go, Python, TypeScript, Kotlin and Swift, PostgreSQL, Kafka, OpenSearch and Terraform. We collaborate through GitHub Enterprise, Jira, Confluence and Slack, and we use PagerDuty for paging.

title: TechSync Company Overview
heading: Leadership
text:
## Leadership

Helen Park is our CEO and Arjun Mehta is our CTO. Tamsin Reid is the CISO, Lucia Romano is the CFO, and Jerome Baptiste is the VP People. The three engineering VPs report to the CTO; see the Engineering Handbook for the organization layout.

## Where to go next

New employees should read the Engineering Handbook and the product overview for whichever product they will work on. Questions about this page can go to the Technical Writing team.

title: Product Overview: TechSync Ship
heading: What Ship does
text:
# Product Overview: TechSync Ship

**Launched:** 2016
**Category:** CI/CD and release orchestration

## What Ship does

TechSync Ship takes code from a pull request to production. It builds artifacts, runs the checks a team has configured, and orchestrates the rollout across environments (dev, staging and prod). Release managers and engineers use Ship to see, in one place, what is deployed where and what is waiting to go out.

title: Product Overview: TechSync Ship
heading: Core capabilities
text:
## Core capabilities

- **Build and test orchestration.** Pipelines are defined as code alongside the service they build.
- **Environment promotion.** A release moves from dev to staging to prod with explicit gates between each step.
- **Release orchestration.** Coordinate several services shipping together, with ordering and dependency awareness.
- **Audit trail.** Every promotion, approval and rollback is recorded and searchable.
- **Approvals.** Reviewers can approve a promotion from the web console or from TechSync Mobile.

title: Product Overview: TechSync Ship
heading: Who uses it
text:
## Who uses it

Ship is used by platform and application teams at customers of every tier. Internally, TechSync's own engineering teams use Ship for their services, so the product gets daily exercise from the people who build it.

## How Ship fits with other products

- **Console** is where most people interact with Ship day to day.
- **Mobile** carries deploy approval requests to the people who need to act on them.
- **Insight** can receive deploy events so that a release marker appears on a graph next to the metrics it may have affected.

## Getting help

Customers can reach support through their normal support channel. Internal engineers can find the Ship team through the Product Engineering directory. For roadmap questions, talk to your account team.

title: Product Overview: TechSync Ledger
heading: The problem Ledger solves
text:
# Product Overview: TechSync Ledger

**Launched:** 2021
**Category:** Usage metering and billing

## The problem Ledger solves

Companies that charge by usage need two things to be right: an accurate count of what each customer used, and a bill that reflects that count. Ledger does both. It collects usage events, aggregates them into billable quantities, and turns those quantities into invoices.

title: Product Overview: TechSync Ledger
heading: Components
text:
## Components

Ledger is made of two main pieces:

1. **Meterflow** receives usage events from your products, de-duplicates them, and rolls them up into hourly and daily totals.
2. **Ledger Core** is the billing engine. It applies pricing plans, computes charges, and produces invoices for each billing period.

title: Product Overview: TechSync Ledger
heading: Highlights
text:
## Highlights

- Flexible pricing plans, including tiered, volume and flat-plus-overage models.
- Usage exports so that customers can reconcile their own records.
- Plan changes that take effect mid-period, with prorated charges calculated for you.
- A public API for reading usage and billing data.
- Alerts for billing events can be delivered through other TechSync products.

title: Product Overview: TechSync Ledger
heading: Audience
text:
## Audience

Finance teams use Ledger to understand revenue; product teams use it to understand consumption; engineering teams integrate it into the services that emit usage. Ledger is offered on all three customer tiers, with limits that vary by tier as described in your order form.

## Further reading

The Ledger public API documentation, the Meterflow export FAQ, and the Product Engineering directory are the best next stops.

title: Product Overview: TechSync Insight
heading: Summary
text:
# Product Overview: TechSync Insight

**Category:** Logs, metrics, traces and search
**General availability:** June 2024

## Summary

TechSync Insight brings the signals you need to run software into one place: logs, metrics and traces, with a search experience that lets you move between them without changing tools. Insight was introduced in 2023 as a beta program and reached general availability in June 2024.

title: Product Overview: TechSync Insight
heading: Availability by tier
text:
## Availability by tier

Insight is generally available to **all customer tiers: Free, Team and Enterprise**. Usage limits differ by tier and are set out in each customer's order form. During the beta in 2023, access was limited to Enterprise customers; that restriction ended when the product reached general availability in June 2024.

title: Product Overview: TechSync Insight
heading: What you can do
text:
## What you can do

- **Search.** Query logs and events with a purpose-built query language and save the searches you use often.
- **Metrics.** Build dashboards from metrics emitted by your services and compare them against deploys.
- **Traces.** Follow a request across services to find where time is spent.
- **Alerting.** Define alert conditions and route notifications to your on-call tools.

title: Product Overview: TechSync Insight
heading: How it is built
text:
## How it is built

Under the hood, Insight uses a query engine (Quarry) and an indexer (Sieve) maintained by the Search team, with OpenSearch as one of the storage back ends. Customers do not need to know these names to use the product, but they help when you read internal documentation.

title: Product Overview: TechSync Insight
heading: Related products
text:
## Related products

- **Ship** can send release markers to Insight.
- **Console** hosts the Insight user interface alongside our other products.
- **Mobile** can surface Insight alerts as push notifications.

## Questions

Customers should contact support. Internal readers can find the owning team in the Product Engineering directory.

title: Product Overview: TechSync Console
heading: One front door
text:
# Product Overview: TechSync Console

## One front door

TechSync Console is the shared web console for TechSync products. Rather than learning a different interface for every product, customers sign in once and find Ship pipelines, Ledger usage and billing views, and Insight dashboards under the same roof.

title: Product Overview: TechSync Console
heading: What you will find in Console
text:

- **Dashboards.** Build and share views that combine information from more than one product.

Console is built on **Prism**, our design system. Prism supplies the components, color tokens and accessibility patterns used across TechSync web interfaces, which is why different products feel consistent even though different teams build them.

Everyone who uses a TechSync product uses Console, from an engineer checking a deploy to a finance analyst downloading a usage report. It is available to customers on the Free, Team and Enterprise tiers.

Console works in current versions of the major desktop browsers. Detailed browser guidance is kept by the team that builds Console, and customers can find it in the help center.

title: Product Overview: TechSync Mobile

text:
# Product Overview: TechSync Mobile

TechSync Mobile puts the two things you most often need away from your desk, alerts and deploy approvals, on your phone.

title: Engineering Handbook: Working Agreements
heading: Engineering Handbook: Working Agreements
text:
# Engineering Handbook: Working Agreements

*Part 1 of the Engineering Handbook. Part 2 covers organizations and roles.*

When roughly 900 engineers work remote-first, habits matter more than meetings. This page collects the working agreements most teams share. Teams add their own on top, but start here.

title: Engineering Handbook: Working Agreements
heading: Write it down
text:
## Write it down

If a decision affects other people, put it in writing: a Confluence page, a Jira ticket, or a pull request description. Chat is for conversation, not for records. When you decide something in a call, post the outcome afterward, with names, so that someone joining next quarter can find it.

title: Engineering Handbook: Working Agreements
heading: Planning cadence
text:
## Planning cadence

- Teams plan in quarterly cycles and refine in two-week sprints.
- Each sprint ends with a short written update on what shipped and what did not.
- Technical Program Management supports planning for work that spans teams.

## Communication norms

- **Default to async.** Assume the reader is in a different time zone and may reply tomorrow.
- **Use threads.** Keep Slack channels readable by replying in threads.
- **Name an owner.** Every action item has one person's name next to it.
- **Mark urgency honestly.** Urgent means someone should drop what they are doing. Most things are not.

title: Engineering Handbook: Working Agreements
heading: Meetings
text:
## Meetings

Meetings need an agenda and a note-taker. If there is no agenda a day before, cancel it or turn it into a document. Rotating the note-taker role spreads the load.

## Documentation habits

Every service should have a README that answers: what is this, who owns it, how do I run it, and where do I ask for help. Technical Writing publishes templates; use them, and ask for a review when a document will be read by people outside your team.

title: Engineering Handbook: Working Agreements
heading: Learning and growth
text:
## Learning and growth

Engineers are encouraged to spend time on learning, internal talks, and mentoring. Managers should ask about growth in every one-on-one, not only at review time.

## Looking after each other

Take your time off. Hand work over clearly when you leave for a break. If you see a colleague stretched thin, say something, to them or to their manager.

title: Engineering Handbook: Orgs, Roles and Cross-Org Functions

text:

title: Customer SLA
heading: TechSync Customer Service Level Agreement
text:
# TechSync Customer Service Level Agreement

**Owner:** CTO office
**Effective:** January 2026

## 1. Purpose

This document states the availability commitment TechSync makes to customers for its hosted products. It applies to every customer, and the commitment depends on the customer's tier.

title: Customer SLA
heading: 2. Availability commitment
text:
## 2. Availability commitment

| Customer tier | Monthly availability commitment |
|---|---|
| Enterprise | 99.95% |
| Team | 99.9% |
| Free | 99.9% |

The Enterprise commitment of 99.95% took effect in January 2026. The Team and Free commitments remain at 99.9%.

title: Customer SLA
heading: 3. How availability is measured
text:
## 3. How availability is measured

Availability is measured per calendar month. It is the percentage of minutes in the month during which the hosted service was able to respond successfully to requests, measured from TechSync's monitoring at the edge of our network.

As a rough guide to scale, a 99.9% month allows about 43 minutes of unavailability, and a 99.95% month allows about 21 minutes.

title: Customer SLA
heading: 4. What does not count as downtime
text:
## 4. What does not count as downtime

- Scheduled maintenance announced to customers in advance.
- Unavailability caused by the customer's own configuration, network or systems.
- Events outside TechSync's reasonable control, such as widespread internet outages.

title: Customer SLA
heading: 5. Reporting and credits
text:
## 5. Reporting and credits

Customers who believe the commitment was missed should open a support request within the period stated in their order form. TechSync will review the monitoring data and, where the commitment was missed, apply the remedy described in the order form.

title: Customer SLA
heading: 6. Status information
text:
## 6. Status information

Current and historical status is published on the TechSync status page. Incident updates follow the customer-facing communication template used by Product Engineering.

## 7. Questions

Questions about this document go to the CTO office. Questions about a specific contract go to your account team.

title: ADR Policy
heading: Architecture Decision Record (ADR) Policy
text:
# Architecture Decision Record (ADR) Policy

**Owner:** Architecture Review Board (chaired by the CTO)

## 1. Why we write ADRs

Architectural choices outlive the people who make them. An Architecture Decision Record captures what was decided, why, and what else was considered, so that the next team does not have to rediscover it.

title: ADR Policy
heading: 2. When an ADR is required
text:
## 2. When an ADR is required

**An ADR is required whenever a change affects more than one team.**

"Affects" means that another team must change its code or configuration, relies on behavior that will change, or carries operational responsibility that changes as a result of the decision.

title: ADR Policy
heading: 3. What an ADR contains
text:
## 3. What an ADR contains

Every ADR includes:

1. **Title and ID.** A short title and a sequential identifier.
2. **Context.** The situation and constraints.
3. **Decision.** What was chosen, in one or two clear sentences.
4. **Alternatives.** Other options considered, and why they were not chosen.
5. **Consequences.** What gets easier, what gets harder, and who is affected.
6. **Affected teams.** Each team named, with a contact.

title: ADR Policy
heading: 4. Statuses
text:
## 4. Statuses

- **Proposed:** open for comment.
- **Accepted:** approved by the Architecture Review Board.
- **Rejected:** reviewed and declined, kept for the record.
- **Deprecated:** no longer in effect, with a pointer to what replaced it.

title: ADR Policy
heading: 5. Review
text:
## 5. Review

The author submits the ADR to the Architecture Review Board. The Board reviews proposals on its regular cadence and may ask the author to involve affected teams before it decides. An ADR takes effect only once it is marked Accepted.

title: ADR Policy
heading: 6. Storage
text:
## 6. Storage

Accepted ADRs are stored in the shared Confluence space for architecture records. Authors link the ADR from related pull requests and design documents.

## 7. Questions

Contact the Architecture Review Board through its Slack channel, or see the ADR Review Process FAQ.

title: ADR Review Process FAQ
heading: ADR Review Process FAQ
text:
# ADR Review Process FAQ

Answers to the questions the Architecture Review Board hears most often. For the policy itself, see the ADR Policy.

**Who reviews ADRs?**
The Architecture Review Board. The CTO chairs it, and members come from across the three engineering orgs.

**How do I submit one?**
Write the ADR using the template in the architecture Confluence space, set its status to Proposed, and post the link in the Board's Slack channel. A Board member will acknowledge it and tell you which review session to expect.

**How long does review take?**
It depends on how many teams are involved and how complete the draft is. Drafts that list affected teams and name a contact for each tend to move faster.

**Do I need approval from the teams I name?**
You should talk to them before you submit. The Board will usually ask whether affected teams have seen the draft, so having their comments in the document saves a round trip.

**What does the Board look for?**
A clear decision statement, real alternatives, honest consequences, and a list of who is affected. Length is not a goal; a one-page ADR is fine.

**Can I change an ADR after it is accepted?**
Small corrections such as typos and links are fine. If the decision itself changes, write a new ADR and link it to the old one so the history stays intact.

**What if I am not sure whether my change needs an ADR?**
Read the ADR Policy. If it is still unclear, ask in the Board's Slack channel.

**Where do I find existing ADRs?**
In the architecture records space in Confluence. Search by keyword or by team name.

**Who do I contact with other questions?**
Post in the Board's Slack channel, or ask your TPM.

title: Service Tiering Policy
heading: 1. Purpose
text:
# Service Tiering Policy

**Owner:** CTO office

## 1. Purpose

Not every service matters equally when something goes wrong. Tiering gives us a shared vocabulary for how critical a service is, so that other policies can set expectations by tier instead of naming services one at a time.

title: Service Tiering Policy
heading: 2. The tiers
text:
## 2. The tiers

| Tier | Definition |
|---|---|
| Tier 0 | Core platform |
| Tier 1 | Customer-facing |
| Tier 2 | Internal |
| Tier 3 | Experimental |

- **Tier 0** covers the platform that other services depend on to run at all.
- **Tier 1** covers services that customers use directly.
- **Tier 2** covers services used only by TechSync employees and internal tooling.
- **Tier 3** covers prototypes and experiments that are not relied on by customers or by other services.

title: Service Tiering Policy
heading: 3. Reference assignments
text:
## 3. Reference assignments

Some assignments are fixed here so that every team uses the same answer:

- **Keystone** (SSO and IAM) is **Tier 0**.
- **Kestrel** (the internal Kubernetes platform) is **Tier 0**.
- **Console** (the shared web console) is **Tier 1**.

The full assignment for every system is kept in the service catalog, which teams update through the CTO office.

title: Service Tiering Policy
heading: 4. How a tier is assigned
text:
## 4. How a tier is assigned

1. The owning team proposes a tier using the definitions above.
2. The CTO office reviews the proposal against the definitions.
3. The agreed tier is recorded in the service catalog.

A tier is a property of the service, not of the team that owns it. If a service gains customers or other services come to depend on it, the owning team should ask for a review.

title: Service Tiering Policy
heading: 5. How other policies use tiers
text:
## 5. How other policies use tiers

Policies for code review, on-call, disaster recovery and similar topics refer to tiers. Read those documents for the details; this policy only defines what the tiers mean.

## 6. Changing a tier

Request a change through the CTO office with a short written rationale. Tier changes take effect once the service catalog is updated.

## 7. Review

The CTO office reviews this policy once a year.

title: Reservoir Table Layout and Partitioning Runbook
heading: Purpose
text:
# Reservoir Table Layout and Partitioning Runbook

**Owner:** Data Platform (DATA) | **Audience:** engineers who create, read, or repair Reservoir tables

## Purpose

This runbook describes how tables are laid out in Reservoir, our data lake, and how to create, inspect, and repair partitions. Reservoir stores tables as Parquet files on S3 in us-east-1, with table metadata kept in the Reservoir catalog.

title: Reservoir Table Layout and Partitioning Runbook
heading: Partitioning standard
text:
## Partitioning standard

Every Reservoir table is partitioned **daily by event date**. The partition value is derived from the event timestamp carried in the record itself, converted to UTC, and written as `dt=YYYY-MM-DD` in the object path:

```
s3://reservoir-prod/<domain>/<table>/dt=2026-07-14/part-0000.parquet
```

Consequences you should plan for:

- A record that arrives late is written to the partition of the day it happened, not the day it arrived. Partitions for the most recent 7 days therefore remain open for rewrite.
- Queries that filter on `dt` are pruned to the matching partitions. Always include a `dt` range in ad hoc queries through Quarry.
- Each record also carries an `_ingested_at` column, populated by the ingestion job. It exists for audit and debugging.

title: Reservoir Table Layout and Partitioning Runbook
heading: Creating a new table
text:
## Creating a new table

1. Register the dataset (see the Dataset Onboarding FAQ) and pick a domain prefix.
2. Define the schema in the Reservoir catalog, naming the event timestamp column that drives `dt`.
3. Apply the Terraform module for the table so bucket policy and catalog entries are created together.
4. Run the smoke-load job against a one-day sample and confirm that one `dt=` folder appears for each distinct event date in the sample.

title: Reservoir Table Layout and Partitioning Runbook
heading: Compaction
text:
## Compaction

A nightly compaction job runs at 02:00 UTC and merges small files inside each open partition into files of roughly 256 MB. Do not run manual compaction on a partition while the nightly job is active; check the job status page first.

title: Reservoir Table Layout and Partitioning Runbook
heading: Repairing a partition
text:
## Repairing a partition

If a partition is missing or contains duplicates:

1. Pause the downstream Streamline consumer group that feeds the table.
2. Move the damaged `dt=` folder to the `_quarantine/` prefix. Do not delete it until the repair is verified.
3. Re-run the batch job for that event date only.
4. Compare row counts against the Streamline topic offsets for the same date window.
5. Resume the consumer group and note the repair in the DATA on-call log.

## Escalation

Questions about layout go to the DATA channel in Slack. Anything affecting more than one domain should go to the Tech Lead before changes are made.

title: Reservoir Dataset Archive Guide
heading: The two tiers
text:
# Reservoir Dataset Archive Guide

How dataset archiving works in Reservoir, what it costs you, and how to get data back.

## The two tiers

Every dataset in Reservoir passes through two storage tiers:

1. **Hot (90 days).** The dataset's partitions sit in the active tier, with full query performance in Quarry.
2. **Archive (12 months).** After 90 days the partitions are moved to compressed archive storage. They are no longer visible in Quarry until restored.

After the 12 months in archive, the data is deleted by the lifecycle job.

title: Reservoir Dataset Archive Guide
heading: What this means for your queries
text:
## What this means for your queries

- Queries over a range older than 90 days will return empty results for that range unless you request a restore first.
- Dashboards that look back further than 90 days should be rebuilt from aggregates stored in a separate table.
- Training jobs that need older data should plan a restore a day ahead.

title: Reservoir Dataset Archive Guide
heading: Restoring archived data
text:
## Restoring archived data

1. Open a ticket in the DATA queue with the dataset name, date range, and reason.
2. DATA checks the classification of the dataset. Confidential data needs the data owner's approval.
3. The restore lands in a scratch prefix, typically within a few hours.
4. Scratch restores are deleted after 7 days.

title: Reservoir Dataset Archive Guide
heading: Costs
text:
## Costs

Archive storage is considerably cheaper than hot storage. Restores are metered per terabyte and appear on your team's cost report.

## FAQ

**Can I keep a dataset hot longer?** Not through this guide. Talk to your engineering manager about the business need.

**Does the archive clock restart on restore?** No. Restores are temporary copies.

**Who can approve a restore?** The DATA on-call engineer, with the data owner's agreement where required.

title: Streamline Topic Naming Conventions
heading: Streamline Topic Naming Conventions
text:
# Streamline Topic Naming Conventions

Streamline is TechSync's Kafka-based event bus. Consistent topic names make ownership obvious and tooling simple. This standard applies to every new topic; existing topics are renamed only when they are rebuilt.

title: Streamline Topic Naming Conventions
heading: 1. Format
text:
## 1. Format

```
<domain>.<entity>.<event>.v<version>
```

Examples: `billing.invoice.finalized.v2`, `search.index.updated.v1`.

Rules:
- Lowercase letters, digits, and hyphens inside a segment; dots between segments.
- Domain is the owning product area, not a team name.
- Event is a past-tense verb (`created`, `updated`, `finalized`).
- Version increments only on a breaking schema change.

title: Streamline Topic Naming Conventions
heading: 2. Special suffixes
text:
## 2. Special suffixes

| Suffix | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `.dlq` | Dead-letter topic for failed messages |
| `.retry` | Retry topic with delayed redelivery |
| `.compacted` | Topic using key compaction |

title: Streamline Topic Naming Conventions
heading: 3. Ownership tags
text:
## 3. Ownership tags

Every topic carries three tags in the Streamline catalog:

- `owner_team`: the team code, for example `PAY`
- `oncall_channel`: the Slack channel for issues
- `data_class`: the classification label recorded in the catalog

title: Streamline Topic Naming Conventions
heading: 4. Keys
text:
## 4. Keys

Choose a key that keeps related events together, for example the account ID. Do not use random keys unless ordering is irrelevant, and document the choice in the catalog entry.

## 5. Requesting a topic

1. Open a request in the DATA queue.
2. Provide the name, owner, expected volume, key, and schema.
3. DATA reviews within two business days and creates the topic through Terraform.

## 6. Anti-patterns

- Team names in topic names, which break when teams are reorganized.
- Environment names in topic names; use separate clusters per environment instead.
- Reusing a topic for unrelated events.

title: Streamline Consumer Lag Troubleshooting
heading: 1. Confirm the symptom
text:
# Streamline Consumer Lag Troubleshooting

Use this runbook when a Lookout alert reports consumer lag on a Streamline topic, or when a team reports that events are arriving late.

## 1. Confirm the symptom

1. Open the Streamline lag dashboard and select the consumer group.
2. Note the current lag and whether it is growing, flat, or shrinking.
3. Check the time the lag started, and compare against recent deploys of the consuming service.

A flat or shrinking lag means the consumer is catching up; keep watching but do not intervene.

title: Streamline Consumer Lag Troubleshooting
heading: 2. Decide the cause
text:
## 2. Decide the cause

| Pattern | Likely cause |
|---|---|
| Lag grows steadily on one consumer group only | Slow or stuck consumer |
| Lag grows on many groups at once | Broker or network issue |
| Lag jumps after a deploy | New code is slower or failing |
| Lag spikes then recovers daily | A batch job or traffic peak |

title: Streamline Consumer Lag Troubleshooting
heading: 3. Slow or stuck consumer
text:
## 3. Slow or stuck consumer

1. Look at the consuming service's logs for exceptions, repeated retries, or long processing times.
2. Check pod restarts in Kestrel.
3. If one instance is stuck, delete that pod and let Kestrel reschedule it.
4. If all instances are slow, scale the deployment up by about 50 percent and watch the dashboard.
5. If a poison message is repeatedly failing, send it to the topic's `.dlq` and move on.

title: Streamline Consumer Lag Troubleshooting
heading: 4. Broker or network issue
text:
## 4. Broker or network issue

1. Check the broker health panel for under-replicated topics or leader elections.
2. Check the Meridian Mesh dashboard for elevated errors between the consumers and brokers.
3. Page the DATA on-call through Lookout if broker health is degraded. Do not restart brokers yourself.

title: Streamline Consumer Lag Troubleshooting
heading: 5. After a deploy
text:
## 5. After a deploy

Roll the consumer back first, then investigate. A rollback is cheap and restores flow while you diagnose.

## 6. Closing out

- Confirm lag has returned to normal for 30 minutes.
- Post a summary in the DATA channel.
- If a poison message was found, open a ticket for the producing team.

title: Reservoir Batch Ingestion Job Runbook
heading: Reservoir Batch Ingestion Job Runbook
text:
# Reservoir Batch Ingestion Job Runbook

How batch ingestion jobs are scheduled, how they retry, and what to do when they fail. Event streams are covered in the Streamline guides; this runbook is only for scheduled batch jobs that load data into Reservoir.

title: Reservoir Batch Ingestion Job Runbook
heading: Job anatomy
text:
## Job anatomy

Each job is a container image run on Kestrel by the scheduler. A job has a source, a transformation, a target table, and a schedule. Jobs are defined in the `reservoir-jobs` repo and deployed through Gatekeeper CI.

```yaml
job: payments-ledger-sync
schedule: "0 * * * *"
source: postgres://ledger-replica/transactions
target: payments.transactions
timeout: 45m
retries: 3
```

title: Reservoir Batch Ingestion Job Runbook
heading: Scheduling
text:
## Scheduling

- Most jobs run hourly; heavy jobs run overnight.
- Do not schedule more than five heavy jobs at the same time. The scheduler dashboard shows current load.
- Jobs must be idempotent: running twice must produce the same result.

title: Reservoir Batch Ingestion Job Runbook
heading: Retries
text:
## Retries

The scheduler retries a failed job with exponential backoff: 2, 4, and then 8 minutes. After the final retry, the job is marked Failed and a Lookout alert goes to the owning team's channel.

title: Reservoir Batch Ingestion Job Runbook
heading: When a job fails
text:
## When a job fails

1. Open the job's page in the scheduler and read the last log lines.
2. Classify the failure:
   - **Source unavailable:** wait for the source to recover, then run the job manually.
   - **Schema mismatch:** coordinate with the source owner; do not change the target table without the DATA team's review.
   - **Timeout:** check source volume; raise the timeout only if the increase is justified in the ticket.
   - **Out of memory:** raise the memory request in the job file and redeploy.
3. Re-run with `reservoir job run <name> --once` after the fix.
4. Confirm the target table has the expected row count with a Quarry query.

title: Reservoir Batch Ingestion Job Runbook
heading: Ownership
text:
## Ownership

Every job has an owner team in its definition. Orphaned jobs are reported monthly and disabled if no owner claims them.

## Change process

Changes go through a pull request reviewed by someone on DATA. Schedule changes for heavy jobs need the Tech Lead's approval.

title: Streamline Schema Registry Guide
heading: Why schemas
text:
# Streamline Schema Registry Guide

Every message on Streamline has a schema registered in the schema registry. This guide explains how to register a schema, how to change it safely, and what the compatibility checks mean.

## Why schemas

Producers and consumers are developed by different teams. A registered schema gives consumers something to code against, and the registry blocks changes that would break them.

title: Streamline Schema Registry Guide
heading: Registering a schema
text:
## Registering a schema

1. Write the Avro schema in your service repo under `schemas/`.
2. Open a pull request. CI registers the schema in a test registry and runs the compatibility check.
3. After merge, the deploy pipeline registers it in the production registry.

title: Streamline Schema Registry Guide
heading: Compatibility mode
text:
## Compatibility mode

All subjects use **backward compatibility**: consumers using the new schema can read data written with the previous schema.

| Change | Allowed? |
|---|---|
| Add an optional field with a default | Yes |
| Remove an optional field | Yes |
| Add a required field without a default | No |
| Rename a field | No |
| Change a field's type | No |

title: Streamline Schema Registry Guide
heading: Breaking changes
text:
## Breaking changes

When you must break compatibility, create a new topic version (for example `.v2`) and run both for a migration period. Tell consumers in the DSEC channel before you start.

## Common errors

- **Incompatible schema:** you added a required field. Give it a default.
- **Subject not found:** the topic name does not match the registered subject.
- **Unknown magic byte:** the producer is not using the registry serializer.

## Tips

Add a `doc` string to every field. Prefer enums with an `UNKNOWN` default for values that may grow. Never reuse a field name for a different meaning.

title: Reservoir Dataset Onboarding FAQ
heading: Reservoir Dataset Onboarding FAQ
text:
# Reservoir Dataset Onboarding FAQ

**What is a dataset?**
A table registered in the Reservoir catalog with a named owner team. Unregistered files are not supported.

**How do I register one?**
Open a request in the DATA queue with the dataset name, owner team, description, and the schema. DATA reviews within two business days.

**Who should be the owner?**
A team, not a person. The owner answers questions and keeps the schema and checks current.

**What do I need before I load data?**
A schema, a source, a job definition in the `reservoir-jobs` repo, and the required data quality checks described in the Data Quality Checks Standard.

**Which domain prefix should I use?**
Choose the product area the data belongs to, such as `payments` or `search`. If none fits, ask in the DATA channel.

**Do I need to tag the dataset?**
Yes. Datasets carry `owner_team`, `service`, and `classification` tags. Untagged datasets are flagged in the monthly cost report.

**How do I read the data?**
Through Quarry. Ask for read access in the Keystone request portal; group names follow the naming standard.

**Can I share a dataset with another team?**
Yes. The owner approves access requests. For questions about how sensitive the data is, see the company data classification standard.

**What if the upstream schema changes?**
Tell the DATA channel before the change. Jobs fail on schema mismatch, and we would rather plan the migration than fix it at night.

**Who do I ask for help?**
The DATA channel, or the intake queue for anything that needs work.

title: Streamline Capacity Planning Notes
heading: Streamline Capacity Planning Notes (DRAFT)
text:
# Streamline Capacity Planning Notes (DRAFT)

**Status: draft, open for comments.** Numbers are estimates and need validation against production metrics before use.

## Goal

Decide how many Streamline brokers and how much disk we need for the next twelve months, and when to add capacity, so that we do not scramble when a large product team launches a new feed.

title: Streamline Capacity Planning Notes
heading: Current state
text:
## Current state

- Three Kafka clusters: dev, staging, and prod. This document concerns prod, in us-east-1.
- Throughput has grown steadily over the last year, with peaks at the start of each business day in North America.
- Brokers run on Kestrel with local SSD-backed volumes.
- Producers are mostly product services, with Ledger Core's Meterflow feed as the largest.

title: Streamline Capacity Planning Notes
heading: Sizing approach
text:
## Sizing approach

We size on three constraints, and the tightest one wins:

1. **Network throughput:** peak inbound plus replication traffic per broker must stay under about 60 percent of the instance limit.
2. **Disk:** projected storage after replication must stay under about 70 percent of volume capacity.
3. **Request handling:** broker CPU should stay under about 50 percent at peak to leave room for failures and rebalances.

title: Streamline Capacity Planning Notes
heading: Method
text:
## Method

1. Take peak hourly inbound volume from the last quarter.
2. Multiply by a growth factor. We propose 1.6 for the next twelve months, based on last year's trend plus known launches.
3. Multiply by the replication factor of three to estimate total broker traffic and storage.
4. Divide by per-broker limits and add one broker of headroom so that a single failure does not exceed limits.

title: Streamline Capacity Planning Notes
heading: Early estimate
text:
## Early estimate

With the proposed growth factor, we expect the current broker count to meet network and CPU limits until about the second quarter of next year, with disk the first constraint to tighten. Disk expansion is cheaper than adding brokers, so the first step is larger volumes.

title: Streamline Capacity Planning Notes
heading: Triggers for action
text:
## Triggers for action

| Signal | Action |
|---|---|
| Disk above 65 percent on any broker for a week | Plan a volume expansion |
| Network above 55 percent at peak for two weeks | Plan an additional broker |
| Any under-replicated topic during peak | Investigate immediately |

title: Streamline Capacity Planning Notes
heading: Risks
text:
## Risks

- Large launches that were not planned in advance.
- A noisy producer that sends far more than its estimate.
- Rebalancing storms when adding brokers.

## Open questions

1. Is a growth factor of 1.6 reasonable?
2. Should we ask product teams for forecasts each quarter?
3. Is it worth moving the largest feed to a dedicated cluster?

Please comment in the draft or in the DATA channel.

title: Streamline Kafka Upgrade Playbook
heading: 1. When to upgrade
text:
# Streamline Kafka Upgrade Playbook

Rolling-upgrade procedure for the Streamline Kafka clusters. Follow it in order. Do not improvise steps in prod.

## 1. When to upgrade

Upgrade for security fixes, bug fixes we need, or when a version nears end of support. Plan upgrades on Tuesday through Thursday, with a second SRE available. Upgrade dev first, then staging, then prod, leaving at least one week between environments unless a security fix requires otherwise.

title: Streamline Kafka Upgrade Playbook
heading: 2. Pre-checks
text:
## 2. Pre-checks

- [ ] Release notes read; breaking changes noted
- [ ] All topics fully in sync (no under-replicated topics)
- [ ] No partition reassignments in progress
- [ ] Consumer lag normal on the main groups
- [ ] Recent broker backup of configuration
- [ ] Rollback plan reviewed
- [ ] Announcement posted in the DATA and DSEC channels

title: Streamline Kafka Upgrade Playbook
heading: 3. Upgrade procedure (per broker)
text:
## 3. Upgrade procedure (per broker)

1. Pick the broker that is not the active controller.
2. Verify health: all topics in sync before you start.
3. Set the broker to a controlled shutdown.
4. Upgrade the broker image through Terraform and let Kestrel restart it.
5. Wait for the broker to rejoin and for every topic to be in sync again.
6. Check the broker's error rate and latency for 10 minutes.
7. Continue to the next broker. Upgrade the controller last.

Do not upgrade more than one broker at a time.

title: Streamline Kafka Upgrade Playbook
heading: 4. Protocol version
text:
## 4. Protocol version

Keep the inter-broker protocol version on the old setting until every broker is upgraded and a day has passed without issue. Then raise it in a separate change.

## 5. Rollback

Before the protocol version is raised:

1. Stop the upgrade.
2. Roll the upgraded brokers back to the previous image one at a time, checking sync status after each.
3. Post what happened in the DATA channel.

After the protocol version is raised, rollback is not supported. Call the Tech Lead.

title: Streamline Kafka Upgrade Playbook
heading: 6. Verification
text:
## 6. Verification

- Producers and consumers report no errors.
- Lag on main consumer groups returns to baseline.
- The schema registry is reachable.

## 7. Post-upgrade

Update the cluster inventory, close the ticket, and note any surprises in the playbook.

## 8. Contacts

DATA on-call through Lookout; DATA Tech Lead for rollback decisions.

title: Reservoir Cost Reports Guide
heading: Where the numbers come from
text:
# Reservoir Cost Reports Guide

Reservoir costs money, and every team that uses it should be able to see its share. This guide explains how to read the cost dashboards and what to do when a number surprises you.

## Where the numbers come from

Costs are pulled daily from the AWS bill and from the Kestrel usage meter, then attributed to teams using the `owner_team` tag on buckets, jobs, and query workloads. Untagged resources land in an "unattributed" line, which we chase every month.

title: Reservoir Cost Reports Guide
heading: Dashboards
text:
## Dashboards

| Dashboard | What it shows |
|---|---|
| Overview | Total Reservoir spend by month |
| By team | Spend per owning team, split into storage, compute, and transfer |
| Top tables | The 20 most expensive tables |
| Queries | Quarry query cost by team and user |

title: Reservoir Cost Reports Guide
heading: Reading the "By team" view
text:
## Reading the "By team" view

- **Storage** grows with data volume. A steady upward slope is normal.
- **Compute** follows jobs and queries. Spikes usually line up with a backfill or a heavy report.
- **Transfer** should be small. A large value often means cross-region reads.

title: Reservoir Cost Reports Guide
heading: When a number surprises you
text:
## When a number surprises you

1. Open the Top tables view and sort by change over the last month.
2. Check whether a new job or backfill started recently.
3. Look at the Queries view for expensive query patterns, such as full scans of large tables.
4. If nothing explains it, ask in the DATA channel with a link to the dashboard.

title: Reservoir Cost Reports Guide
heading: Reducing cost
text:
## Reducing cost

- Filter on the table's date column in queries to avoid reading everything.
- Remove tables nobody reads; the Top tables view lists last access.
- Schedule heavy jobs overnight.
- Right-size job memory and timeouts.

## Monthly review

Each month DATA posts a summary with the biggest movers and any unattributed cost. Team leads are expected to reply to items that concern them.

title: Data Quality Checks Standard
heading: 1. Why
text:
# Data Quality Checks Standard

**Owner:** Data Platform | **Applies to:** every dataset that other teams consume from Reservoir

## 1. Why

A dataset that is late, empty, or wrong costs every consumer time. Checks catch the problem at the source.

title: Data Quality Checks Standard
heading: 2. Required checks
text:
## 2. Required checks

Every consumed dataset must have these checks, defined in its job file:

| Check | What it verifies |
|---|---|
| Freshness | The dataset has been updated within its freshness target |
| Volume | Row counts are within an expected range compared with recent history |
| Nulls | Key columns have no unexpected nulls |
| Uniqueness | Declared keys are unique |
| Schema | Columns and types match the registered schema |

title: Data Quality Checks Standard
heading: 3. Thresholds
text:
## 3. Thresholds

Each dataset declares its own thresholds in the job file. Defaults: volume within 30 percent of the trailing median; freshness target set to the job's schedule plus a tolerance of one hour.

## 4. Failures

- A failed check marks the run as failed and sends a Lookout alert to the dataset owner.
- Downstream jobs wait until the check passes.
- Owners must acknowledge and explain a failure in the alert ticket.

title: Data Quality Checks Standard
heading: 5. Skipping or changing a check
text:
## 5. Skipping or changing a check

A check may only be disabled temporarily with a ticket stating the reason, owner, and date by which it will return. Permanent changes to thresholds are made in the job file through a pull request.

## 6. Reporting

DATA publishes a monthly quality report listing failed checks by dataset and owner.

## 7. Adding checks

Teams are encouraged to add checks beyond the required set, for example distribution checks on key metrics. Share useful ones in the DATA channel.
