title: ADR: Streamline Topic Compaction
heading: Context
text:
# ADR: Streamline Topic Compaction

**Status:** Accepted | **Date:** August 2025 | **Deciders:** Data Platform tech lead, engineering manager, two staff engineers

## Context

Several consumers rebuild their local state by reading a topic from the beginning. For entity-state topics, such as account profile changes, most of that data is overwritten by later messages for the same key, so rebuilds are slow and wasteful. We needed a way to let consumers rebuild quickly without a separate snapshot store.

title: ADR: Streamline Topic Compaction
heading: Decision
text:
## Decision

Entity-state topics will use Kafka log compaction, keeping the latest message per key. Topics that hold compacted state carry the `.compacted` suffix and a mandatory key.

## Consequences

**Positive**
- Rebuilds read only the latest state, which is much faster.
- No separate snapshot system to run.
- Consistent with the naming standard.

**Negative**
- Consumers lose intermediate history on compacted topics. Anyone who needs history must use a separate event topic.
- Deleting a record requires a tombstone message.
- Compaction adds some broker load.

title: ADR: Streamline Topic Compaction
heading: Alternatives considered
text:
## Alternatives considered

1. **Snapshots in PostgreSQL.** Familiar, but adds an extra system and a consistency problem between the snapshot and the topic.
2. **Rebuild from full history.** Simple, but slow, and gets slower as volume grows.
3. **Snapshots in Reservoir.** Adds latency and couples event consumers to the lake.

## Follow-up

- Update the topic request form to ask whether the topic is state or event.
- Add a lint check that rejects `.compacted` topics without keys.

title: Data Platform Glossary
heading: Data Platform Glossary
text:
# Data Platform Glossary

Terms you will hear on the Data Platform team and in conversations with people who use our systems.

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Backfill** | Loading or recomputing historical data after a change or a gap |
| **Batch job** | A scheduled job that loads data into Reservoir in groups rather than one event at a time |
| **Catalog** | The Reservoir registry of datasets, schemas, owners, and tags |
| **Compaction** | Rewriting data to remove stale or small pieces; applies to Kafka topics and to files in Reservoir |
| **Consumer group** | A set of consumers that share the work of reading a Streamline topic |
| **Dataset** | A table registered in the Reservoir catalog with an owner |
| **DLQ** | Dead-letter queue: a topic that holds messages that failed processing |
| **Idempotent** | An operation that gives the same result when run more than once |
| **Lag** | How far a consumer is behind the newest message in a topic |
| **Producer** | A service that writes messages to Streamline |
| **Quarry** | The query engine used to read Reservoir tables |
| **Reservoir** | The TechSync data lake |
| **Schema registry** | The service that stores message schemas and checks compatibility |
| **Streamline** | The Kafka-based event bus |
| **Tombstone** | A message with an empty value used to delete a key from a compacted topic |
| **Topic** | A named stream of messages in Streamline |

heading: Abbreviations
text:
## Abbreviations

- **ADR:** architecture decision record
- **DATA:** the Data Platform team code
- **DSEC:** Data & Security, our org
- **SRE:** site reliability engineer

## Suggest a term

title: FeatureHub Ingestion and Offline Store Guide
heading: FeatureHub Ingestion and Offline Store Guide
text:
# FeatureHub Ingestion and Offline Store Guide

FeatureHub is the feature store used by teams that train and serve models on Foundry. This guide explains how the offline store is populated from Reservoir and how to configure a new feature view. It is written for ML engineers who are new to FeatureHub.

title: FeatureHub Ingestion and Offline Store Guide
heading: How the offline store is built
text:
## How the offline store is built

The offline store is materialized from Reservoir tables by a scheduled FeatureHub job. The job does not copy raw data; it reads the Parquet files of the source table and computes the feature columns you define.

Reservoir tables are **partitioned daily by ingest date**, which means each `dt=` folder holds the rows that were loaded on that day. This matters for two reasons:

1. A daily materialization run reads one new partition, which is the one for the day just ingested.
2. Rows with an old event timestamp can appear in a recent partition, so point-in-time joins must always use the event timestamp column, never the partition value.

To catch stragglers the job re-reads a lookback window of the 3 most recent partitions on every run. You can raise the window per feature view if your source is known to deliver late.

title: FeatureHub Ingestion and Offline Store Guide
heading: Configuring a feature view
text:
## Configuring a feature view

A feature view is a YAML file in the FeatureHub repo:

```yaml
name: payments_txn_counts
source:
  reservoir_table: payments.transactions
  timestamp_column: event_ts
entities: [account_id]
lookback_partitions: 3
features:
  - name: txn_count_1h
    agg: count
    window: 1h
```

Steps:

1. Open a PR adding the YAML under `views/`.
2. CI validates the schema and checks that the source table exists in the Reservoir catalog.
3. After merge, the next scheduled run creates the offline table. First runs of large views can take several hours.

title: FeatureHub Ingestion and Offline Store Guide
heading: Backfills
text:
## Backfills

To backfill history for a new view, set `backfill_from` to the first date you need and submit the backfill job. Because partitions follow ingest date, a backfill for a given calendar day reads the partitions loaded on that day; if you need events that happened on that day but arrived later, widen the range forward by a few days.

title: FeatureHub Ingestion and Offline Store Guide
heading: Common problems
text:
## Common problems

- **Features look empty for yesterday:** the upstream load may not have finished. Check the ingestion job status before re-running.
- **Duplicate entity rows:** confirm the view declares every entity key.
- **Slow materialization:** reduce `lookback_partitions` or narrow the column list.

Questions go to the ML Infrastructure channel.

title: Foundry Research Sandbox Security Review Exception
heading: Summary
text:
# Foundry Research Sandbox Security Review Exception

**Approved by:** Rachel Goldstein, VP Data & Security | **Approved:** March 2026 | **Owner:** ML Infrastructure (MLI)

## Summary

Researchers using Foundry need to spin up exploratory environments quickly. The full threat-model security review that DSEC requires before a service reaches staging is too heavy for short-lived experimentation. This document grants a narrow exception: the three **named Foundry research sandboxes** listed below complete a **lightweight checklist** instead of the full review.

title: Foundry Research Sandbox Security Review Exception
heading: Sandboxes covered
text:
## Sandboxes covered

| Sandbox | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `rs-nlp-explore` | Language model experiments |
| `rs-vision-explore` | Image model experiments |
| `rs-tabular-explore` | Tabular modeling experiments |

No other Foundry environment is covered. In particular, Foundry production serving, FeatureHub, and any service that is customer-facing are **not** covered and follow the full review.

title: Foundry Research Sandbox Security Review Exception
heading: Conditions
text:
## Conditions

All of the following must remain true. If any stops being true, the exception ends for that sandbox immediately.

- The sandbox is not customer-facing.
- It contains **no production data**. Only public or synthetic datasets may be loaded.
- It has no network path to production systems, enforced by a deny-egress network policy in Kestrel.
- It holds no production credentials from Vaultline.
- It never runs in the staging or prod environments.

title: Foundry Research Sandbox Security Review Exception
heading: Lightweight checklist
text:
## Lightweight checklist

The sandbox owner completes this once at creation and again at each six-month review:

1. Name a human owner and backup.
2. Attest that no production data is present, with the dataset inventory attached.
3. Confirm the deny-egress policy is applied.
4. Confirm no production secrets are mounted.
5. Confirm Keystone group access is limited to named researchers.
6. A MLI Security Engineer countersigns in the checklist ticket.

title: Foundry Research Sandbox Security Review Exception
heading: Promotion
text:
## Promotion

A sandbox workload that is to be promoted toward staging or prod, or that is given any production data, leaves this exception and must pass the full DSEC review first.

## Contact

Questions go to the MLI Engineering Manager or the MLI Security Engineer on rotation.

title: Foundry Operator Onboarding Guide
heading: Foundry Operator Onboarding Guide
text:
# Foundry Operator Onboarding Guide

Welcome to ML Infrastructure! This guide gets you from "new laptop" to "can run and watch a training job on Foundry" in about three days. Don't try to do it all on day one; we've ordered things so that the slow parts (access requests) start first.

title: Foundry Operator Onboarding Guide
heading: Day 1: access
text:
## Day 1: access

Open the access requests below in the Keystone request portal. Most are approved within a business day.

- Group `foundry-users`: submit jobs and read dashboards
- Group `foundry-operators`: manage clusters and quotas (needed for on-call)
- Group `featurehub-readers`: read the feature store
- Your team's GPU quota pool (ask your manager which one)

While you wait, install the tooling:

```
brew install foundry-cli kubectl
foundry login
```

title: Foundry Operator Onboarding Guide
heading: Day 1: multi-factor setup for production
text:
## Day 1: multi-factor setup for production

Foundry operators need production access for on-call work. Production sign-ins use multi-factor authentication, and **an authenticator app is acceptable** for this. Install one on your phone, register it in Keystone under Security settings, and save your recovery codes in the company password manager. Test it by signing in to the production Foundry console. If it prompts you for a six-digit code and lets you in, you are done.

title: Foundry Operator Onboarding Guide
heading: Day 2: your first job
text:
## Day 2: your first job

1. Clone the `ml-examples` repo.
2. Pick the `hello-gpu` example. It trains a tiny model for about two minutes.
3. Submit it with `foundry job submit -f hello-gpu.yaml`.
4. Watch it with `foundry job logs <id> --follow`.
5. Find the run in the experiment tracker and confirm that metrics were logged.

If the job stays Pending, check that your quota pool has free GPUs. The FAQ explains how to ask for more.

title: Foundry Operator Onboarding Guide
heading: Day 3: serving and rollouts
text:
## Day 3: serving and rollouts

Read the Model Serving Rollout Guide and shadow an on-call engineer during a canary rollout. You will not be asked to run one alone until your second month.

## On-call readiness checklist

- [ ] In the `foundry-operators` group
- [ ] Production sign-in tested
- [ ] Added to the paging rota
- [ ] Read the training job and serving runbooks
- [ ] Introduced yourself in the ML Infrastructure channel

## Who to ask

Your onboarding buddy first, then the ML Infrastructure Tech Lead. There are no silly questions here; our best runbooks started as someone's confused message.

title: Foundry Training Job Submission Runbook
heading: Prerequisites
text:
# Foundry Training Job Submission Runbook

Terse reference for submitting and monitoring training jobs.

## Prerequisites

- Member of `foundry-users`
- GPU quota pool assigned to your team
- Job spec in version control

## Job spec

```yaml
name: ranker-v7
image: registry.internal/ml/ranker:2026.04
resources:
  gpu: a100
  count: 4
  memory: 128Gi
checkpoint:
  interval: 20m
  path: s3://foundry-ckpt/ranker-v7/
retries: 2
tags:
  cost_center: search
```

title: Foundry Training Job Submission Runbook
heading: Submit
text:
## Submit

1. Validate: `foundry job validate -f job.yaml`
2. Submit: `foundry job submit -f job.yaml`
3. Record the job ID in your experiment notes.

## Monitor

- Logs: `foundry job logs <id> --follow`
- Metrics: the Foundry job dashboard, GPU utilization panel
- Alerts: Lookout pages the owning team only for jobs tagged `critical`

title: Foundry Training Job Submission Runbook
heading: Common failures
text:
## Common failures

| Symptom | Likely cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Pending for more than 30 min | Quota exhausted | Check pool usage; wait or ask MLI for temporary quota |
| OOMKilled | Memory request too low | Raise `memory`, or reduce batch size |
| ImagePullBackOff | Wrong tag or registry permission | Check image tag and service account |
| Loss becomes NaN | Learning rate or data issue | Resume from the last checkpoint with a lower rate |

title: Foundry Training Job Submission Runbook
heading: Resuming from a checkpoint
text:
## Resuming from a checkpoint

Add `resume_from: <checkpoint path>` to the spec and resubmit. Foundry will pick up at the last saved step.

## Cancelling

`foundry job cancel <id>`. Cancel jobs you no longer need; idle GPUs still cost money.

## Escalation

ML Infrastructure channel during business hours; the MLI on-call through Lookout for cluster-wide failures.

title: Foundry Model Serving Rollout Guide
heading: Before you start
text:
# Foundry Model Serving Rollout Guide

This runbook covers rolling out a new model version to a Foundry serving endpoint with a canary.

## Before you start

- The model is registered in the model registry with a version tag.
- Offline evaluation results are attached to the release ticket.
- You are in the `foundry-operators` group.
- A second engineer is available as a reviewer.

title: Foundry Model Serving Rollout Guide
heading: Rollout stages
text:
## Rollout stages

| Stage | Traffic | Minimum soak |
|---|---|---|
| Shadow | 0% (mirrored) | 30 minutes |
| Canary | 5% | 1 hour |
| Partial | 25% | 1 hour |
| Full | 100% | n/a |

title: Foundry Model Serving Rollout Guide
heading: Steps
text:
## Steps

1. Create the rollout: `foundry serve rollout create --model <name>:<version> --stage shadow`.
2. Compare shadow results with the current version in the comparison dashboard. Latency and error rate must be within the thresholds in the release ticket.
3. Advance to canary. Watch p95 latency, error rate, and the business metric named in the ticket.
4. Advance to partial, and then to full, only after each soak period has passed with metrics inside their thresholds.
5. Record each stage change in the release ticket.

title: Foundry Model Serving Rollout Guide
heading: Automatic rollback
text:
## Automatic rollback

Foundry rolls back automatically if the error rate exceeds the threshold for 5 consecutive minutes during canary or partial. A Lookout alert is sent to the owning team.

## Manual rollback

`foundry serve rollout rollback --to <previous-version>` returns all traffic to the previous version within about a minute. Use it without hesitation if anything looks wrong. A rollback can be repeated safely.

## After rollout

- Keep the previous version deployed and warm for 24 hours.
- Update the model card with the new version and evaluation results.
- Close the release ticket.

title: FeatureHub Feature Definition Standard
heading: 1. Naming
text:
# FeatureHub Feature Definition Standard

**Owner:** ML Infrastructure | **Applies to:** every feature view registered in FeatureHub

## 1. Naming

- Feature names use `snake_case`, are descriptive, and include the unit or window: `txn_count_1h`, `avg_basket_value_30d`.
- View names are named for the entity and subject area: `account_payments`, `user_search_activity`.
- Do not include team names or version numbers in names. Versions are tracked by FeatureHub.

title: FeatureHub Feature Definition Standard
heading: 2. Ownership
text:
## 2. Ownership

1. Every feature view has an owner team, recorded in its YAML.
2. Every feature has a description that explains what it measures in one sentence.
3. Owners are responsible for answering questions and for removal when the feature is no longer used.

title: FeatureHub Feature Definition Standard
heading: 3. Types and nulls
text:
## 3. Types and nulls

- Declare the data type of every feature.
- State how nulls are handled: `drop`, `zero`, or `default:<value>`.
- Never leave null handling implicit.

## 4. Documentation fields

| Field | Required |
|---|---|
| `description` | Yes |
| `owner_team` | Yes |
| `entities` | Yes |
| `freshness_target` | Yes |
| `notes` | No |

title: FeatureHub Feature Definition Standard
heading: 5. Deprecation
text:
## 5. Deprecation

Mark a feature `deprecated: true` and announce it in the ML Infrastructure channel. Remove it only after no consumer has read it for a full release cycle.

## 6. Review

Each new or changed view is reviewed by an MLI engineer who is not the author, following the company code review policy.

title: Foundry GPU Capacity FAQ
heading: Foundry GPU Capacity FAQ
text:
# Foundry GPU Capacity FAQ

**How do I get GPU quota?**
Each team has a quota pool. Ask your engineering manager which pool you belong to, then request access to it through the Keystone request portal.

**What if my team's pool is full?**
Check usage on the Foundry capacity dashboard. If other jobs are idle, ask the owner to release them. If the pool is genuinely too small, open a quota request.

**How do I request more quota?**
Open a ticket in the MLI queue with the GPU type, the count, how long you need it, and which project it supports. Requests are reviewed weekly.

**How long does it take?**
Temporary increases of a few days are often approved the same week. Permanent increases follow the annual budget cycle and need your VP's agreement.

**Which GPU types exist?**
Foundry offers a few GPU classes. Check the capacity dashboard for what is available today; availability changes with procurement.

**Can I run on spot capacity?**
Yes, for jobs that checkpoint regularly. Spot jobs can be interrupted, and Foundry will resume from the last checkpoint if you set `resume_from`.

**Why is my job Pending?**
Usually because the pool has no free GPUs of the type you requested. See the training job runbook for the other causes.

**Who pays?**
Costs are charged back to your team through the `cost_center` tag in the job spec.

**Where can I ask other questions?**
In the ML Infrastructure channel.

title: Model Registry Conventions
heading: 1. Model names
text:
# Model Registry Conventions

Rules for registering models and tracking versions in the Foundry model registry.

## 1. Model names

- Lowercase letters, digits, and hyphens: `search-ranker`, `fraud-scorer`.
- The name identifies the task, not the architecture.
- One name per production use case. Experimental variants use a `-exp` suffix.

title: Model Registry Conventions
heading: 2. Versions
text:
## 2. Versions

Use semantic versions: `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`.

- **MAJOR:** the input or output contract changes.
- **MINOR:** retrained on new data or with a new architecture, same contract.
- **PATCH:** configuration or packaging fix, no change to behavior.

title: Model Registry Conventions
heading: 3. Stages
text:
## 3. Stages

A registered version moves through stages: `dev`, `staging`, `prod`. Promotion to `prod` requires:

1. Offline evaluation results attached.
2. A model card.
3. A reviewer from outside the model's team.
4. A completed release ticket.

title: Model Registry Conventions
heading: 4. Required metadata
text:
## 4. Required metadata

| Field | Example |
|---|---|
| `owner_team` | `search` |
| `training_run` | link to the experiment |
| `feature_views` | FeatureHub views used |
| `metrics` | AUC, latency, and so on |
| `contact` | team channel |

title: Model Registry Conventions
heading: 5. Model cards
text:
## 5. Model cards

Every `prod` model has a card describing purpose, training data, known limitations, and evaluation. Update it with every MINOR or MAJOR version.

## 6. Retiring models

Mark the model `deprecated` and tell consumers. Remove it once nothing has called it for a full release cycle.

title: Foundry Experiment Tracking Guide
heading: The basics
text:
# Foundry Experiment Tracking Guide

Experiment tracking lets you answer "what did we run, with which settings, and what happened?" six months from now. This guide covers how to log runs from Foundry training jobs.

## The basics

Every training job is automatically linked to an experiment with the job name. Inside your training code, you can log parameters, metrics, and artifacts.

```python
from foundry import tracking

with tracking.run(experiment="search-ranker") as run:
    run.log_params({"lr": 0.001, "batch_size": 256})
    for step, loss in enumerate(train()):
        run.log_metric("loss", loss, step=step)
    run.log_artifact("model.pt")
```

title: Foundry Experiment Tracking Guide
heading: What to log
text:
## What to log

- **Parameters:** everything that affects the result, including the random seed.
- **Metrics:** training and validation metrics at regular intervals.
- **Data references:** the FeatureHub views and versions used.
- **Code version:** Foundry records the commit automatically; do not override it.
- **Artifacts:** the model file and any evaluation reports.

title: Foundry Experiment Tracking Guide
heading: Naming
text:
## Naming

Experiments are named for the task, such as `search-ranker`. Runs get an automatic ID; add a short human-friendly note with `run.set_note("larger batch")`.

## Comparing runs

In the tracking UI, select multiple runs and choose Compare to see parameters and metrics side by side. You can chart any metric against steps or time.

title: Foundry Experiment Tracking Guide
heading: Linking to the registry
text:
## Linking to the registry

When a run produces a model you want to keep, register it from the run page. The registry entry links back to the run, so reviewers can find the evidence.

## Tips

- Log early. A run that crashed at step 20 can still teach you something.
- Do not log large files as metrics; use artifacts.
- Tag runs that are part of a sweep with the same `sweep_id`.

title: ADR: Foundry Serving Autoscaling
heading: Context
text:
# ADR: Foundry Serving Autoscaling

**Status:** Accepted | **Date:** January 2026

## Context

Foundry serving endpoints previously scaled on CPU utilization. For GPU-backed models, CPU is a poor signal: an endpoint can be saturated on the GPU while CPU looks calm. Several endpoints were slow during traffic peaks and wasteful overnight.

title: ADR: Foundry Serving Autoscaling
heading: Decision
text:
## Decision

Serving endpoints will autoscale on **request concurrency per replica**, with GPU utilization as a secondary signal. The autoscaler runs on Kestrel.

Initial settings:

| Setting | Value |
|---|---|
| Minimum replicas | 2 |
| Target concurrency | per-model, set in the serving spec |
| Scale-up reaction | 1 minute |
| Scale-down delay | 10 minutes |

title: ADR: Foundry Serving Autoscaling
heading: Consequences
text:
## Consequences

- Better latency during spikes because replicas are added based on actual queueing.
- Lower idle cost because the scale-down delay is short.
- Model owners must set a realistic target concurrency from load tests; a wrong value causes flapping.
- Cold starts for large models remain slow, so a minimum of 2 replicas is kept for all production endpoints.

title: ADR: Foundry Serving Autoscaling
heading: Alternatives considered
text:
## Alternatives considered

1. **Keep CPU-based scaling.** Rejected for the reason above.
2. **Fixed replica counts.** Predictable but expensive.
3. **Scheduled scaling.** Good for known daily peaks but fails on unexpected traffic.

## Follow-up

- Add target concurrency to the serving spec template.
- Add a dashboard panel for queue depth per replica.
- Review the settings after one quarter of data.

title: FeatureHub Backfill Playbook
heading: FeatureHub Backfill Playbook (DRAFT)
text:
# FeatureHub Backfill Playbook (DRAFT)

**Status: draft, under review by the MLI Tech Lead.** Do not use for production backfills until it is approved.

## When you need a backfill

- You added a new feature to an existing feature view and need historical values.
- A bug in a feature definition was fixed and past values must be recomputed.
- A source table gap was filled and downstream features should be recalculated.

title: FeatureHub Backfill Playbook
heading: Before you start
text:
## Before you start

1. Confirm the feature view's YAML change is merged.
2. Pick the date range. Keep it as small as you can; large backfills compete with regular materialization for resources.
3. Estimate the cost with `featurehub backfill plan` and attach the output to the ticket.
4. Check the Foundry capacity dashboard to confirm there is room.

title: FeatureHub Backfill Playbook
heading: Procedure
text:
## Procedure

1. Submit the backfill: `featurehub backfill submit --view <name> --from <date> --to <date>`.
2. The job runs in chunks. Watch progress in the FeatureHub dashboard.
3. If a chunk fails, FeatureHub retries it twice. After that the job pauses; do not restart from the beginning. Use `featurehub backfill resume <id>`.
4. When the job finishes, run `featurehub backfill verify <id>`. It compares row counts and a sample of values against the expected computation.

title: FeatureHub Backfill Playbook
heading: Cutting over
text:
## Cutting over

Backfilled values are written to a shadow table. After verification:

1. Announce the cutover in the ML Infrastructure channel.
2. Run `featurehub backfill promote <id>`.
3. Watch dependent training jobs for one cycle.

title: FeatureHub Backfill Playbook
heading: Rollback
text:
## Rollback

`featurehub backfill revert <id>` restores the previous table. Keep the shadow table until at least one dependent job has trained successfully.

## Things that go wrong

- **Backfill is slow:** the range is too wide, or the pool is busy. Narrow the range.
- **Verification shows missing rows:** the source did not have data for that range; check with the source owner.
- **Dependent jobs behave differently:** a feature's definition changed along with the backfill. Review the YAML diff.

## Open items before approval

- Add expected runtimes by view size.
- Agree on the approval needed for large backfills.

title: Foundry Cost Allocation Guide
heading: How charges are calculated
text:
# Foundry Cost Allocation Guide

Foundry costs are charged back to the teams that cause them. This guide explains how allocation works, so that your team's bill is accurate and predictable.

## How charges are calculated

Costs fall into three buckets:

| Bucket | Driver | Allocated by |
|---|---|---|
| Training | GPU-hours consumed by jobs | `cost_center` tag on the job |
| Serving | Replica-hours of each endpoint | `cost_center` tag on the endpoint |
| Shared | Registry, tracking, dashboards | Split in proportion to the other two |

title: Foundry Cost Allocation Guide
heading: Tagging
text:
## Tagging

Every job spec and serving spec must contain a `cost_center` tag, using the codes published by Finance. Jobs without a tag are blocked at submission, so you will find out immediately rather than at the end of the month.

```yaml
tags:
  cost_center: search
  project: ranker-v7
```

title: Foundry Cost Allocation Guide
heading: Reports
text:
## Reports

Weekly and monthly reports are available in the Foundry cost dashboard. Each report lists spend by `cost_center`, by project, and by user.

## Common questions

- **Why is the shared bucket not zero?** It covers platform components that nobody can use alone.
- **Can I move spend to another cost center?** Only with the approval of both cost center owners, through a ticket.
- **What about idle GPUs?** They are charged to the reserving team. Cancel jobs you no longer need.
- **Do spot GPUs cost less?** Yes, and the report shows them separately.

## Disputes

If a charge looks wrong, open a ticket in the MLI queue with the job ID or endpoint name. The MLI engineering manager decides within a week.

title: ML Infrastructure Team Charter
heading: Mission
text:
# ML Infrastructure Team Charter

## Mission

ML Infrastructure (MLI) gives machine-learning practitioners at TechSync a reliable, efficient, and safe way to train, evaluate, and serve models. We want researchers to spend their time on models, not on clusters.

title: ML Infrastructure Team Charter
heading: Who we are
text:
## Who we are

MLI is one of four teams in Data & Security. Olivia Brandt is the engineering manager and Hassan Qureshi is the tech lead.

## What we own

- **Foundry:** ML training and serving platform
- **FeatureHub:** the feature store
- The model registry, experiment tracking, and GPU capacity

title: ML Infrastructure Team Charter
heading: What we do not own
text:
## What we do not own

- The data lake (Reservoir) or the event bus (Streamline); these belong to Data Platform.
- Identity and secrets for our systems; these belong to IT & Compliance and AppSec.
- The models themselves; model owners belong to the product teams that build them.

title: ML Infrastructure Team Charter
heading: Who we serve
text:
## Who we serve

Product teams in Product Engineering, search and billing teams using models, and researchers.

## Principles

1. **Self-service first.** If a task needs a ticket, we try to automate it.
2. **Safe rollouts.** Every production model change goes through a staged rollout.
3. **Cost visible.** Every GPU-hour is attributable to a team.
4. **Reproducible.** A run can be reconstructed from its recorded inputs.

title: ML Infrastructure Team Charter
heading: How we work
text:
## How we work

- Weekly sync, monthly retrospective, and shared quarterly planning with the rest of DSEC.
- Requests come through the DSEC intake queue.
- Operational issues are handled by the MLI on-call through Lookout.

Time from experiment to serving, GPU utilization, rollout failure rate, and satisfaction of our users measured in a twice-yearly survey.

title: Postmortem: Foundry Serving Latency Regression
heading: Postmortem: Foundry Serving Latency Regression
text:
# Postmortem: Foundry Serving Latency Regression

**Severity:** Sev2 | **Incident date:** 19 May 2026 | **Duration:** about 2 hours 40 minutes | **Authors:** MLI SRE

title: Postmortem: Foundry Serving Latency Regression
heading: Summary
text:
## Summary

After a model rollout on a customer-facing recommendation endpoint, p95 latency roughly doubled for several hours. No requests failed, so the automatic rollback did not trigger. The latency regression was found by a customer-facing team's alert, not by Foundry's own alerts.

title: Postmortem: Foundry Serving Latency Regression
heading: Impact
text:
## Impact

- p95 latency rose from about 120 ms to about 260 ms on the affected endpoint.
- Downstream pages that call the endpoint loaded visibly slower.
- No data loss, and no errors above baseline.

## Timeline (UTC)

| Time | Event |
|---|---|
| 14:05 | Rollout reaches the partial stage (25 percent). Metrics inside thresholds. |
| 14:50 | Rollout advances to full. |
| 15:20 | Latency begins to climb as traffic increases through the afternoon. |
| 16:10 | A downstream team's latency alert fires; they message the MLI channel. |
| 16:25 | MLI SRE opens an incident and starts investigating. |
| 16:55 | Autoscaler dashboards show replicas at the minimum while queue depth is high. |
| 17:10 | Manual scale-up applied; latency starts to fall. |
| 18:45 | Latency back to baseline. Rollout of the previous version prepared as a fallback but not needed. |

title: Postmortem: Foundry Serving Latency Regression
heading: Root cause
text:
## Root cause

The new model was larger and slower per request. The serving spec still carried the target concurrency of the old model, set far too high for the new one. The autoscaler therefore believed the replicas had capacity, and it did not add replicas as load rose.

title: Postmortem: Foundry Serving Latency Regression
heading: Contributing factors
text:
## Contributing factors

1. The rollout gates measured error rate and median latency, but not queue depth.
2. The partial stage soaked during a quiet period; the traffic peak came after full rollout.
3. No check compared the serving spec's target concurrency with the model's load test results.

title: Postmortem: Foundry Serving Latency Regression
heading: What went well
text:
## What went well

- The manual scale-up worked immediately.
- The downstream team reported clearly and quickly.

## What went poorly

- Foundry's own alerts did not catch a slow-but-healthy endpoint.
- The rollout guide did not require updating the concurrency target for a new model.

title: Postmortem: Foundry Serving Latency Regression
heading: Action items
text:
## Action items

| Action | Owner | Due |
|---|---|---|
| Add p95 latency and queue-depth thresholds to the automatic rollback | MLI SRE | June 2026 |
| Require target concurrency to be re-validated in the release ticket | MLI Tech Lead | June 2026 |
| Add a soak requirement that spans peak traffic for customer-facing endpoints | MLI SRE | July 2026 |
| Alert on high queue depth with minimum replicas | MLI SRE | June 2026 |

title: Sentinel Dependency Scanning Standard
heading: 1. Purpose
text:
# Sentinel Dependency Scanning Standard

**Owner:** AppSec (SEC) | **Applies to:** every repository hosted in GitHub Enterprise that builds a deployable artifact

## 1. Purpose

Sentinel is our code and dependency scanner. This standard defines when scans run and what a scan result is allowed to do to a change.

title: Sentinel Dependency Scanning Standard
heading: 2. Requirements
text:
## 2. Requirements

**2.1 Scan trigger.** Sentinel scans **run on every pull request**. The scan is a stage in the Gatekeeper CI pipeline, executed on Forge runners, and is added automatically to repositories created from Scaffold templates. Repositories not created from a template must add the `sentinel-scan` stage before their first production deploy.

**2.2 Merge gating.** A pull request **cannot be merged while it has an open Critical finding**. The merge check is enforced as a required status check in GitHub Enterprise and cannot be bypassed by repository admins.

**2.3 High and lower findings.** High findings do not block the merge. Sentinel opens a tracking ticket assigned to the owning team and posts a summary comment on the pull request. Medium and Low findings are reported in the weekly digest only.

**2.4 Scan scope.** Each scan covers direct and transitive dependencies resolved from lockfiles, container base images referenced by Dockerfiles, and first-party source files for the supported languages (Go, Python, TypeScript, Kotlin, Swift).

title: Sentinel Dependency Scanning Standard
heading: 3. Waivers and false positives
text:
## 3. Waivers and false positives

A finding believed to be a false positive is marked through the triage workflow described in the False Positive Triage FAQ. A SEC engineer must approve the suppression, and suppressions are recorded with an expiry date. Waivers for true findings are not available for Critical severity.

title: Sentinel Dependency Scanning Standard
heading: 4. Responsibilities
text:
## 4. Responsibilities

- Service owners keep the `sentinel-scan` stage enabled and respond to tickets.
- SEC maintains rule sets and the scan queue.
- DEVT maintains the Gatekeeper CI stage definitions.

## 5. Review

This standard is reviewed by the SEC tech lead and engineering manager each year.

title: AppSec Critical Vulnerability Remediation Runbook
heading: Why we hold ourselves to a tighter clock
text:
# AppSec Critical Vulnerability Remediation Runbook

**Owner:** AppSec (SEC) | **Covers:** services owned by SEC, which are Sentinel and Vaultline

## Why we hold ourselves to a tighter clock

Sentinel and Vaultline sit in the path of every pull request and every secret in the company. A Critical vulnerability in either is more urgent than the same finding elsewhere. So for SEC-owned services, **Critical findings must be fixed within 3 days** of confirmation.

title: AppSec Critical Vulnerability Remediation Runbook
heading: The 3-day clock
text:
## The 3-day clock

| Day | What must happen |
|---|---|
| Day 0 | Finding confirmed. Page the SEC on-call, open a Critical ticket, name an incident lead. |
| Day 1 | Fix approach agreed. Patch or mitigation in progress. Engineering manager informed. |
| Day 2 | Fix built and tested in staging. Peer review done. |
| Day 3 | Fix deployed to production and verified. Ticket closed with evidence. |

title: AppSec Critical Vulnerability Remediation Runbook
heading: Roles
text:
## Roles

- **Incident lead:** a Security Engineer who owns the ticket until it is closed.
- **Reviewer:** a second engineer who is not the author of the fix.
- **SEC Engineering Manager:** receives a daily summary and unblocks resources.

title: AppSec Critical Vulnerability Remediation Runbook
heading: If the fix is not ready
text:
## If the fix is not ready

If a fix cannot ship by Day 3, the incident lead must apply a mitigation (disable a feature, add a deny rule, rotate affected credentials) and notify the SEC Engineering Manager. A mitigation does not close the ticket; the permanent fix keeps its own tight deadline set by the SEC Tech Lead.

title: AppSec Critical Vulnerability Remediation Runbook
heading: Checklist for the incident lead
text:
## Checklist for the incident lead

- [ ] Ticket opened with severity evidence
- [ ] Scope assessed: which versions and environments
- [ ] Mitigation considered on Day 0
- [ ] Customer or internal communications drafted if data is at risk
- [ ] Verification steps recorded
- [ ] Retro note added to the SEC weekly sync agenda

## Tooling

Use Sentinel to confirm that the vulnerable version no longer appears in any build, and use Vaultline audit logs to check for abuse during the exposure window.

title: Vaultline Dynamic Secrets Runbook
heading: 1. What dynamic secrets are
text:
# Vaultline Dynamic Secrets Runbook

**Owner:** AppSec (SEC), which owns and operates Vaultline.

## 1. What dynamic secrets are

Vaultline can mint short-lived credentials on demand for databases, cloud roles, and internal services. A workload asks for a credential, receives it with a lease, and Vaultline revokes it automatically when the lease ends.

title: Vaultline Dynamic Secrets Runbook
heading: 2. Lease limits
text:
## 2. Lease limits

**Vaultline dynamic secrets have a maximum lease of 1 hour.**

| Setting | Value |
|---|---|
| Default lease | 15 minutes |
| Maximum lease | 1 hour |
| Renewal | Allowed until the 1-hour ceiling is reached |
| After the ceiling | Workload must request a new credential |

The maximum is enforced by Vaultline itself. A role configured with a longer value in Terraform is capped at 1 hour when credentials are issued, and the pipeline lint will fail the change.

title: Vaultline Dynamic Secrets Runbook
heading: 3. Requesting dynamic credentials
text:
## 3. Requesting dynamic credentials

1. Create a Vaultline role for the target engine through the policy-as-code repo.
2. Bind the role to the workload's Kestrel service account.
3. Have the workload call the credential endpoint at startup and again before the lease expires.
4. Log the lease ID with each request to make revocation and audit traceable.

title: Vaultline Dynamic Secrets Runbook
heading: 4. Troubleshooting
text:
## 4. Troubleshooting

- **Lease expired errors:** the workload held the credential longer than its lease. Add a renewal timer at about two-thirds of the lease.
- **Renewal denied:** the 1-hour ceiling was reached. Request a new credential instead of renewing.
- **Permission denied on request:** check the role binding and the namespace of the service account.
- **Credentials revoked early:** an operator may have revoked the lease; check the Vaultline audit log.

title: Vaultline Dynamic Secrets Runbook
heading: 5. Manual revocation
text:
## 5. Manual revocation

Security Engineers can revoke all leases for a role with `vaultline lease revoke -prefix <role>`. Announce in the SEC channel before running it in prod.

## 6. Escalation

Page the SEC on-call through Lookout for Vaultline unavailability.

title: Sentinel Rule Tuning Guide
heading: Sentinel Rule Tuning Guide
text:
# Sentinel Rule Tuning Guide

Sentinel ships with a default rule set, and AppSec adjusts it so that findings are useful and noise is low. This guide describes how we tune rules and how you can propose changes. It is written for Security Engineers, though service owners with an opinion about a noisy rule are welcome to contribute.

title: Sentinel Rule Tuning Guide
heading: Rule anatomy
text:
## Rule anatomy

A rule has an ID, a language or ecosystem, a pattern, a severity, and a message explaining the problem and how to fix it. Rules live in the `sentinel-rules` repository and are loaded by Sentinel on its next rule refresh.

title: Sentinel Rule Tuning Guide
heading: When to tune
text:
## When to tune

Tune a rule when at least one of the following is true:

- More than half of its findings are marked false positive in triage.
- The message does not tell the reader what to do.
- The severity does not match the real-world impact.
- It misses a class of issue found by a pen test or a bug bounty report.

title: Sentinel Rule Tuning Guide
heading: How to tune
text:
## How to tune

1. Gather evidence: link at least five findings that show the problem.
2. Draft the change in a branch of `sentinel-rules`.
3. Run the rule test suite. Each rule has positive and negative sample files.
4. Add a sample that reproduces the original problem.
5. Open a pull request and request review from a second Security Engineer.
6. After merge, watch the rule's finding volume for a week.

title: Sentinel Rule Tuning Guide
heading: Severity guidance
text:
## Severity guidance

| Severity | Typical meaning |
|---|---|
| Critical | Directly exploitable with high impact, such as remote code execution |
| High | Exploitable under realistic conditions, or leaks sensitive data |
| Medium | Needs unusual conditions or has limited impact |
| Low | Hygiene issue |

When in doubt, rate lower and revisit once a real exploit path is shown.

title: Sentinel Rule Tuning Guide
heading: Writing good messages
text:
## Writing good messages

Say what is wrong, why it matters, and the fix, in that order. Link to internal guidance if it exists.

## Retiring rules

A rule that has produced no true positives in a year may be retired. Record the decision in the rule's changelog.

title: Sentinel False Positive Triage FAQ
heading: Sentinel False Positive Triage FAQ
text:
# Sentinel False Positive Triage FAQ

**Q: Sentinel flagged something that is clearly not a problem. What now?**
Open the finding and choose **Mark as false positive**. Add a short reason. It goes to the SEC triage queue.

**Q: What makes a good reason?**
Say why the finding cannot be exploited in your context. "The vulnerable function is never called" is good. "Not an issue" is not.

**Q: Who decides?**
A Security Engineer on the triage rotation reviews each request. They may approve, ask for more detail, or reject.

**Q: How long does triage take?**
Usually within one business day.

**Q: What happens when it is approved?**
Sentinel suppresses the finding for that exact location and rule. The suppression has an expiry date, so it is rechecked later.

**Q: How long do suppressions last?**
Up to six months, depending on the reviewer's judgment. When one expires, the finding reappears and you can request it again with an updated reason.

**Q: Can I suppress a whole rule?**
No. Suppressions are per finding. If a rule is generally noisy, ask SEC to tune it instead.

**Q: What if I disagree with a rejection?**
Reply in the triage ticket with more evidence, or ask in the SEC channel. The SEC Tech Lead has the final say.

**Q: Does a suppression hide the finding from audit?**
No. Suppressions, reasons, and reviewers are retained in Sentinel's history.

title: Vaultline Secrets Engine Setup Guide
heading: Concepts in one minute
text:
# Vaultline Secrets Engine Setup Guide

This guide shows how to mount a secrets engine in Vaultline for a new team or service. It is aimed at engineers who have never done this before.

## Concepts in one minute

- **Secrets engine:** a plugin that stores or generates a type of secret.
- **Mount path:** where the engine lives, such as `kv/payments/`.
- **Policy:** a set of permissions bound to paths.
- **Auth method:** how a workload proves who it is. At TechSync, workloads authenticate with their Kestrel service account.

title: Vaultline Secrets Engine Setup Guide
heading: Choosing an engine
text:
## Choosing an engine

| Need | Engine |
|---|---|
| Static values such as API keys | KV (version 2) |
| Database access | Database engine |
| TLS certificates | PKI |
| Cloud permissions | AWS engine |

title: Vaultline Secrets Engine Setup Guide
heading: Setup steps
text:
## Setup steps

1. **Pick a path.** Use `<team>/<service>/`.
2. **Write the Terraform.** Add a mount and a policy file to the policy-as-code repo.
3. **Open a pull request.** A SEC engineer reviews paths and permissions.
4. **Apply.** After merge, the pipeline mounts the engine.
5. **Bind the auth role.** Link your service account's namespace to the policy.
6. **Test.** From a pod in dev, read a test value.

title: Vaultline Secrets Engine Setup Guide
heading: Policy basics
text:
## Policy basics

- Grant the minimum paths and capabilities the workload needs.
- Separate read and write policies.
- Use one policy per service, not per person.

## Audit

Vaultline logs every request to the audit log. Teams can export audit events through the audit export guide.

title: Vaultline Secrets Engine Setup Guide
heading: Common mistakes
text:
## Common mistakes

- Using the root path for application secrets.
- Sharing one policy across unrelated services.
- Copying a secret into an environment variable file.

## Help

SEC channel in Slack; for outages, page the SEC on-call.

title: Vaultline Audit Log Export Guide
heading: What an audit event contains
text:
# Vaultline Audit Log Export Guide

Vaultline records every request it receives. This guide explains how to get those audit events out of Vaultline and into places where teams can search them.

## What an audit event contains

Each event describes who made the request (the authenticated identity), what they asked for (the path and operation), when, and whether it succeeded. Secret values are never written to the audit log; values are hashed.

title: Vaultline Audit Log Export Guide
heading: How export works
text:
## How export works

1. Vaultline writes audit events to an audit device configured by SEC.
2. A shipper forwards events to a Streamline topic, `security.vaultline.audit.v1`.
3. A consumer indexes the events into OpenSearch, where the security dashboards read them.

You do not configure the audit device yourself; SEC manages it. You may request access to the dashboards or a filtered feed for your team.

title: Vaultline Audit Log Export Guide
heading: Requesting a feed for your team
text:
## Requesting a feed for your team

Teams that want to see access to their own secret paths can request a filtered view.

1. Open an intake request with the paths you own.
2. Name the Slack channel for any alerts.
3. SEC reviews and creates a filtered dashboard.

title: Vaultline Audit Log Export Guide
heading: Searching events
text:
## Searching events

In the OpenSearch dashboard, useful fields are:

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `auth.display_name` | Identity making the request |
| `request.path` | Secret path requested |
| `request.operation` | read, create, update, delete, list |
| `response.status` | Success or error |

Example question: "Who read anything under `kv/payments/` yesterday?" Filter on `request.path` and `request.operation`.

title: Vaultline Audit Log Export Guide
heading: Investigations
text:
## Investigations

For an investigation, SEC can join Vaultline events with Keystone sign-in events. Request this through a Security Engineer; do not export raw events to personal drives.

## Troubleshooting

- **Events missing:** check the shipper's status page; if it is unhealthy, page the SEC on-call.
- **Events delayed:** look at consumer lag on the audit topic.
- **Dashboard empty:** confirm your filter paths match the actual mount names.

title: Threat Modeling Workshop Guide
heading: Threat Modeling Workshop Guide
text:
# Threat Modeling Workshop Guide

A guide for engineers who want to run a threat modeling workshop with their team. The aim is to find the ways a system could be attacked or misused, early enough that it is cheap to design them away. You do not need to be a security expert. You need to know your system and be curious about how it could go wrong.

title: Threat Modeling Workshop Guide
heading: Who to invite
text:
## Who to invite

Four to eight people is ideal:

- The service's tech lead and one or two engineers who built it
- A Security Engineer from AppSec as co-facilitator
- Someone from a neighboring team that calls or depends on the service
- Optionally, a product representative who knows how customers use it

title: Threat Modeling Workshop Guide
heading: Before the workshop (about two days)
text:
## Before the workshop (about two days)

1. **Describe the system.** One page: what it does, who uses it, what data it holds.
2. **Draw a first data-flow diagram.** Boxes for components, arrows for data, dashed lines for trust boundaries. It does not need to be perfect.
3. **List assets.** What would hurt if it were stolen, changed, or unavailable?
4. **Share both documents** with the invitees a day before.

title: Threat Modeling Workshop Guide
heading: Running the session (90 minutes)
text:
## Running the session (90 minutes)

| Minutes | Activity |
|---|---|
| 0-10 | Walk through the diagram; correct mistakes |
| 10-20 | Agree on assets and trust boundaries |
| 20-60 | Go through each element and each boundary using STRIDE |
| 60-80 | Rate and group the threats |
| 80-90 | Assign actions and owners |

title: Threat Modeling Workshop Guide
heading: Using STRIDE
text:
### Using STRIDE

For each element, ask:

- **Spoofing:** can someone pretend to be this user or service?
- **Tampering:** can data be changed in transit or at rest?
- **Repudiation:** could someone deny an action, and could we prove otherwise?
- **Information disclosure:** where could data leak?
- **Denial of service:** how could this be made unavailable?
- **Elevation of privilege:** can someone gain access they should not have?

Write each threat as a sentence: "An attacker who can ... could ... which would ...". Avoid solutions in the first pass.

title: Threat Modeling Workshop Guide
heading: Rating threats
text:
## Rating threats

Use a simple scale of high, medium, low, based on likelihood and impact. Resist the temptation to debate precision. If the group is split, round up and move on.

## After the workshop

- Turn each high and medium threat into a Jira ticket with an owner.
- Update the diagram with what you learned.
- Store the diagram and threat list next to the service's design document.
- Revisit when the architecture changes in a meaningful way.

title: Threat Modeling Workshop Guide
heading: Facilitator tips
text:
## Facilitator tips

- Keep quiet people involved by asking for their view directly.
- Park solution debates; note them and move on.
- Celebrate finding things. A long threat list is a success, not a failure.

## Help

Ask in the SEC channel to find a co-facilitator.

title: Sentinel and Gatekeeper CI Integration
heading: Sentinel and Gatekeeper CI Integration
text:
# Sentinel and Gatekeeper CI Integration

How the `sentinel-scan` stage is wired into a Gatekeeper CI pipeline, and how to troubleshoot it. Read this if you are adding the stage to a repository that was not created from a Scaffold template, or if the stage misbehaves.

title: Sentinel and Gatekeeper CI Integration
heading: Pipeline overview
text:
## Pipeline overview

A repository's pipeline is defined in `pipeline.yaml`. Stages run on Forge runners in the order given. The Sentinel stage sits after the build and before the deploy stages.

```yaml
stages:
  - build
  - test
  - sentinel-scan
  - package
  - deploy-staging
  - deploy-prod
```

title: Sentinel and Gatekeeper CI Integration
heading: Adding the stage
text:
## Adding the stage

1. Add `sentinel-scan` to `pipeline.yaml` using the snippet from the Scaffold template.
2. Make sure the repository has lockfiles committed. The stage reads them to resolve dependencies.
3. Set the service's owner team in the `CODEOWNERS` file so findings are routed.
4. Run the pipeline in a branch and confirm the stage reports a result.

title: Sentinel and Gatekeeper CI Integration
heading: Reading the result
text:
## Reading the result

The stage outputs a summary with finding counts by severity and a link to the detailed report in Sentinel. The same summary is posted to the pull request.

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Likely cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Stage times out | Large dependency tree or a busy queue | Retry once; if it repeats, ask SEC about runner capacity |
| "No lockfile found" | Lockfile not committed | Commit the lockfile |
| Stage passes but no summary appears | Missing permissions for the comment bot | Check the repository's app installation |
| Unexpected finding on unchanged code | Rule update | Check the rule changelog in `sentinel-rules` |
| Stage cannot reach Sentinel | Network policy | Check egress to the Sentinel service in Meridian Mesh |

title: Sentinel and Gatekeeper CI Integration
heading: Runner and cache tips
text:
## Runner and cache tips

- Use the shared dependency cache to speed up resolution.
- Do not install your own scanner; use the stage.
- Pin the stage version only if you have a reason; the default tracks the latest tested version.

## Who owns what

- SEC owns the Sentinel service and the stage's behavior.
- DEVT owns Gatekeeper CI and the pipeline framework.
- Service owners own their pipeline file and the findings in it.

## Getting help

The SEC channel for scanner questions, and the DEVT channel for pipeline questions.

title: Pen Test Coordination Process
heading: 1. Planning
text:
# Pen Test Coordination Process

AppSec coordinates external penetration tests so that vendors get what they need and engineering teams are not surprised. This describes the steps.

## 1. Planning

- Each year, AppSec proposes the list of systems to test, based on risk, changes, and customer requirements.
- The CISO's office approves the list and budget.
- AppSec books vendors well in advance, since good testers have long lead times.

title: Pen Test Coordination Process
heading: 2. Scoping
text:
## 2. Scoping

For each engagement, a Security Engineer writes a scope document:

- Systems and environments in scope
- Systems explicitly out of scope
- Accounts and test data the vendor will use
- Testing windows
- Rules of engagement

Owning teams review the scope and confirm the testing window works for them.

title: Pen Test Coordination Process
heading: 3. Before testing
text:
## 3. Before testing

1. Sign the contract and any required non-disclosure agreements.
2. Create vendor accounts through Keystone with limited access.
3. Tell the owning teams, SRE, and the support team of the testing window.
4. Make sure the on-call engineer for the target system knows how to reach the AppSec coordinator.

title: Pen Test Coordination Process
heading: 4. During testing
text:
## 4. During testing

- The AppSec coordinator is the vendor's single point of contact.
- If the vendor finds something serious, they notify the coordinator immediately and do not wait for the final report.
- Testers must stay in scope. If the vendor needs to go beyond it, the coordinator and the owning team decide together.

title: Pen Test Coordination Process
heading: 5. After testing
text:
## 5. After testing

1. The vendor delivers a report.
2. AppSec reviews it, confirms findings, and rates severity.
3. Findings enter the normal vulnerability remediation process.
4. Owning teams get a briefing from AppSec and the vendor.
5. A summary goes to the CISO's office.

## 6. Retesting

Where appropriate, AppSec asks the vendor to retest fixed findings.

## 7. Contacts

AppSec coordinator on the engagement; the SEC channel for general questions.

title: ADR: Sentinel SBOM Generation
heading: Context
text:
# ADR: Sentinel SBOM Generation

**Status:** Accepted | **Date:** October 2025

## Context

Customers and auditors increasingly ask for a software bill of materials (SBOM) for what we ship. Today Sentinel works out the dependency list on demand, which is not repeatable: the same release can produce different results depending on when it is analyzed. We need an SBOM that is tied to a specific build.

title: ADR: Sentinel SBOM Generation
heading: Decision
text:
## Decision

An SBOM in CycloneDX format will be generated **at build time** in the Gatekeeper CI pipeline, on Forge runners, for every deployable artifact. The SBOM is stored next to the artifact in the artifact registry, and Sentinel reads it from there.

title: ADR: Sentinel SBOM Generation
heading: Consequences
text:
## Consequences

**Positive**
- Each release has an immutable, auditable SBOM.
- Customer SBOM requests can be answered from stored files.
- Sentinel can look up a released artifact's components without rebuilding the dependency tree.

**Negative**
- A small increase in build time, estimated at under a minute for typical services.
- Teams with unusual build steps may need custom configuration.
- SBOM storage grows with each build.

title: ADR: Sentinel SBOM Generation
heading: Alternatives considered
text:
## Alternatives considered

1. **Generate on request.** Cheap, but not reproducible.
2. **Third-party SBOM service.** Adds cost and a new vendor review.
3. **Generate in Sentinel only.** Couples SBOM content to Sentinel's analysis rather than the build.

## Rollout

SEC will add the build step to Scaffold templates first, then work with service owners to enable it in existing repositories.

title: AppSec Team Onboarding Guide
heading: AppSec Team Onboarding Guide
text:
# AppSec Team Onboarding Guide

Welcome to AppSec. We build the tools that scan our code and guard our secrets, and we help every engineering team build securely. You will find the work varied, and the team friendly. This guide is on top of the DSEC org onboarding guide, which covers company tools and general first-month tasks.

title: AppSec Team Onboarding Guide
heading: What we own
text:
## What we own

- **Sentinel:** code and dependency scanning
- **Vaultline:** secrets management

title: AppSec Team Onboarding Guide
heading: Your first two weeks
text:
## Your first two weeks

**Week 1**
- Meet your buddy and the tech lead, Amara Okafor.
- Get access to the `sentinel-rules` and Vaultline policy-as-code repositories.
- Read the Sentinel and Vaultline documents linked from the DSEC tooling landing page.
- Sit in on a triage session and a security review.

**Week 2**
- Take a ticket from the triage queue, with your buddy reviewing your work.
- Shadow the on-call engineer for a day.
- Co-facilitate a threat modeling session using the workshop guide.

title: AppSec Team Onboarding Guide
heading: How the team works
text:
## How the team works

- Weekly sync on Tuesdays; notes go in Confluence.
- A triage rotation handles false-positive requests. You join the rota after your first month.
- An on-call rotation covers Sentinel and Vaultline availability. You join after your first three months.
- Pull requests to our repositories are reviewed under the company code review policy.
- We write decisions down as ADRs when they affect other teams.

title: AppSec Team Onboarding Guide
heading: Habits we value
text:
## Habits we value

1. **Explain, do not just block.** A good finding message tells the engineer what to do next.
2. **Make the safe path the easy path.** If a control annoys people, find out why.
3. **Be honest about uncertainty.** "I do not know yet" is a good answer.
4. **Share what you learn.** Post interesting findings in the SEC channel.
