title: Postmortem: Sentinel Scan Queue Backlog
heading: Postmortem: Sentinel Scan Queue Backlog
text:
# Postmortem: Sentinel Scan Queue Backlog

**Severity:** Sev3 | **Incident date:** 10 June 2026 | **Duration:** about 5 hours | **Authors:** SEC SRE

title: Postmortem: Sentinel Scan Queue Backlog
heading: Summary
text:
## Summary

On the morning of 10 June, the Sentinel scan queue grew until scans were waiting more than an hour to start. Engineers saw pipelines sitting in the `sentinel-scan` stage. No scans were skipped and no findings were lost, but many teams waited for their pipelines to finish. The queue drained after we added runner capacity and paused a large scheduled job.

title: Postmortem: Sentinel Scan Queue Backlog
heading: Impact
text:
## Impact

- Pipelines in many repositories were delayed by up to about 70 minutes.
- Developer complaints in the DSEC and DEVT channels.
- No data loss, and no security impact.

## Timeline (Pacific time)

| Time | Event |
|---|---|
| 07:45 | Queue depth begins to rise as the Pacific workday starts |
| 08:30 | Median wait passes 20 minutes; no alert fires |
| 09:10 | A developer reports slow pipelines in the DEVT channel |
| 09:25 | SEC on-call opens an incident |
| 09:50 | Cause identified: a weekly rescan of all repositories began at the same time as the morning load |
| 10:05 | Weekly rescan paused; extra runners requested from Compute |
| 10:40 | Extra runners available; queue begins to drain |
| 12:55 | Queue back to normal |

title: Postmortem: Sentinel Scan Queue Backlog
heading: Root cause
text:
## Root cause

The weekly rescan of every repository against updated rules was scheduled at the start of the Pacific workday. It added many scan jobs in a short window, on top of normal pipeline traffic. Runner capacity for Sentinel was sized for the normal load and did not account for the rescan.

title: Postmortem: Sentinel Scan Queue Backlog
heading: Contributing factors
text:
## Contributing factors

1. No alert on queue wait time, only on service availability.
2. The rescan schedule had not been changed since the repository count was much smaller.
3. Requests for temporary runner capacity relied on a manual ticket to Compute.

title: Postmortem: Sentinel Scan Queue Backlog
heading: What went well
text:
## What went well

- A developer reported the problem quickly, with clear symptoms.
- Pausing the rescan was safe and fast.
- Compute approved extra runners within 35 minutes.

## What went poorly

- We learned about the problem from users.
- The rescan could not be rescheduled without editing its configuration by hand.

title: Postmortem: Sentinel Scan Queue Backlog
heading: Action items
text:
## Action items

| Action | Owner | Due |
|---|---|---|
| Add an alert on median queue wait time | SEC SRE | July 2026 |
| Move the weekly rescan to Sunday evening | SEC Tech Lead | June 2026 |
| Document how to request temporary runner capacity | SEC Tech Lead | July 2026 |
| Review Sentinel runner sizing against repository growth | SEC Engineering Manager | August 2026 |

title: Vaultline Policy-as-Code Conventions
heading: Vaultline Policy-as-Code Conventions (DRAFT)
text:
# Vaultline Policy-as-Code Conventions (DRAFT)

**Status: first draft for SEC review.** Comments welcome in the document or in the SEC channel.

## Purpose

Vaultline mounts, policies, and auth roles are managed with Terraform in the policy-as-code repository. These conventions keep that repository consistent as more teams add to it.

title: Vaultline Policy-as-Code Conventions
heading: Repository layout
text:
## Repository layout

```
vaultline-policy/
  mounts/
    <team>/<service>.tf
  policies/
    <team>/<service>-read.hcl
    <team>/<service>-write.hcl
  roles/
    <team>/<service>.tf
```

title: Vaultline Policy-as-Code Conventions
heading: Naming
text:
## Naming

- Mount paths follow `<team>/<service>/`.
- Policy files are named `<service>-read.hcl` and `<service>-write.hcl`.
- Auth roles use the service account name.

title: Vaultline Policy-as-Code Conventions
heading: Policy guidelines
text:
## Policy guidelines

1. Prefer explicit paths to wildcards.
2. Split read and write policies.
3. One policy per service.
4. Add a comment at the top of each policy file naming the owner team and the channel.

## Review

- Each pull request needs approval from a Security Engineer.
- The reviewer checks that paths match the team's namespace and that no policy grants access to another team's secrets.
- CI runs lint checks for naming, wildcard usage, and missing owner comments.

title: Vaultline Policy-as-Code Conventions
heading: Applying
text:
## Applying

Merge to main triggers the pipeline. Applies to dev and staging are automatic; prod applies need the SEC tech lead's approval.

## Open questions

1. Should wildcard use require an exception ticket?
2. Do we want separate repositories per org?
3. How should we handle emergency access changes?

title: Keystone Sev1 Paging and Escalation Procedure
heading: Service details
text:
# Keystone Sev1 Paging and Escalation Procedure

## Service details

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Service | Keystone (SSO and IAM) |
| Owner | IT & Compliance (ITC) |
| Tier | 0 |
| Paging | Lookout, routed to PagerDuty |
| Primary channel | #itc-incidents |

title: Keystone Sev1 Paging and Escalation Procedure
heading: When this applies
text:
## When this applies

Use this procedure when a Keystone alert is classified Sev1: SSO sign-in is failing for a large share of employees, token issuance is down, or directory sync has stopped and group changes are not applying.

title: Keystone Sev1 Paging and Escalation Procedure
heading: Acknowledgement target
text:
## Acknowledgement target

**Keystone Sev1 pages are acknowledged within 15 minutes, because IT systems are internal.** Our users are employees, not customers, and a short delay in acknowledgement does not affect customer-facing availability. The 15-minute clock starts when Lookout fires the page.

title: Keystone Sev1 Paging and Escalation Procedure
heading: Escalation ladder
text:
## Escalation ladder

| Elapsed since page | Action |
|---|---|
| 0 min | Page goes to the primary on-call |
| 15 min, no ack | Page auto-escalates to the secondary on-call |
| 30 min, no ack | ITC Engineering Manager is paged |
| 45 min, no ack | SRE guild duty lead is notified |

title: Keystone Sev1 Paging and Escalation Procedure
heading: First actions after acknowledging
text:
## First actions after acknowledging

1. Post in #itc-incidents: "Sev1 acknowledged, investigating".
2. Open an incident ticket and note the start time.
3. Check the Keystone status dashboard for token error rates and directory sync lag.
4. If sign-in is down, announce a workaround for break-glass accounts through the IT helpdesk page.
5. Post a status update every 30 minutes until mitigated.

title: Keystone Sev1 Paging and Escalation Procedure
heading: Handoff and closure
text:
## Handoff and closure

When mitigated, move the incident to monitoring, record the resolution time, and schedule the postmortem. Hand off to the next on-call with a summary in the channel.

## Common pitfalls

- Muting the PagerDuty app on a phone while travelling. Use the swap calendar instead.
- Acknowledging the page but not posting in the channel.
- Forgetting to update the incident ticket after mitigation.

title: Keystone SSO Configuration Guide
heading: 1. Session model
text:
# Keystone SSO Configuration Guide

Reference for engineers integrating an application with Keystone SSO. Keystone is a Tier 0 service owned by IT & Compliance.

## 1. Session model

Keystone issues a session when a user signs in. Applications receive an ID token and a refresh token bound to that session.

**Keystone SSO sessions last at most 8 hours.** Applications that use Keystone SSO, including Console, cannot extend a session past that limit. When the 8 hours end, the user is sent back through sign-in.

title: Keystone SSO Configuration Guide
heading: 2. Settings
text:
## 2. Settings

| Setting | Value | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `session_max_age` | 8h | Hard ceiling, not configurable per app |
| `session_idle_timeout` | 30m | May be lowered per app, never raised |
| `id_token_ttl` | 15m | Refreshed silently while the session lives |
| `refresh_token_ttl` | Bound to session | Cannot outlive `session_max_age` |

title: Keystone SSO Configuration Guide
heading: 3. What applications may and may not do
text:
## 3. What applications may and may not do

- You **may** shorten the effective session by setting a lower idle timeout or forcing re-authentication for sensitive actions.
- You **may not** issue your own long-lived application cookie that keeps a user signed in after the Keystone session has ended.
- You **may not** exchange an expired refresh token for a new session.

title: Keystone SSO Configuration Guide
heading: 4. Behaviour you should expect
text:
## 4. Behaviour you should expect

- A user who signs in at 08:00 will be asked to sign in again by 16:00 at the latest, even if active the whole time.
- Single sign-out revokes all application sessions for that user within about a minute.
- Console and other first-party apps follow the same ceiling. Support engineers cannot extend a session on a user's behalf.

title: Keystone SSO Configuration Guide
heading: 5. Integration checklist
text:
## 5. Integration checklist

1. Register the application in Keystone and select the OIDC flow.
2. Set redirect URIs for dev, staging, and prod separately.
3. Handle the expired-session redirect without losing unsaved work.
4. Test an idle timeout and a max-age expiry in staging.

## 6. Contact

ITC Keystone channel. For outages follow the Sev1 paging procedure.

title: Access Review Onboarding Guide for Compliance Analysts
heading: Access Review Onboarding Guide for Compliance Analysts
text:
# Access Review Onboarding Guide for Compliance Analysts

Welcome to IT & Compliance. Access reviews are one of the biggest recurring pieces of work for analysts, and this guide walks you through what a cycle looks like so you are not surprised when your first one starts.

title: Access Review Onboarding Guide for Compliance Analysts
heading: The calendar
text:
## The calendar

TechSync runs access reviews **twice a year**. Cycles open on the first business day of **January** and **July**. Reviewers get 20 business days to finish. The rest of the year is for audit preparation, SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001 evidence work, and cleaning up the previous cycle's loose ends.

Put the next two cycle start dates in your calendar on day one.

title: Access Review Onboarding Guide for Compliance Analysts
heading: Your first cycle, step by step
text:
## Your first cycle, step by step

1. **Week -1:** Request the Keystone group and entitlement exports for the systems assigned to you. Check that the owner listed for each system is still correct.
2. **Day 1:** Create one review ticket per system and assign the system owner and the managers.
3. **Day 1:** Send the kickoff message in the access-review Slack channel with the due date.
4. **Weeks 1-3:** Answer reviewer questions. Typical ones: "Who is this contractor?" and "Why does this group have admin?" Your answer is usually in Keystone or the HR system.
5. **Day 15:** Send reminders to anyone with open tickets.
6. **Day 20:** Escalate unfinished reviews to the reviewer's manager.
7. **After close:** Confirm that every "remove" decision has a matching removal ticket, then store the exports, decisions, and removal tickets in Compass.

title: Access Review Onboarding Guide for Compliance Analysts
heading: Tips from the team
text:
## Tips from the team

- Keep a running list of reviewers who are repeatedly late; managers appreciate a heads-up before the window opens.
- Contractors are the most common source of surprise accounts.
- Do not edit exports. If a number looks wrong, ask the Keystone team to regenerate.

## Who to ask

Your onboarding buddy, the ITC Tech Lead, or the compliance channel.

title: Open-Source License Exception for Internal-Only Tooling
heading: Open-Source License Exception for Internal-Only Tooling
text:
# Open-Source License Exception for Internal-Only Tooling

**Approved by:** Tamsin Reid (CISO) and Legal | **Approved:** February 2026 | **Owner:** IT & Compliance (ITC)

title: Open-Source License Exception for Internal-Only Tooling
heading: Why this exists
text:
## Why this exists

ITC maintains small automation around Compass and Keystone: evidence collectors, export scripts, directory helpers. Several of the best libraries for these jobs are GPL-licensed. Because our scripts never leave the company, a separate legal review for every library adds delay without reducing risk.

title: Open-Source License Exception for Internal-Only Tooling
heading: What is allowed
text:
## What is allowed

ITC engineers **may use GPL-licensed libraries (GPL and LGPL) in ITC internal-only tools without a per-use legal review.** Each use must be logged in the ITC license register with the library, version, tool, and date.

title: Open-Source License Exception for Internal-Only Tooling
heading: Scope limits
text:
## Scope limits

This exception applies only to tools that meet **all** of these conditions:

- Owned by ITC.
- Run only inside TechSync infrastructure.
- **Never distributed outside TechSync**, in any form: not to customers, not to partners, not to contractors outside our network, and not bundled in any product artifact.

It does not cover AGPL libraries, which require legal review in every case.

title: Open-Source License Exception for Internal-Only Tooling
heading: What is not covered
text:
## What is not covered

- Anything shipped to customers.
- Any tool owned by another team.
- Any library under a license other than GPL or LGPL.

## If a tool's use changes

If an internal tool is ever proposed for distribution outside TechSync, the exception stops applying to it. The tool must go through legal review before release.

## Register review

The ITC engineering manager reviews the license register each quarter and reports to AppSec.

title: Compass Evidence Collection How-To
heading: Compass Evidence Collection How-To
text:
# Compass Evidence Collection How-To

A step-by-step guide to putting evidence into Compass, written for engineers who have never done it. For the rules about what evidence is needed and the naming convention, see the Compliance Evidence Handbook. This guide covers the clicks.

title: Compass Evidence Collection How-To
heading: What you need before you start
text:
## What you need before you start

- Access to Compass (request the `co-compass-users` group in the Keystone request portal)
- The evidence itself, as a file or a link
- The name of the control it supports, from the request you received

title: Compass Evidence Collection How-To
heading: Uploading evidence
text:
## Uploading evidence

1. Sign in to Compass through Keystone.
2. Open **Controls** and search for the control by name or ID.
3. Choose **Add evidence**.
4. Attach the file, or paste the link if the evidence lives in Jira or Confluence.
5. Select the period the evidence covers. Compass offers the audit period by default.
6. Write one sentence describing what the file shows.
7. Select **Submit**. Compass records who uploaded it and when.

title: Compass Evidence Collection How-To
heading: What makes good evidence
text:
## What makes good evidence

- It names the system, the date, and the person who collected it.
- It can be read without special tools.
- It shows the control working, not just that it exists.

## Replacing or fixing evidence

You cannot edit submitted evidence. If you uploaded the wrong file, upload the correct one and add a comment on the old entry explaining why. A compliance analyst will mark the old one as replaced in the record.

title: Compass Evidence Collection How-To
heading: Linking a ticket
text:
## Linking a ticket

If your evidence is a Jira ticket, paste its URL. Compass keeps a link but not a copy, so make sure the ticket is accessible to auditors. If it is in a restricted project, ask a compliance analyst how to handle it.

title: Compass Evidence Collection How-To
heading: Bulk uploads
text:
## Bulk uploads

For many files at once, ask a compliance analyst for the bulk template. It takes a spreadsheet with one row per file.

## Common problems

| Problem | What to do |
|---|---|
| Cannot find the control | Search by ID; if it is missing, tell the compliance channel |
| Upload fails | Check the file size and type; compress large files |
| Wrong period selected | Upload again with the right one and comment on the old entry |
| No permission | Request the group again; approvals can take a day |

## Where to ask

The compliance channel, or a message to the analyst who sent the request.

title: Keystone Role and Group Naming Standard
heading: 1. Group names
text:
# Keystone Role and Group Naming Standard

Consistent names make access easy to understand and to review. This standard applies to all groups and roles created in Keystone.

## 1. Group names

```
<scope>-<system>-<role>
```

- **scope:** `org` code, or `co` for company-wide
- **system:** the lowercase system or application name
- **role:** what the group can do

Examples: `dsec-foundry-users`, `plat-kestrel-admins`, `co-console-viewers`.

title: Keystone Role and Group Naming Standard
heading: 2. Standard role words
text:
## 2. Standard role words

| Role | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `viewers` | Read-only |
| `users` | Normal use |
| `operators` | Operate and configure |
| `admins` | Full control, including access management |
| `oncall` | Members of the paging rota |

Do not invent synonyms such as `power-users` or `superusers`.

title: Keystone Role and Group Naming Standard
heading: 3. Ownership
text:
## 3. Ownership

Every group has an owner in Keystone: a team, not an individual. The owner approves membership requests.

## 4. Lifecycle

- Create groups through the Keystone request portal.
- Rename only through a ticket; renaming breaks downstream references.
- A group with no members for 12 months is flagged for removal.

title: Keystone Role and Group Naming Standard
heading: 5. Role bundles
text:
## 5. Role bundles

Roles that apply across several systems use the prefix `role-`, for example `role-sre-baseline`. Only IT & Compliance creates role bundles.

## 6. Anti-patterns

- Groups named for people.
- Groups that mix unrelated systems.
- Using `admins` where `operators` is enough.

title: Keystone Application Onboarding Checklist
heading: Before you start
text:
# Keystone Application Onboarding Checklist

Use this to integrate an internal application with Keystone. Copy it into your ticket and tick items as you go.

## Before you start

- [ ] The application has an owner team and an on-call channel.
- [ ] You know whether users are employees only, or employees and contractors.
- [ ] You have read the Role and Group Naming Standard.

title: Keystone Application Onboarding Checklist
heading: Registration
text:
## Registration

- [ ] Register the application in the Keystone request portal.
- [ ] Choose OIDC unless the app only supports SAML.
- [ ] Add redirect URIs separately for dev, staging, and prod.
- [ ] Record the client ID in your service's configuration, not the client secret. Store the secret in Vaultline.

title: Keystone Application Onboarding Checklist
heading: Groups and roles
text:
## Groups and roles

- [ ] Create the groups the app needs, following the naming standard.
- [ ] Assign an owning team for every group.
- [ ] Map groups to application roles in your app's configuration.

## Provisioning

- [ ] Decide whether the app needs SCIM provisioning. If it keeps its own user records, it does.
- [ ] If yes, configure the SCIM endpoint and test joiner, mover, and leaver cases in staging.

title: Keystone Application Onboarding Checklist
heading: Testing
text:
## Testing

- [ ] Sign in as a user with each role and confirm the expected access.
- [ ] Sign in as a user with no group and confirm they are denied.
- [ ] Confirm sign-out behaves as intended.

## Go-live

- [ ] Review with an ITC engineer.
- [ ] Announce in the ITC channel.
- [ ] Add the application to the Compass inventory.

## Afterwards

Revisit your groups and roles whenever the app's features change.

title: SOC 2 Type II Audit Prep Runbook
heading: SOC 2 Type II Audit Prep Runbook
text:
# SOC 2 Type II Audit Prep Runbook

This runbook is for ITC compliance analysts coordinating the SOC 2 Type II audit. It covers the work from kickoff through the auditor's report. Engineers who supply evidence should read the org-wide audit calendar and the evidence handbook instead.

title: SOC 2 Type II Audit Prep Runbook
heading: Roles
text:
## Roles

| Role | Responsibility |
|---|---|
| Lead analyst | Runs the plan, talks to auditors |
| Analysts | Own a share of the controls and chase evidence |
| ITC Engineering Manager | Removes blockers, reviews status |
| CISO's office | Signs the management assertion and receives findings |

title: SOC 2 Type II Audit Prep Runbook
heading: Phase 1: Kickoff (March)
text:
## Phase 1: Kickoff (March)

1. Confirm the audit period and scope with the auditors.
2. Export the control list from Compass and check that every control has an owning team.
3. Send the control owners a message with their list and the evidence calendar.
4. Create a tracker with one row per control: owner, evidence status, due date.

title: SOC 2 Type II Audit Prep Runbook
heading: Phase 2: Evidence collection (April to May)
text:
## Phase 2: Evidence collection (April to May)

1. Owners upload evidence to Compass as described in the evidence handbook.
2. Each week, run the gap check:
   - List controls with no evidence in the current period.
   - Open a ticket for each, assigned to the control owner.
   - Post the summary in the compliance channel.
3. Review uploaded evidence for quality: timestamps, names, and period selected. Send back anything unclear.
4. Escalate controls still open after two reminders to the owner's engineering manager.

title: SOC 2 Type II Audit Prep Runbook
heading: Phase 3: Fieldwork (June)
text:
## Phase 3: Fieldwork (June)

1. Create a shared folder for auditor requests and an index of what is in it.
2. Brief any engineer an auditor wishes to speak to; share the questions in advance when you can.
3. Log each auditor request with the date, the response, and who answered.
4. Hold a daily 15-minute check-in during fieldwork with the lead analyst, analysts, and the auditors.

title: SOC 2 Type II Audit Prep Runbook
heading: Phase 4: Findings and report (July to August)
text:
## Phase 4: Findings and report (July to August)

1. Log every auditor finding with the control, the cause, and a proposed fix.
2. Agree fixes with owners and set due dates.
3. Review the draft report with the CISO's office before it is final.
4. After the report is issued, run a lessons-learned session with all control owners.

title: SOC 2 Type II Audit Prep Runbook
heading: Checklist before fieldwork
text:
## Checklist before fieldwork

- [ ] Every control has an owner and evidence for the whole audit period
- [ ] Evidence index is up to date
- [ ] Auditor access to Compass is configured and tested
- [ ] Engineers likely to be interviewed have been briefed
- [ ] Previous findings show as remediated
- [ ] Management assertion draft is ready

title: SOC 2 Type II Audit Prep Runbook
heading: Tips from past audits
text:
## Tips from past audits

- Auditors value consistency. If a control is described differently in two places, fix it before they notice.
- Keep a list of "who knows how this works" for each control.
- Do not argue with auditors in front of engineers; take it offline.
- Write down the answers you give, so the next analyst can reuse them.

title: SOC 2 Type II Audit Prep Runbook
heading: After the audit
text:
## After the audit

Update this runbook with anything that went differently from the plan. Archive the tracker and the evidence index for the following year's team.

## Contacts

The lead analyst, the compliance channel, and the CISO's office for formal communications.

title: ISO 27001 Surveillance Audit Notes
heading: ISO 27001 Surveillance Audit Notes
text:
# ISO 27001 Surveillance Audit Notes

Notes from the debrief after last cycle's ISO 27001 surveillance audit. Written for the next analyst who owns the audit, so they can see what was asked and what to prepare. Informal.

**Date of debrief:** 6 Nov 2025 | **Present:** two analysts, the ITC engineering manager, and a representative of the CISO's office

title: ISO 27001 Surveillance Audit Notes
heading: Overall
text:
## Overall

The auditors completed the surveillance audit with two minor observations and no major nonconformities. They described TechSync's documentation as easy to follow, which was a nice change from the first year.

## What they asked about

- **Asset inventory:** how we keep the Compass inventory of systems current. We showed them the regular refresh and the owner list.
- **Supplier management:** how vendors are reviewed. They sampled three and asked for the review records.
- **Incident handling:** they picked two recent postmortems and asked how actions were tracked to completion.
- **Secure development:** they asked how scanning is built into pipelines and how findings are tracked.
- **Training:** records that engineers completed required courses.

title: ISO 27001 Surveillance Audit Notes
heading: Observations
text:
## Observations

1. **Supplier reviews:** one review had no recorded date. We have added a date field to the template.
2. **Document control:** one policy page had no visible owner. The owner was fixed during the audit.

Both are minor; each has a ticket and an owner.

title: ISO 27001 Surveillance Audit Notes
heading: What worked
text:
## What worked

- Having a named person per control meant answers were quick.
- The evidence index was complete, so we did not hunt for files.
- Engineers who were interviewed had been briefed and were relaxed.

## What to do differently

- Start the supplier record check earlier.
- Do a document-ownership sweep a month before the audit.
- Offer auditors a shorter walkthrough of Compass at the start; they spent time finding their way around.

title: ISO 27001 Surveillance Audit Notes
heading: Actions
text:
## Actions

| Action | Owner | Due |
|---|---|---|
| Add date field to supplier review template | Analyst | done |
| Run ownership sweep on policy pages | Analyst | before next audit |
| Prepare a 15-minute Compass tour | Lead analyst | before next audit |

## Notes for next time

The auditors were friendly and fair. They said they prefer to be told early about anything that changed in the year rather than discover it. A short "what changed" list prepared in advance would help.

title: Compass Control Mapping Reference
heading: Compass Control Mapping Reference
text:
# Compass Control Mapping Reference

Compass tracks controls and the evidence that shows they operate. This reference shows how our control families map to the frameworks TechSync is audited against, SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001, and who owns the evidence.

title: Compass Control Mapping Reference
heading: How to read the table
text:
## How to read the table

- **Family:** the group of controls in Compass.
- **SOC 2 area:** the broad trust services area.
- **ISO 27001 theme:** the broad Annex A theme.
- **Evidence owner:** the team that supplies evidence.

| Family | SOC 2 area | ISO 27001 theme | Evidence owner |
|---|---|---|---|
| Change management | Common criteria: change management | Operational security | Developer Tooling, SRE guild |
| Incident response | Common criteria: incident handling | Incident management | SRE guild |
| Business continuity | Availability | Continuity | SRE guild |
| Vendor management | Common criteria: risk mitigation | Supplier relationships | IT & Compliance |
| People security | Common criteria: control environment | People controls | People team |
| Asset management | Common criteria: system operations | Asset management | IT & Compliance |
| Secure development | Common criteria: change management | Secure development | AppSec |
| Risk management | Common criteria: risk assessment | Risk assessment | CISO's office |

title: Compass Control Mapping Reference
heading: Using the mapping
text:
## Using the mapping

1. Find your system's family in Compass.
2. Open the control and read what evidence is expected.
3. Upload or link the evidence as described in the evidence handbook.

## Adding or changing a mapping

Mapping changes are made by IT & Compliance after review with the auditors. Raise a docs or change request in the intake queue.

## Notes

- A single control can satisfy more than one framework requirement.
- Auditors may request evidence outside the table; ask the compliance channel if you are unsure who owns it.

title: IT Helpdesk Intake FAQ
heading: IT Helpdesk Intake FAQ
text:
# IT Helpdesk Intake FAQ

**How do I contact the IT helpdesk?**
Use the IT helpdesk page in Confluence, or post in the IT help channel. For anything that blocks your work, use the page so that a ticket is created.

**What can the helpdesk do?**
Laptop and peripheral issues, software installs, group membership requests, account problems, and onboarding setup.

**What can the helpdesk not do?**
Security exceptions, policy questions, and questions about specific systems owned by other teams. They route those to the right place.

**How do I get access to a system?**
Use the Keystone request portal and search for the group named in your team's onboarding guide. The group owner approves.

**My account is locked. What now?**
Contact the helpdesk. They confirm your identity and unlock it.

**I lost my laptop.**
Report it immediately through the helpdesk. They will disable your device and arrange a replacement.

**How long do requests take?**
Most are handled within one business day. Anything involving hardware purchases takes longer.

**Who approves software purchases?**
Your engineering manager approves, and IT & Compliance reviews the vendor.

**Can I install my own tools?**
Common developer tools are allowed. For others, ask the helpdesk; they will check with AppSec if there is a risk.

**How do I join a Slack channel I cannot see?**
Ask a channel member for an invite. The helpdesk does not manage channel membership.

**Who do I ask if my question is not here?**
The IT help channel.

title: Keystone Directory Sync Troubleshooting
heading: 1. Symptoms
text:
# Keystone Directory Sync Troubleshooting

Keystone synchronizes users and groups from the HR directory. Use this runbook when group changes or new accounts are not appearing.

## 1. Symptoms

- A new hire's account is missing.
- Group membership changes do not apply.
- The sync dashboard shows a growing "pending changes" count.

title: Keystone Directory Sync Troubleshooting
heading: 2. First checks
text:
## 2. First checks

1. Open the directory sync dashboard and note the time of the last successful run.
2. Check for a failed run and read its error summary.
3. Check whether the HR directory itself is reachable.

## 3. Error patterns

| Error | Meaning | Action |
|---|---|---|
| `auth_failed` | Service credential rejected | Rotate the connector credential through Vaultline, then re-run |
| `schema_mismatch` | HR directory changed a field | Update the mapping file and re-run |
| `rate_limited` | Too many requests | Wait and re-run with a smaller batch |
| `partial_apply` | Some records failed | Download the failure report and fix records individually |

title: Keystone Directory Sync Troubleshooting
heading: 4. Re-running a sync
text:
## 4. Re-running a sync

`keystone sync run --full` re-reads the whole directory. Prefer `--incremental` first. Full runs take about 20 minutes and cause a brief increase in load.

## 5. Checking a single user

Use `keystone user show <email>` and compare groups against the HR directory record. If the HR record is wrong, ask the people team to fix it at the source; do not edit Keystone by hand.

## 6. Escalation

If the sync is down and new hires cannot start, escalate to the ITC on-call through Lookout. Post updates in the ITC incidents channel.

title: ADR: Keystone SCIM Provisioning
heading: Context
text:
# ADR: Keystone SCIM Provisioning

**Status:** Accepted | **Date:** September 2025

## Context

Applications that integrate with Keystone need user and group records. Today each app either reads claims at sign-in only, or relies on a custom sync written by its owning team. The custom syncs differ in quality, and some leave accounts behind when people leave the company.

title: ADR: Keystone SCIM Provisioning
heading: Decision
text:
## Decision

Keystone will offer **SCIM 2.0 provisioning** as the standard way for applications to receive user and group changes. New integrations should use SCIM where the application supports it. Existing custom syncs will be migrated over time.

title: ADR: Keystone SCIM Provisioning
heading: Consequences
text:
## Consequences

**Positive**
- Joiners, movers, and leavers propagate to applications through a single, tested mechanism.
- Less custom code for application teams to maintain.
- Easier to show an auditor how deprovisioning works.

**Negative**
- Applications without SCIM support still need a connector or a custom sync.
- ITC must operate a SCIM endpoint and monitor delivery failures.
- Migration of existing integrations takes effort from other teams.

title: ADR: Keystone SCIM Provisioning
heading: Alternatives considered
text:
## Alternatives considered

1. **Keep custom syncs.** Flexible but inconsistent.
2. **Event-based provisioning through Streamline.** Fits our stack, but is non-standard for third-party applications.
3. **Buy a provisioning product.** Adds cost and another vendor.

## Follow-up

- Publish the SCIM endpoint details and an onboarding checklist.
- Migrate Console and the largest internal applications first.
- Report adoption in the ITC weekly sync.

title: Postmortem: Keystone Directory Sync Failure
heading: Postmortem: Keystone Directory Sync Failure
text:
# Postmortem: Keystone Directory Sync Failure

**Severity:** Sev3 | **Incident date:** 21 April 2026 | **Duration:** about 20 hours | **Authors:** ITC SRE

title: Postmortem: Keystone Directory Sync Failure
heading: Summary
text:
## Summary

A change in the HR directory's export format caused Keystone's directory sync to fail from the evening of 20 April until the following afternoon. During that time, group membership changes did not apply and four new employees could not sign in on their first day. Existing users were not affected, and no access was granted incorrectly.

title: Postmortem: Keystone Directory Sync Failure
heading: Impact
text:
## Impact

- Four new hires without accounts on their start day, delayed by about half a day.
- About thirty group membership requests delayed by one business day.
- Increased load on the IT helpdesk.
- No incorrect access was granted and no accounts were lost.

title: Postmortem: Keystone Directory Sync Failure
heading: Timeline (Pacific time)
text:
## Timeline (Pacific time)

| Time | Event |
|---|---|
| Mon 18:05 | HR directory deploys a change that renames a field in its export |
| Mon 18:30 | Overnight sync run fails with a schema mismatch; alert goes to a low-priority channel |
| Tue 08:40 | The helpdesk reports that new hires cannot sign in |
| Tue 09:10 | ITC on-call opens an incident |
| Tue 10:30 | Cause found: the renamed field breaks the mapping file |
| Tue 12:15 | Mapping updated and tested in staging |
| Tue 13:40 | Mapping deployed; full sync run started |
| Tue 14:10 | Sync completes; new accounts appear |
| Tue 15:00 | Incident closed after the backlog of group changes is applied |

title: Postmortem: Keystone Directory Sync Failure
heading: Root cause
text:
## Root cause

The HR directory team renamed a field without telling ITC. Our mapping file referred to the old name, so the sync run failed on every record.

## Contributing factors

1. The sync failure alert was routed to a channel that nobody watched overnight.
2. No contract existed between the HR directory team and ITC describing which fields we depend on.
3. New-hire accounts were created only by the overnight sync, with no manual path documented.

title: Postmortem: Keystone Directory Sync Failure
heading: What went well
text:
## What went well

- The helpdesk escalated quickly with a clear description.
- The mapping fix was small and the staging test was fast.
- No incorrect access resulted.

## What went poorly

- The first alert was missed.
- Recovery depended on the on-call engineer knowing the mapping file well.

title: Postmortem: Keystone Directory Sync Failure
heading: Action items
text:
## Action items

| Action | Owner | Due |
|---|---|---|
| Route sync failure alerts to the ITC on-call through Lookout | ITC SRE | May 2026 |
| Write an interface contract with the HR directory team | ITC Tech Lead | June 2026 |
| Document the manual account creation procedure | ITC SRE | May 2026 |
| Add a schema check on the export before each run | ITC Tech Lead | July 2026 |

title: Security Review Process
heading: Why we review
text:
# Security Review Process

**Applies to:** all services built by teams in Data & Security (DATA, MLI, SEC, ITC)

## Why we review

Every service we ship can touch credentials, customer-derived data, or internal identity. The security review is how DSEC makes sure risks are found while changes are still cheap to make.

title: Security Review Process
heading: The rule
text:
## The rule

A **full threat-model review must be completed before any new service, or any service with a major architectural change, is deployed to staging.** Services that have not passed review may run in dev only.

## What a full review contains

1. **Intake.** The service owner opens a review request in the DSEC intake queue with a one-page description, the data classes handled, and an architecture diagram.
2. **Threat model.** The owner, with an AppSec reviewer, produces a data-flow diagram and a STRIDE-based threat model. Trust boundaries, external dependencies, and secrets usage must be listed explicitly.
3. **Review meeting.** A 60-minute session with an AppSec Security Engineer and a Staff Engineer from a different DSEC team.
4. **Findings.** Findings are logged in Jira with owner and severity. High and Critical findings must be fixed or formally accepted by the engineering manager before staging.
5. **Sign-off.** The AppSec reviewer signs off in the review ticket, and the ticket link is added to the service's Compass record.

Reviews are scheduled within 10 business days of a complete intake.

title: Security Review Process
heading: When to re-review
text:
## When to re-review

Re-run the full process if the service adds a new external integration, changes the data classes it handles, changes its authentication model, or moves between tiers.

## Roles

- **Service owner:** prepares materials, fixes findings.
- **AppSec reviewer:** leads the threat model and signs off.
- **Staff Engineer reviewer:** challenges design assumptions.
- **Engineering manager:** accepts residual risk.

## Records

All review artifacts are kept with the Jira ticket and linked from Compass for audit.

title: Compliance Evidence Handbook
heading: 1. What counts as evidence
text:
# Compliance Evidence Handbook

A practical guide for DSEC teams on collecting, naming, and storing evidence for audits and internal reviews. Evidence is what lets us show an auditor that a control actually operated. It lives in Compass.

## 1. What counts as evidence

- System exports (access lists, configuration dumps) with a visible timestamp
- Tickets showing a decision and its follow-up work
- Signed approvals (Jira sign-off is fine)
- Screenshots, only when no export is possible

Evidence must be readable without special tooling and must identify the system, the date, and the person who collected it.

title: Compliance Evidence Handbook
heading: 2. Naming
text:
## 2. Naming

Use `<system>_<control>_<YYYY-MM-DD>_<collector>`. For example: `keystone_access-list_2026-04-03_analyst1`.

title: Compliance Evidence Handbook
heading: 3. Uploading to Compass
text:
## 3. Uploading to Compass

1. Open the control in Compass and choose **Add evidence**.
2. Attach the file or link and select the review period.
3. Add one sentence describing what the file proves.
4. Submit within 5 business days of the work being completed.

title: Compliance Evidence Handbook
heading: 4. Access review evidence
text:
## 4. Access review evidence

Each quarterly access review produces three items: the exported access list, the reviewer decisions, and the removal tickets.

- **Tier 0, Tier 1, and Tier 2 services:** all three items are uploaded to Compass.
- **Tier 3 experimental services:** uploading to Compass is **optional**. A reviewer sign-off recorded in the Jira review ticket is sufficient, since these services hold no customer data and change frequently.

title: Compliance Evidence Handbook
heading: 5. Audit seasons
text:
## 5. Audit seasons

During SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001 audit windows, the Compliance Analysts run a weekly gap check. Teams with missing evidence get a Slack reminder and a Jira ticket.

## 6. Common mistakes

- Uploading a screenshot when an export was available.
- Missing timestamps.
- Leaving the review period blank.

## 7. Questions

Ask in the compliance channel or open a ticket with the IT & Compliance team.

title: DSEC Org Charter and Team Map

text:
## How we work together

- **Interface contracts.** When one DSEC team depends on another's system, the contract is written down and owned by the providing team.

title: DSEC Org Charter and Team Map

text:
## Cross-org functions we work with

Technical Program Management, the SRE guild, Technical Writing, and the Architecture Review Board, which the CTO chairs.

## Working agreements

1. Documentation is part of the work. Every system has a runbook with a named owner.
2. We name decisions in ADRs when more than one team is affected.
3. We prefer boring, reliable technology: Kubernetes on EKS, PostgreSQL, Kafka, OpenSearch, Terraform.
4. We are remote-first, so write things down and favor async updates.

## Where to start

New to DSEC? Read the onboarding guide, then the tooling landing page for links to each system's documentation.

title: DSEC Quarterly Planning Process
heading: Calendar
text:
# DSEC Quarterly Planning Process

Technical Program Management runs a planning cycle for DSEC each quarter. This page describes the calendar, the artifacts, and who does what, so that nobody is surprised by a deadline.

## Calendar

| Week | Milestone |
|---|---|
| -4 | TPM opens the planning doc and shares last quarter's results |
| -3 | Teams draft objectives and key results (OKRs) |
| -2 | Tech leads review cross-team dependencies |
| -1 | Engineering managers and the VP review the combined plan |
| 0 | Plans are published; the quarter starts |
| 6 | Mid-quarter check-in |
| 12 | Quarter closes and scores are recorded |

title: DSEC Quarterly Planning Process
heading: Artifacts
text:
## Artifacts

- **Team OKR page:** 3 to 5 objectives per team, each with measurable key results.
- **Dependency table:** every request one team makes of another, with an owner and a date.
- **Capacity sheet:** engineers available after on-call, leave, and holidays.

title: DSEC Quarterly Planning Process
heading: Roles
text:
## Roles

- **TPM:** runs the calendar, chases drafts, and publishes the final plan.
- **Engineering managers:** own their team's commitments.
- **Tech leads:** own the technical feasibility of each key result.
- **VP:** resolves trade-offs between teams.

title: DSEC Quarterly Planning Process
heading: Rules of thumb
text:
## Rules of thumb

1. No more than 70 percent of a team's capacity is planned; the rest is reserved for incidents and unplanned work.
2. A key result that depends on another team must have that team's agreement written in the dependency table before the plan is published.
3. Changes after week 0 are logged in the planning doc, not edited silently.

## Scoring

Key results are scored from 0.0 to 1.0. A score of 0.7 is considered a good result for a stretch goal. Scores are discussed in the retrospective, not used in individual performance conversations.

title: DSEC Technical Writing Style Guide
heading: DSEC Technical Writing Style Guide
text:
# DSEC Technical Writing Style Guide

Good documentation is a product. This guide sets the shared conventions for runbooks, standards, guides, and other documents written by DSEC teams. It is short on purpose: follow it, and when it does not cover something, choose clarity.

title: DSEC Technical Writing Style Guide
heading: 1. Know the document type
text:
## 1. Know the document type

Every document is one of a small set of types, and the type decides the shape.

| Type | Reader's question | Shape |
|---|---|---|
| Runbook | "Something is happening; what do I do?" | Numbered steps, expected output, escalation |
| Standard | "What must I do?" | Numbered requirements, scope, owner |
| Guide | "How do I get started?" | Narrative with examples |
| Reference | "What exactly does this setting do?" | Tables, no story |
| FAQ | "Quick question" | Question, short answer, link |
| ADR | "Why did we choose this?" | Context, decision, consequences |
| Meeting notes | "What was said?" | Attendees, discussion, actions |

Do not mix types in one document. If a runbook needs background, link to a guide.

title: DSEC Technical Writing Style Guide
heading: 2. The header block
text:
## 2. The header block

Start each page with an owner, a status, and a last-reviewed date. Readers use these to judge whether to trust the page. Use these status words: draft, approved, deprecated.

## 3. Voice and tone

- Write to one reader, using "you".
- Use the active voice. "Restart the consumer" beats "The consumer should be restarted".
- Prefer short sentences. If a sentence has three commas, split it.
- Avoid jokes in runbooks. A tired on-call engineer at 3 a.m. should not have to decode them.
- Guides can be warm. Welcome the reader and explain why, not just how.

title: DSEC Technical Writing Style Guide
heading: 4. Structure
text:
## 4. Structure

1. Lead with the purpose in one or two sentences.
2. Put prerequisites before steps.
3. Number steps that must happen in order; bullet items that need not.
4. Put the most likely failure next to the step where it occurs.
5. End with who to ask.

title: DSEC Technical Writing Style Guide
heading: 5. Names and terms
text:
## 5. Names and terms

Use the canonical names of systems exactly: Reservoir, Streamline, Foundry, FeatureHub, Sentinel, Vaultline, Keystone, Compass. Spell out an abbreviation on first use. Refer to people by role unless the document requires a name.

title: DSEC Technical Writing Style Guide
heading: 6. Formatting
text:
## 6. Formatting

- Headings in sentence case.
- Code and commands in fenced blocks, with the language noted.
- Tables for comparisons of three or more items.
- Avoid screenshots of text; paste the text.
- Link rather than copy. Copies drift.

title: DSEC Technical Writing Style Guide
heading: 7. Examples
text:
## 7. Examples

Weak: "Failures may occur during the job."
Better: "If the job fails with `OOMKilled`, raise `memory` in the spec and resubmit."

## 8. Review

Ask one person who did not write the page to follow it from start to finish. Every place they hesitate is a place to fix.

## 9. Help

Technical Writing holds office hours every Thursday, and you can post drafts in the DSEC docs channel.

title: Cross-Team Interface Contracts in DSEC
heading: 1. What needs a contract
text:
# Cross-Team Interface Contracts in DSEC

DSEC teams depend on one another constantly: MLI reads from Reservoir, SEC provides secrets to everyone, ITC provides identity. A written contract keeps those dependencies from becoming surprises.

## 1. What needs a contract

Any interface that another DSEC team relies on: an API, an event stream, a table, a CLI, a queue. If you would be upset when it changed without notice, it needs a contract.

title: Cross-Team Interface Contracts in DSEC
heading: 2. What a contract contains
text:
## 2. What a contract contains

1. **Owner:** the providing team and an on-call contact.
2. **Interface description:** endpoints, topics, or tables, with schemas.
3. **Compatibility promise:** what may change without notice and what needs a heads-up.
4. **Support:** channel and response expectations during business hours.
5. **Deprecation process:** how consumers are told, and how long they get to migrate.

title: Cross-Team Interface Contracts in DSEC
heading: 3. Where contracts live
text:
## 3. Where contracts live

Each contract is a page in the providing team's documentation space, linked from the DSEC tooling landing page. The providing team keeps it current.

## 4. Changing a contract

- **Additive changes** (new optional fields, new endpoints) may ship with an announcement in the DSEC channel.
- **Breaking changes** require two weeks' notice to consumers, a migration path, and agreement from the main consuming teams.
- **Removal** requires that no consumer has used the interface for a full release cycle.

title: Cross-Team Interface Contracts in DSEC
heading: 5. Consumer responsibilities
text:
## 5. Consumer responsibilities

Read the contract before depending on an interface. Report problems to the owner instead of working around them. Do not rely on behaviour the contract does not promise.

## 6. Disagreements

If the two teams cannot agree on a change, tech leads meet first, then engineering managers, then the VP.

title: DSEC New Hire Onboarding Guide
heading: DSEC New Hire Onboarding Guide
text:
# DSEC New Hire Onboarding Guide

Welcome to Data & Security! We are glad you are here. This guide covers your first 30 days across the whole org. Your own team will add a team-specific guide on top of this one, and your manager will walk you through it.

A note before the details: nobody expects you to absorb everything in a week. Most people tell us the first month feels like drinking from a hose. That is normal, and we have tried to put the most important things first.

title: DSEC New Hire Onboarding Guide
heading: Before day one
text:
## Before day one

Your manager and IT will arrange your laptop and accounts. You do not need to do anything, but if something looks missing on day one, tell your buddy.

## Week 1: get settled

- Meet your manager and your onboarding buddy, who is an engineer on your team.
- Complete the company onboarding modules in the learning portal.
- Join the DSEC Slack channels: the main DSEC channel, your team's channel, and the DSEC docs channel.
- Request the group memberships your team lists through the Keystone request portal. Most requests are approved within a business day.
- Clone the main repositories for your team from GitHub Enterprise and build one of them locally.
- Read the DSEC Org Charter and Team Map and the Architecture Principles.

title: DSEC New Hire Onboarding Guide
heading: Week 2: learn the systems
text:
## Week 2: learn the systems

- Walk through the architecture of the systems your team owns with your buddy.
- Read the five most recent postmortems for your team's systems. They tell you more about real behavior than any diagram.
- Shadow an engineer on a routine task, such as a deploy or a ticket triage.
- Attend your team's planning, design review, and demo.

title: DSEC New Hire Onboarding Guide
heading: Weeks 3 and 4: make a first contribution
text:
## Weeks 3 and 4: make a first contribution

- Pick a small ticket from the good-first-issue list on your team's board.
- Open a pull request and get it reviewed.
- Ship it. A small change in production in your first month is a goal we care about.
- Present what you learned at your team's demo.

title: DSEC New Hire Onboarding Guide
heading: Who is who
text:
## Who is who

| Team | Owns | Ask them about |
|---|---|---|
| Data Platform | Reservoir, Streamline | Data lake, event streams |

title: DSEC Architecture Principles
heading: DSEC Architecture Principles
text:
# DSEC Architecture Principles

These principles guide design in Data & Security. They are not rules to be applied mechanically; they are the questions a design reviewer will ask, and the answers they will want to hear. We keep them short so that people remember them.

title: DSEC Architecture Principles
heading: 1. Safe by default
text:
## 1. Safe by default

The easiest way to use a system should also be the safest. Defaults should be restrictive, secrets should never appear in code or configuration files, and a new service should get least privilege without anyone asking. If a design requires users to remember a security step, ask how to automate it.

title: DSEC Architecture Principles
heading: 2. Minimize the data you hold
text:
## 2. Minimize the data you hold

Collect and keep only what you need. Prefer derived or aggregated data to raw data when it serves the purpose. Every copy of customer-derived data is a liability that has to be protected, tracked, and eventually removed.

title: DSEC Architecture Principles
heading: 3. Make failure cheap
text:
## 3. Make failure cheap

Assume dependencies will fail. Design so that a failed component degrades one feature, not the whole service. Prefer timeouts, retries with backoff, and idempotent operations. A job that can safely run twice is worth more than a clever job that must run once.

title: DSEC Architecture Principles
heading: 4. Boring technology
text:
## 4. Boring technology

We run on Kubernetes on EKS, PostgreSQL, Kafka, OpenSearch, and Terraform for a reason. Use the established stack unless a design shows a need it cannot meet. A new technology needs an owner, a support plan, and a way out.

title: DSEC Architecture Principles
heading: 5. Observable from day one
text:
## 5. Observable from day one

A system you cannot see is a system you cannot fix. Emit structured logs, expose metrics, and propagate trace context from the first deployed version. Alerts must have an owner and an action; an alert nobody can act on is noise.

title: DSEC Architecture Principles
heading: 6. Design for the operator
text:
## 6. Design for the operator

Write the runbook while designing the system. If the runbook is hard to write, the system is hard to operate. Include the failure modes, the dashboards, and the rollback path.

## 7. Compatible by default

Other teams build on our interfaces. Prefer additive changes, version interfaces explicitly, and give consumers time to migrate. Breaking a consumer without notice costs more trust than the change is worth.

title: DSEC Architecture Principles
heading: 8. Mind the regions
text:
## 8. Mind the regions

Our primary region is us-east-1, with disaster recovery in us-west-2 and EU customer data in eu-west-1. Designs must say where data lives and how it moves between regions.

title: DSEC Architecture Principles
heading: 9. Cost is a design constraint
text:
## 9. Cost is a design constraint

Estimate cost in the design, in order of magnitude. A design that scales cost linearly with a growing dataset needs a plan for the day the bill is a surprise.

## 10. Write it down

Decisions with long-term consequences are recorded so that new team members can understand why a system looks the way it does. A decision that lives only in someone's head disappears when they change teams.

title: DSEC Architecture Principles
heading: Review checklist
text:
## Review checklist

Reviewers will ask:

- What are the trust boundaries, and who can cross them?
- What data does it hold, and where?
- What happens when each dependency is down?
- How do we know it is working?
- How does an operator roll it back?
- What does it cost at ten times today's load?
- Which interface does another team consume, and is that interface documented?

## Using this document

Bring these principles to the design review as a starting point. If a design departs from one, explain why; reviewers are looking for a reasoned answer, not for compliance.

title: DSEC Stakeholder Communication Guide
heading: Who your stakeholders are
text:
# DSEC Stakeholder Communication Guide

Most trouble on projects starts with someone finding out too late. This guide sets habits for keeping stakeholders informed without burying them.

## Who your stakeholders are

Stakeholders are anyone who depends on your work, funds it, or is affected by it: other engineering orgs, Support, Legal, the CISO's office, Finance. List yours in the project page on day one.

title: DSEC Stakeholder Communication Guide
heading: Status updates
text:
## Status updates

Use the same three-part format every time:

1. **Where we are:** one sentence, with a color (green, yellow, red).
2. **What changed since last time.**
3. **What we need:** decisions, people, or dates.

Send updates on the cadence you promised. A short update on time beats a perfect one that is late.

title: DSEC Stakeholder Communication Guide
heading: Colors mean something
text:
## Colors mean something

- **Green:** on track; no help needed.
- **Yellow:** a risk exists; we have a plan; tell people early.
- **Red:** we will miss a commitment unless something changes; ask for help now.

Do not turn yellow into red at the last minute; people make better decisions with notice.

title: DSEC Stakeholder Communication Guide
heading: Escalation etiquette
text:
## Escalation etiquette

1. Raise it with the other team's tech lead first.
2. If unresolved after a week, bring in both engineering managers.
3. Take it to the VP only with a written summary of the options and what you recommend.

Escalations are about problems, not people. Write them so that they could be read aloud to the other party.

title: DSEC Stakeholder Communication Guide
heading: During incidents
text:
## During incidents

Follow the incident lead's instructions on channel and cadence. Do not start side threads asking for updates; read the main channel first.

## Meetings

Send an agenda in advance. Record decisions and actions in the notes within a day. If a meeting has no decision to make, consider an email.

## Tone

Be direct and kind. Say what you know, what you do not, and when you will know more.

title: DSEC Budget and Capacity Planning Cycle
heading: Annual calendar
text:
# DSEC Budget and Capacity Planning Cycle

This describes how DSEC plans money and people each year, so engineering managers know what is due and when.

## Annual calendar

| Month | Activity |
|---|---|
| September | Finance opens the planning cycle; DSEC managers review current spend |
| October | Teams submit headcount and vendor requests |
| November | Cloud spend forecasts due |
| December | VP reviews the combined plan with Finance, under the CFO |
| January | Budgets confirmed and communicated |
| Mid-year | Re-forecast based on actual spend |

title: DSEC Budget and Capacity Planning Cycle
heading: What goes into the plan
text:
## What goes into the plan

1. **Headcount:** new roles with a short justification tied to the roadmap.
2. **Cloud spend:** AWS costs per team, split into compute, storage, and data transfer. Forecasts should reflect known launches.
3. **Vendors and tools:** licenses, audit fees, and penetration testing engagements.
4. **Training and travel:** per-person allowances.

title: DSEC Budget and Capacity Planning Cycle
heading: Forecasting cloud cost
text:
## Forecasting cloud cost

- Start from the last three months of actuals in the cost dashboards.
- Adjust for planned launches and decommissions.
- Add a contingency of about 10 percent.
- Explain any increase larger than 15 percent in words.

title: DSEC Budget and Capacity Planning Cycle
heading: Capacity planning
text:
## Capacity planning

Engineering managers record each engineer's availability, leaving room for on-call, leave, and holidays. TPM combines these into the capacity sheet used in quarterly planning.

## Roles

- **Engineering managers:** prepare team inputs.
- **VP:** consolidates and negotiates.
- **TPM:** keeps the calendar and templates.
- **Finance partner:** reviews forecasts and flags anomalies.

## In-year changes

Spend increases of more than 10 percent of a team's budget during the year need VP approval and a note in the planning doc.

title: DSEC Interview Rubric
heading: The loop
text:
# DSEC Interview Rubric

A short guide for interviewers on the DSEC hiring loop and how to score candidates.

## The loop

1. Recruiter screen
2. Hiring manager conversation
3. Technical interview: coding or practical exercise
4. Systems design interview
5. Collaboration and values interview
6. Debrief

title: DSEC Interview Rubric
heading: Scoring
text:
## Scoring

Each interviewer scores one competency from 1 to 4:

| Score | Meaning |
|---|---|
| 4 | Strong evidence; clearly above the bar |
| 3 | Meets the bar |
| 2 | Some concerns; mixed evidence |
| 1 | Clear concerns |

Write your notes before you read anyone else's. Scores and notes are submitted before the debrief.

title: DSEC Interview Rubric
heading: Competencies
text:
## Competencies

- **Technical depth** in the relevant area (data, ML, security, or identity)
- **Systems thinking:** failure modes, trade-offs, operations
- **Communication:** clarity, listening, written clarity
- **Collaboration:** how they work with other teams
- **Ownership:** follow-through and judgment

title: DSEC Interview Rubric
heading: Debrief rules
text:
## Debrief rules

- Start with the lowest scores.
- Talk about evidence, not impressions.
- The hiring manager decides after listening to everyone.

## Don'ts

Do not ask about family plans, age, or health. Do not compare a candidate to a former colleague.

# DSEC Learning and Reading Program

We try to keep learning visible in DSEC. This page lists the regular activities and how to join in.

title: DSEC Learning and Reading Program

title: DSEC Learning and Reading Program

text:
## Paper reading group

Every second Tuesday, a small group reads one paper (often from systems, ML, or security conferences) and discusses it. The presenter picks the paper at least a week ahead.

## Conference and course learning

Engineers can attend one external conference or course each year, subject to the learning budget process described by your manager. After attending, please share notes at a brown bag or in the docs channel.

title: DSEC Learning and Reading Program
heading: Mentoring
text:
## Mentoring

DSEC runs a mentoring match twice a year. Mentors and mentees are matched by interest, not by team. The sign-up form is posted in the DSEC channel.

If you want to see how another DSEC team works, ask your manager to arrange a one-week shadowing. People often return with ideas for their own team.

The program is run by a rotating group of three volunteers. If you want to help, post in the learning channel.
